\section{org-pwa}
\label{sec:org4caae54}
A mobile-first outliner for editing \texttt{.org} files in the browser. It works offline, needs no server and no account to use locally, and installs as a PWA.

This guide covers how to use it and, for anyone coming from Emacs, where it differs from real org-mode (see \hyperref[sec:org17920f6]{Differences from Emacs org-mode}).

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{What org-pwa is (and isn't)}
\label{sec:orgcb024ec}
org-pwa is a \textbf{touch-first outline editor}, not a port of Emacs. It reads and writes real \texttt{.org} files and keeps anything it doesn't understand exactly as written. Editing is built around tapping and gestures rather than Emacs keybindings, and it implements a useful subset of org-mode, not all of it.

It is not org-mode with full parity: Babel runs JavaScript, and the rest is a subset (see \hyperref[sec:org17920f6]{Differences from Emacs org-mode}). It is for opening a real org file on your phone, reorganizing the outline, checking off tasks, editing tables and saving back to disk, GitHub or a WebDAV server.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Getting started}
\label{sec:org920e912}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Open the app and tap \textbf{File → Open} if no file is open.
\item The place bar at the top names where the list is looking; tap it to change place. It opens where you were last, in the folder you were last in for that place. The command palette's \textbf{Files (Dired)…} (\texttt{dired}) opens the same list in the folder of the current file.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{GitHub}: browse a repo set up in Settings and tap a file. \textbf{Type a path instead…} is always there for a path the listing doesn't show.
\item \textbf{WebDAV}: the same, for a WebDAV server set up in Settings.
\item \textbf{This device}: in Chrome or Edge on desktop, choose a folder once and its files are listed like the other places (the browser asks again for access in each new session). \textbf{Choose another file…} opens the system picker; Save writes straight back to the same file. In the Android app, the org-pwa folder is listed here.
\item \textbf{Import file} (instead of \textbf{This device} where File System Access is missing, such as iOS): reads a file once. Save downloads a new copy for you to put back (see \hyperref[sec:orgb821724]{Platform support}).
\end{itemize}

A place that is not set up says so and links to Settings; if the last place cannot be used, the list opens the most recent one that can and tells you. On a wide screen the places are listed beside the files.

\item Edit. Edits apply at once and are cached locally, so nothing is lost if you close the tab before saving.
\item Tap \textbf{Save} to write the file back to where it came from, or \textbf{Save As} to choose another destination.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Menus and popups}: on a phone or tablet the menus and popups open as a bottom sheet. On a wide screen with a mouse the menus drop down under their button (\textbf{↑}, \textbf{↓}, \textbf{Home}, \textbf{End} and \textbf{Enter} move through them), and popups are centered dialogs. \textbf{Esc} closes either, and \textbf{Enter} accepts a question dialog such as a file path.

The modeline (see \hyperref[sec:orgf259c86]{Modeline and minibuffer}) shows the filename, where it came from and whether it has unsaved edits. Once a second tab is open, the tab bar (see \hyperref[sec:orgb31a5d3]{Tabs}) marks unsaved tabs with a dot.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Editing your outline}
\label{sec:orge56f2ad}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Headings}: tap the title to show its actions: edit title, edit text, edit details (the general editor, below), add a sub-heading, TODO, move up and down, archive, attach (see \hyperref[sec:orgc5944b1]{Attachments}), delete, promote and demote. Most close the row after running; move and promote/demote stay open so you can repeat them. \textbf{Delete} always asks first, listing what would be lost, and every delete or discard confirmation in the app defaults to \textbf{Cancel}, so a stray Enter or tap never deletes. With a keyboard, the arrow keys move between the buttons and \textbf{Esc} closes the row.
\item \textbf{TODO state}: tap the TODO badge to cycle the \texttt{\#+TODO:} sequence (default \texttt{TODO}, \texttt{DONE}) one step at a time. The action menu's \textbf{TODO} button (\texttt{C-c C-t}) does the same, except that for a heading with no keyword in a file with more than one parallel \texttt{\#+TODO:} workflow it opens a picker of every state of every workflow (see \hyperref[sec:org08c2b92]{Progress logging}).
\item \textbf{Fold and unfold}: tap the chevron to toggle a heading's subtree, or swipe left on a heading to cycle collapsed → children only → fully expanded.
\item \textbf{Move}: drag the grip at the right of a heading to move it with its subtree (Settings → Editing and startup → Keyboard → \textbf{Drag handle on headings} moves it to the left or turns it off). The blue line snaps between two headings; moving sideways steps through the levels that fit, rightward being deeper, and a tag names the result (\textbf{into} a heading, \textbf{same level as} one, or \textbf{top level}). Letting go over the top bar or the mode line, or pressing Escape, cancels.
\item \textbf{Complete or archive}: swipe right. A heading with an active TODO keyword jumps to the first DONE-type keyword. Otherwise it opens the Archive, Refile or Cancel prompt, and an archived heading unarchives directly.
\item \textbf{Archive} (\textbf{Unarchive} for an archived heading) moves the subtree to its \texttt{org-archive-location} or back, from a panel that shows the destination first (see \hyperref[sec:org2712015]{Archiving}). The \texttt{:ARCHIVE:} tag and \texttt{ARCHIVE\_*} properties can be edited or removed in the general editor.
\item \textbf{Moving in steps} (↑ ↓ ← →): ↑ and ↓ reorder a heading among its siblings with its subtree. ← promotes the heading with its subtree one level, as \texttt{org-promote-subtree} does: it stays where it is in the text, and the siblings after it become its children. → demotes it one level: after a sibling it becomes that sibling's last child, as a first child it stays under its parent. A top-level heading can't be promoted, and a short status message says so.
\item \textbf{The general editor} (📋 \textbf{Edit details}) is a popup with five tabs, so nothing is a long scroll: \textbf{Dates}, \textbf{Tags}, \textbf{Props}, \textbf{Files} and \textbf{More} (priority and tables). A tab you have edited shows a dot, and a note beside the buttons names them ("Changed: Dates, Tags"). Each tab shows how many items it holds.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{SCHEDULED, DEADLINE and a plain timestamp}: date and time pickers, a repeat selector (every N hours, days, weeks, months or years) and an optional warning delay (\texttt{-3d} shows a deadline three days early). The three are independent, each with its own \textbf{Clear}. See \hyperref[sec:org8b51351]{Agenda} for how a plain timestamp differs (it doesn't carry forward, and lives in the title).
\item \textbf{Tags}: removable chips (tap to remove) and an input with an \textbf{Add} button (Enter also adds). Suggestions appear as you type: every tag used in the open document (from an agenda view, in your agenda files) plus tags declared on a \texttt{\#+TAGS:} line or listed in \texttt{org-tag-alist} or \texttt{org-tag-persistent-alist}, most used first, narrowed to what you typed and excluding tags the heading already has. One tap adds one.
\item \textbf{Priority}: a button for each priority of the range (A, B, C unless \texttt{org-priority-highest} and \texttt{org-priority-lowest} say otherwise) and None.
\item \textbf{Properties}: an editable key/value row for each, with a remove button and an \textbf{Add property} row. The Key field completes from every key used in the open document (from an agenda view, in your agenda files), most used first, plus ones the app reads or writes (\texttt{CUSTOM\_ID}, \texttt{EFFORT}, \texttt{Effort\_ALL}, \texttt{ID}, the \texttt{ARCHIVE\_*} set); other keys still work. A row with a blank key is dropped on commit. A property that is new or changed is written as Org writes it, with the \texttt{:KEY:} padded to ten columns (\texttt{:ID:       abc}). This is also how you set a \texttt{CUSTOM\_ID} for \texttt{[[\#id]]}-style links (see \hyperref[sec:org3674ada]{Links and images}).
\end{itemize}

Three buttons govern every tab: \textbf{Cancel} discards everything and closes, \textbf{Reset} restores every field to how it was when the editor opened, and \textbf{OK} commits every tab and closes. Nothing is written until \textbf{OK}. Above them are three immediate actions. \textbf{Add table} inserts a table into the body and closes the editor. \textbf{Delete table} removes the heading's most recently added table after a confirmation, and is disabled when there is none. \textbf{Attach} closes the editor and opens the attachment picker (see \hyperref[sec:orgc5944b1]{Attachments}). If any field has changed, these three first ask \textbf{Commit and continue}, \textbf{Discard and continue} or \textbf{Keep editing}; with no changes they act at once.

Existing properties also show as a small read-only line under the heading while drawers are visible for it (\texttt{\#+STARTUP: showeverything}, or manually cycled to fully expanded; see \hyperref[sec:org3339e1e]{Folding and \#+STARTUP}). Tapping it opens the action menu.

\item \textbf{Text above the first heading}: the paragraphs, lists and tables before the first heading, and the file's \texttt{\#+KEY: value} lines, show at the top of the Org view, whatever \texttt{\#+STARTUP} says (as in Emacs, where that text is never folded). The text edits like any other, and the \texttt{\#+} lines keep their place; the \texttt{\#+} lines themselves are read-only here and are edited in View → Text. A file with no headings shows only this.
\item \textbf{Block content} (\texttt{\#+BEGIN\_SRC}, \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_QUOTE}, \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_EXAMPLE} and so on) is shown read-only, under the same drawer-visibility rule as properties. Folded, it shows a "collapsed block" label: tap it to reveal the content, and tap it again to re-fold. Edit blocks in \hyperref[sec:orge6ba82b]{Text view}. Any \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_NAME} and \texttt{\#+END\_NAME} pair works, and three names are displayed specially:
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{QUOTE}: inline markup is interpreted, and the block is indented on both margins with a left border.
\item \texttt{VERSE}: inline markup is interpreted, and every source line stays its own line.
\item \texttt{CENTER}: inline markup is interpreted, and its paragraphs are centered.
\end{itemize}

Everything else (\texttt{SRC}, \texttt{EXAMPLE}, \texttt{COMMENT}, custom names) is shown literally.

Export (see \hyperref[sec:org8e45f5f]{Export}) turns \texttt{SRC} into a code block with its language kept, \texttt{QUOTE} into a blockquote and drops \texttt{COMMENT}. A \texttt{SRC} language is not syntax-highlighted in the outline, and only \texttt{js} blocks can run (see \hyperref[sec:orgf955b76]{Source blocks}).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{A heading's "text"}
\label{sec:org0f64ad4}
Org has no separate description field: everything after a heading, up to the next heading, belongs to it, and can include several paragraphs, lists and tables in any order. \textbf{Edit text} opens all of it as one block of raw org syntax in a popup, like Settings' \textbf{Menu labels} editor (see \hyperref[sec:orgdebc8db]{Menu customization}): a large textarea with \textbf{Cancel} (discard and close), \textbf{Reset} (reload the original text and keep the popup open) and \textbf{OK} (save and close). The heading's rendered body is hidden from the outline while the popup is open. Typing \texttt{- [ ]} at the start of a line becomes a checklist item on save, as in the file.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Undo/redo and History}
\label{sec:org10b54c5}
Every edit can be undone and redone: text, TODO state, priority, tags, properties, moving, archiving, capturing, all of it. The command palette's \textbf{Undo history} opens a panel with \textbf{‹ Undo} and \textbf{Redo ›} buttons, a list of every step since the file was opened (current position marked) and a \textbf{diff} toggle on each entry showing what it changed.

Undo and redo keep the folds you see: a heading stays open or closed as it was, matched by its title and its parents' titles; a heading the text change renamed or added opens as the file's \texttt{\#+STARTUP} says.

The history is a tree. An edit made after an Undo starts a branch instead of discarding what was undone, and the panel shows the branches side by side, each indented from the step it follows. Tap any entry, on any branch, to jump there. Undo goes to the step before; Redo goes to the branch you were last on (the status line says \texttt{branch 2 of 3} when there is a choice). Dimmer entries are the ones Redo reaches, dimmest the other branches. The saved history keeps up to 200 steps, and branches you left go before the line you are working on.

A step is one completed edit action (saving a title, toggling a checkbox, archiving a heading), not a keystroke, and an edit that changes nothing adds none.

History is unlimited while a file stays open. It survives closing and reopening (the 200 most recent steps) only if the text on reopen matches what the app last had; if the file changed elsewhere, the old history is dropped. Undo and redo reapply the file's \texttt{\#+STARTUP} visibility instead of keeping fold state.

Landing on a step identical to the last saved text clears the modified indicator.

\textbf{If the filename shows modified (red) and nothing you did explains it}, check the first history entry. If it reads "Opened (resumed unsaved local version)" instead of "Opened", the file had an unsaved edit from an earlier session, and reopening resumed it instead of starting from what is stored. Save to make that version the real one, or jump back in the history list if it wasn't what you wanted.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Lists, tables, and body text}
\label{sec:orgca65121}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Lists}: ordered, unordered, checkboxes, description lists (\texttt{term \textbackslash{}:: description}) and nested sub-lists. Tap an item's text for edit, add-below and delete actions. \textbf{Add item below} puts the new item right under the item's line, as \texttt{M-RET} does, with the item's sub-items following it, and numbers an ordered list again (a description item gets an empty term only when the list's first item has one; an item with nothing after its bullet gets the new item above it; blank lines between items are kept). Lists inside drawers and example blocks edit like any other list. \textbf{Add checkbox below} does the same with a box. Deleting an item removes its text and sub-items.
\item \textbf{Checkboxes} toggle between unchecked and done. A box that has boxes under it shows what they add up to (\texttt{[-]} when some are done), as in Org, so tapping it changes nothing. A progress cookie (\texttt{[3/8]}, \texttt{[40\%]}, or the blank \texttt{[/]}) in a heading's title or a list item is recalculated when a checkbox changes: a heading counts the top-level items of its own lists, an item counts its sub-list. \texttt{:COOKIE\_DATA: recursive} counts nested items too. Changing a TODO state recalculates the parent heading's cookie from its TODO children (\texttt{:COOKIE\_DATA: recursive} reaches all descendants; \texttt{checkbox} keeps a heading on checkbox counting, \texttt{todo} on TODO counting). Percentages round down.
\item \textbf{Tables}: tap a cell to edit it in place. The \textbf{⎌} button beside the field discards the edit and restores the cell's text (on a phone there is no Escape key). Row and column controls sit below the table; \textbf{⋯ Table} opens more (see \hyperref[sec:orgff72a3f]{Table pad}). Every edit aligns the table the way \texttt{org-table-align} does (deleting a row leaves the others as they are), and the references in \texttt{\#+TBLFM:} follow an inserted or deleted row or column. \texttt{\#+TBLFM:} formulas are evaluated (see \hyperref[sec:orgf56fea3]{Table formulas}). \textbf{Header rows} are the rows before the table's first horizontal rule (\texttt{|-{}-{}-+-{}-{}-|}) and show bold; a table with no rule has no header, and a later rule only separates groups.
\item \textbf{Paragraphs}: tap the text for edit, add-below and delete actions.
\item \textbf{Captions, names and image sizes}: \texttt{\#+CAPTION:}, \texttt{\#+NAME:}, \texttt{\#+ATTR\_HTML:} (or \texttt{\#+ATTR\_ORG:}), \texttt{\#+HEADER:} and \texttt{\#+RESULTS:} lines directly above a paragraph, image, table or block describe it. A caption shows in italics with its markup rendered; \texttt{\#+ATTR\_HTML: :width 300 :align center} sizes and centers the images in that paragraph (a plain number is pixels; \texttt{\%} and \texttt{em} work). The other lines stay visible as small muted text, exactly as written.
\end{itemize}

Undo/redo covers every edit (see \hyperref[sec:org10b54c5]{Undo/redo and History}).

\subsubsection{Table pad}
\label{sec:orgff72a3f}
\textbf{⋯ Table}, below a table, opens a pad of buttons that act at the highlighted cell, the one you last tapped; the arrows at its top move it. Each button is an Org command, and holding one shows its key. They are in the command palette too (\texttt{org-table-insert-row}, \texttt{org-table-kill-row}, \texttt{org-table-sort-lines} and the rest). In a table the M-arrow keys do these instead of moving headings.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Key & What it does\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{M-S-↓}, \texttt{M-S-↑} & Insert a row above the cursor; delete the row\\[0pt]
\texttt{M-↑}, \texttt{M-↓} & Move the row up or down (a rule counts as a row)\\[0pt]
\texttt{M-S-→}, \texttt{M-S-←} & Insert a column at the cursor; delete the column\\[0pt]
\texttt{M-←}, \texttt{M-→} & Move the column left or right\\[0pt]
\texttt{C-c -} & Insert a rule below the row\\[0pt]
\texttt{C-c RET} & Insert a rule and go to the row below it\\[0pt]
\texttt{C-c \textasciicircum{}} & Sort the rows between the nearest rules (the whole table if there are none) by the cursor's column\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Sort} asks the way Emacs does: \texttt{a} alphabetic (ignoring case, by character code), \texttt{n} numeric (text that is not a number counts as 0), \texttt{t} time (timestamps and durations such as \texttt{1:30}; other text counts as 0) or \texttt{f} function, and a capital letter reverses. \texttt{f} asks for the name of a function that gets the key from a field (a function that exists, such as \texttt{length} or one from your Lisp init), then for one that compares two keys; leave that empty for \texttt{<} on numbers and \texttt{string<} on strings. Rows that tie keep their order. The formulas follow a moved row or column; a sort leaves them alone.

With the cursor in the qty column of

\begin{verbatim}
| fruit  | qty |
|--------+-----|
| apple  |   3 |
| banana |  12 |
| cherry |   7 |
\end{verbatim}

\texttt{C-c \textasciicircum{} n} puts the rows in the order apple, cherry, banana (3, 7, 12).

\subsubsection{Table formulas}
\label{sec:orgf56fea3}
\texttt{\#+TBLFM:} formulas use Org's formula language with Calc's functions. \textbf{🔢 Calc} below a table recalculates it; \textbf{Recalculate all tables} in the command palette (\texttt{org-table-recalculate-buffer-tables}) does every table as one undo step. A malformed formula is reported and only its own table is skipped. Only the first \texttt{\#+TBLFM:} line directly below a table counts. Worked examples, with the results Emacs gives, are in \texttt{examples/table-formulas.org}.

\begin{verbatim}
| Item | Price | Qty |   Tot |
|------+-------+-----+-------|
| Pen  |  1.50 |   4 |  6.00 |
| Book | 12.00 |   2 | 24.00 |
#+TBLFM: $4=$2*$3;%.2f
\end{verbatim}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Name & What it does\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{+ - * / \% \textbackslash{}} & Arithmetic as in Calc: \texttt{/}, \texttt{\%} and \texttt{\textbackslash{}} bind looser than \texttt{*} (\texttt{14/4*2} is \texttt{14/8}), a minus looser than \texttt{\textasciicircum{}} (\texttt{-2\textasciicircum{}2} is \texttt{-4}). \texttt{\textbackslash{}} divides and rounds down; whole numbers stay exact at any size; \texttt{5/0} is left as written\\[0pt]
\texttt{\textasciicircum{}} & Exponent, right-associative (\texttt{2\textasciicircum{}3\textasciicircum{}2} is 512)\\[0pt]
\texttt{sqrt(x)} & Square root; a negative input gives a complex number\\[0pt]
\texttt{floor}, \texttt{ceil}, \texttt{round}, \texttt{trunc} & Round toward −∞, +∞, nearest (.5 goes away from zero) and zero; a second argument keeps decimals: \texttt{round(\$1, 2)}\\[0pt]
\texttt{sin}, \texttt{cos}, \texttt{tan}, \texttt{arcsin}, \texttt{arccos}, \texttt{arctan} & Degrees by default (flags \texttt{D} and \texttt{R}); Calc's names, not \texttt{asin}\\[0pt]
\texttt{ln}, \texttt{log10}, \texttt{log(x, base)}, \texttt{exp}, \texttt{exp10} & Logarithms (\texttt{log(x)} is natural) and powers of e and 10\\[0pt]
\texttt{pi}, \texttt{inf} & Constants written bare\\[0pt]
\texttt{2\#101}, \texttt{16\#ff}, \texttt{1e3} & Numbers in a base from 2 to 36 and in scientific notation, in a field or a formula\\[0pt]
\texttt{\$name} & A constant from \texttt{\#+CONSTANTS:}, or a named column, parameter or field\\[0pt]
\texttt{vsum}, \texttt{vmean}, \texttt{vcount}, \texttt{vmin}, \texttt{vmax}, \texttt{vmedian} & Aggregates of a range; \texttt{vcount} counts non-blank cells\\[0pt]
\texttt{vvar}, \texttt{vpvar}, \texttt{vsdev}, \texttt{vpsdev} & Sample and population variance and standard deviation\\[0pt]
\texttt{if(c,t,f)} & \texttt{t} if \texttt{c} is non-zero or non-empty, else \texttt{f}; only that branch is evaluated\\[0pt]
\texttt{and}, \texttt{or}, \texttt{not} & Function forms of the logical operators\\[0pt]
\texttt{string(ref)}, \texttt{"text"} & A cell's raw text, and a string literal (a string result shows as character codes, as in Calc)\\[0pt]
\texttt{date(ref)}, \texttt{date(Y,M,D)}, \texttt{now()}, \texttt{deg(x)}, \texttt{date-to-time(ref)} & Dates (below)\\[0pt]
\texttt{format-time-string(fmt, time, utc)} & Emacs's, with every \texttt{\%} code of \hyperref[sec:orgab0be70]{Capture templates}\\[0pt]
\texttt{uconv(value, "from", "to")} & Unit conversion (below)\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Logic}: \texttt{==} (or \texttt{=}), \texttt{!=}, \texttt{<}, \texttt{>}, \texttt{<=}, \texttt{>=} give 1 or 0 and bind tighter than \texttt{\&\&} and \texttt{||}, which short-circuit like \texttt{if}, so \texttt{if(\$1 != 0, 100 / \$1, 0)} never divides by zero. \texttt{!x} is NOT. \texttt{string(\$1) == "Sales"} compares text; a bare \texttt{\$1 == "Sales"} reads the cell as a number.

\textbf{Constants}: \texttt{\#+CONSTANTS: c=299792458 g=9.81} defines \texttt{\$c} and \texttt{\$g}. Several lines combine and a later value wins.

\textbf{Names in the table}: the first cell of a row marks it, as in Org.
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{!} names the columns below it: with \texttt{| ! | Item | Price | Qty | Tot |}, \texttt{\$5=\$Price*\$Qty} works (the marker column is column 1).
\item \texttt{\$} gives parameters as \texttt{name=value} cells, used as \texttt{\$name}. A parameter \texttt{\%=\%.2f} is added, as in Emacs, to a formula that has flags such as \texttt{N} but no format of its own.
\item \texttt{\_} and \texttt{\textasciicircum{}} name the field below or above each of its cells. \texttt{\$name} reads that field, and \texttt{\$name=} on the left sets it: \texttt{\$total=vsum(@2..@4)}.
\item \texttt{\#} and \texttt{*} rows are calculated when the table has any marked row, and then only those. Rows marked \texttt{!} \texttt{\$} \texttt{\_} \texttt{\textasciicircum{}} or \texttt{/} never are.
\end{itemize}

Names start with a letter and use letters, digits and \texttt{\_}. A column name wins over a parameter, and a parameter over a constant.

\textbf{Dates}: a cell with an Org timestamp is a date when referenced. Subtracting dates gives days (decimals if a time is present); adding a number shifts the date and keeps its day name: \texttt{\$1 + 14} on \texttt{<2026-08-25>} gives \texttt{[2026-09-08 Tue]}. \texttt{date(\$1)} is Calc's day number (\texttt{739631} for \texttt{[2026-01-15]}), \texttt{date(739631)} turns it back, and \texttt{date(2026, 2, 29)} rolls over to 1 March. \texttt{(\$2 - \$1) * 24;\%.2f} is hours between two timestamps. As in Calc, adding two dates adds their day numbers, and a date times a number stays symbolic. \texttt{date-to-time} also reads ISO 8601, RFC 822 and US dates. \texttt{format-time-string("\%Y-\%m-\%d", \$1)} gives \texttt{2026-01-15}; \texttt{time} defaults to now and a non-zero \texttt{utc} formats in UTC.

\textbf{References}: \texttt{\$N} is a column of the current row, \texttt{@N\$M} a field, \texttt{@-N} and \texttt{@+N} rows relative to the target, \texttt{@<} \texttt{@>} \texttt{\$<} \texttt{\$>} the first and last row or column, and \texttt{\$1..\$3} or \texttt{@1\$1..@3\$2} a range (\texttt{@2..@6} means those rows of the formula's own column). Rows count every row including the header. \texttt{@I}, \texttt{@II} \ldots{} are horizontal rules (\texttt{@IIII} is the fourth), \texttt{@III+2} is two rows after one, and \texttt{vsum(@I..@II)} covers the rows between two. The shorthand \texttt{\$M=} skips rows before the first rule.

\textbf{Targets and order}: a target is a field (\texttt{@N\$M=}), a range (\texttt{@N\$M..@N\$M=}) or a column (\texttt{\$M=}). Several formulas on one line are separated by \texttt{::} and run, as in Org, sorted by target: column formulas row by row, then field formulas.

\textbf{Blank and text cells}: a blank in a direct reference reads as 0 but is left out of a range. Text that is not a number leaves the formula as written (\texttt{label + 5}), as in Emacs; the \texttt{N} flag reads it as 0. A formula that fails writes \texttt{\#ERROR} in that cell and the rest still updates; one that cannot be parsed is reported.

\textbf{Flags}: a trailing \texttt{;flags} string.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Flag & Effect\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{\%.Nf}, \texttt{fN} & Fixed, N decimals: \texttt{\$1/3;f2} gives \texttt{0.33}. Whole results are left alone\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%.Ne}, \texttt{\%g} & C-style: \texttt{12345.678;\%.2e} gives \texttt{1.23e+04}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%d} & Truncates toward zero\\[0pt]
\texttt{nN}, \texttt{sN}, \texttt{eN} & Normal, scientific and engineering notation with N figures: \texttt{3.14159265;n5} gives \texttt{3.1416}\\[0pt]
\texttt{pN} & Computes at N significant digits (arbitrary precision); add \texttt{nN} to show them: \texttt{1/3;p20n20}\\[0pt]
\texttt{E}, \texttt{N} & \texttt{E} keeps blanks as \texttt{nan}; \texttt{N} reads non-numeric text (and with \texttt{E}, blanks) as 0\\[0pt]
\texttt{D}, \texttt{R} & Degrees (the default) or radians for trig\\[0pt]
\texttt{T}, \texttt{U}, \texttt{t} & Durations: cells like \texttt{HH:MM[:SS]} are read as durations, and the result is \texttt{HH:MM:SS}, \texttt{HH:MM} or decimal hours. \texttt{org-table-duration-hour-zero-padding} pads hours\\[0pt]
\texttt{F} & Exact fractions, written with a colon as Calc does: \texttt{1/3;F} is \texttt{1:3}\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Text after the semicolon that is neither a flag nor a \texttt{\%} format is written into the cell as it stands, as Emacs does.

\textbf{Units}: \texttt{uconv(\$1, "mi/hr", "m/s")} converts with the mathjs unit library, including compound units (\texttt{kg/m\textasciicircum{}3}). Temperatures convert as readings (\texttt{0 degC} is \texttt{32 degF}). An incompatible pair or unknown unit gives \texttt{\#ERROR}. Units follow Calc's names; \texttt{tsp} and \texttt{tbsp} also work. The full list is at \url{https://mathjs.org/docs/datatypes/units.html}.

\textbf{Complex numbers, vectors and algebra}:
\begin{itemize}
\item Complex: \texttt{(re, im)} or \texttt{(r; θ)}, with \texttt{i} the number (0, 1): \texttt{(1, 2) * (3, 4)} is \texttt{(-5, 10)}. \texttt{re}, \texttt{im}, \texttt{conj}, \texttt{abs}, \texttt{arg}, \texttt{polar} and \texttt{rect} work.
\item Vectors and matrices: \texttt{[1, 2, 3]} and \texttt{[[1, 2], [3, 4]]}; \texttt{+ -} and \texttt{* /} by a number are elementwise, \texttt{*} is a dot or matrix product, and \texttt{det}, \texttt{inv}, \texttt{trn}, \texttt{tr}, \texttt{cross} and \texttt{vlen} work.
\item Algebra: letters are variables and what cannot be reduced is written as Calc writes it (\texttt{x + x} is \texttt{2 x}). \texttt{simplify}, \texttt{esimplify}, \texttt{expand}, \texttt{deriv(sin(x)*x, x)}, \texttt{prfac(360)}, and \texttt{solve(a*x+b=c, x)} for equations, inequalities and systems. \texttt{fsolve} writes \texttt{s1} and \texttt{n1} for the choices in a periodic solution. Intervals (\texttt{[1 .. 5]}) add, multiply and take powers.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Raw Elisp}: a formula starting with a quote, \texttt{'(orgtbl-ascii-draw value min max width)}, draws a bar in the cell with Org's 11-character gradient.

\subsubsection{Plots}
\label{sec:org8a22961}
A \texttt{\#+PLOT:} line directly above a table (stacked lines combine) graphs its data. \textbf{📊 Plot} below the table shows the graph inline as SVG; tap again to hide it. The app reads org-plot's own options, so an unmodified line works. See \texttt{examples/plots.org}.

\begin{verbatim}
#+PLOT: title:"Sales" ind:1 deps:(2 3) with:lines
| Month | Pens | Books |
|-------+------+-------|
| Jan   |   40 |    12 |
| Feb   |   55 |    18 |
\end{verbatim}

\texttt{type:2d} (the default) and \texttt{type:radar} are drawn; \texttt{with:} is \texttt{lines}, \texttt{points}, \texttt{boxes} (also \texttt{histograms}) or \texttt{impulses}.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Option & Meaning\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{title} & A quoted string\\[0pt]
\texttt{ind} & The column for the x position (2d) or axis label (radar); without it the x position is the row number\\[0pt]
\texttt{deps} & The columns to plot; default every column except \texttt{ind} (every column when there is no \texttt{ind})\\[0pt]
\texttt{labels} & Quoted series names, by column number; default the header row\\[0pt]
\texttt{transpose} & \texttt{yes} swaps rows and columns first (how a radar chart gets its axes)\\[0pt]
\texttt{min}, \texttt{max}, \texttt{xmin}, \texttt{xmax} & The y range, and the x range when \texttt{ind} is numeric\\[0pt]
\texttt{ticks} & The number of y gridlines; default 5\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Options that only script gnuplot (\texttt{set}, \texttt{line}, \texttt{script}, \texttt{file}, \texttt{map}, \texttt{timefmt}) are accepted and ignored, so a copied line never errors. Editing the table re-renders the graph the next time it is shown.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Inline text markup}
\label{sec:orgc52a359}
All six of org's emphasis markers work in headings, paragraphs and list items:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
Markup & Syntax & Renders as\\[0pt]
\hline
Bold & \texttt{*bold text*} & \textbf{bold text}\\[0pt]
Italic & \texttt{/italic text/} & \emph{italic text}\\[0pt]
Underline & \texttt{\_underline text\_} & underlined\\[0pt]
Strikethrough & \texttt{+strikethrough text+} & \sout{strikethrough text}\\[0pt]
Verbatim & \texttt{=verbatim text=} & \texttt{verbatim text} (literal, not further parsed)\\[0pt]
Code & \texttt{\textasciitilde{}code text\textasciitilde{}} & \texttt{code text} (literal, not further parsed)\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

A marker opens after the start of a line, whitespace or one of \texttt{-(\{'"}, and isn't followed by whitespace. It closes where it isn't preceded by whitespace and is followed by the end of the line, whitespace or one of \texttt{-.,;:!?'")\}[\textbackslash{}}. Bold, italic, underline and strikethrough nest (\texttt{*bold /italic/ bold*}); verbatim and code never do.

\textbf{Horizontal rule}: a line of only dashes, at least five (\texttt{-{}-{}-{}-{}-}), is a horizontal rule. Whitespace around the dashes is fine; any other character on the line makes it a paragraph.

\textbf{Hard line break}: a line ending in two backslashes (\texttt{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}}) forces a line break, in paragraphs, QUOTE and CENTER blocks and every export format. Otherwise the source lines of a paragraph or list item reflow together with a space, as in org.

\textbf{Subscript and superscript}: \texttt{x\_i} and \texttt{x\textasciicircum{}2} work without braces, and braces (\texttt{x\_\{alpha\}}, \texttt{10\textasciicircum{}\{100\}}) are always accepted. \texttt{org-use-sub-superscripts} (see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables}) controls them in the outline and in every export except ASCII (which prints \texttt{\_x} either way); a file's \texttt{\#+OPTIONS: \textasciicircum{}:} wins:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Value & Behavior\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{t} (default) & Both \texttt{x\_i} and \texttt{x\_\{i\}} are interpreted\\[0pt]
\texttt{\{\}} & Only the braced form \texttt{x\_\{i\}} is interpreted; a bare \texttt{x\_i} stays literal text\\[0pt]
\texttt{nil} & Disabled entirely; \texttt{\_} / \texttt{\textasciicircum{}} are always literal characters\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\texttt{\_} also marks underline: underline needs whitespace, a line start or punctuation before it (\texttt{\_underlined\_}), subscript a non-space character (\texttt{a\_b}). Script content is literal, so \texttt{x\_\{*bold*\}} doesn't interpret the \texttt{*bold*}.

\textbf{Footnotes}: \texttt{[fn:label]} is a reference, shown as a small tappable superscript that jumps to the definition, even under a folded heading. A definition can be inline, \texttt{[fn:label:the note text]}, anonymous, \texttt{[fn::an anonymous note]}, or a separate line starting \texttt{[fn:label]} (like \texttt{[fn:1] The actual definition.}). HTML export uses a jump-linked superscript with a back-linked Footnotes section.

Table cells render inline markup too; tap one to edit its raw text and tap away to commit.

\subsubsection{Footnote commands}
\label{sec:org4659b10}
In the outline, open a paragraph, a list item or a heading's text with \textbf{Edit text}, put the cursor after the words the note belongs to and tap \textbf{Footnote}. A sheet (a dialog on a large screen) asks for the label, already the next free number, and the note, with a switch to write it inline; \textbf{Insert} adds the reference and the note under \texttt{* Footnotes}, and Undo takes it back. Tap a reference to see its note and \textbf{Edit note}, \textbf{Go to the note} or \textbf{Delete footnote}; a reference with no note offers \textbf{Create the note}. With a paragraph selected from the keyboard, the \textbf{Footnote} command opens that paragraph's sheet.

In Text view, \textbf{Footnote} (\texttt{org-footnote-action}, \texttt{C-c C-x f}, palette) does the right thing at the cursor: on a reference it jumps to the definition (offering to create one if there is none), on a definition's label it jumps back to the reference, and anywhere else it adds a new footnote. Where a footnote can't go (start of a line, source blocks, comments, links, inside another reference) it offers the one-key menu: \texttt{s\textasciitilde{}ort, \textasciitilde{}r\textasciitilde{}enumber, \textasciitilde{}S} both, \textasciitilde{}n\textasciitilde{}ormalize, \textasciitilde{}d\textasciitilde{}elete.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Insert footnote} (\texttt{org-footnote-new}): a reference at the cursor and the start of its definition under \texttt{* Footnotes} at the end of the file, with the cursor there to write it. The label is the next unused number; an existing label adds another reference to it, and an empty one makes an anonymous \texttt{[fn::]}.
\item \textbf{Normalize footnotes} (\texttt{org-footnote-normalize}): every footnote becomes a numbered one in reading order, inline and anonymous notes become definitions, and all definitions move under \texttt{* Footnotes} (\texttt{DEFINITION NOT FOUND.} for a reference nobody defined).
\item \textbf{Sort footnotes} (\texttt{org-footnote-sort}) puts the definitions in the order of their references. \textbf{Renumber footnotes} (\texttt{org-footnote-renumber-fn:N}) numbers \texttt{fn:1}, \textasciitilde{}fn:2\textasciitilde{}… by first reference.
\item \textbf{Delete footnote} (\texttt{org-footnote-delete}): the one at the cursor, or the label you give, with every definition and reference.
\end{itemize}

Insert, sort, renumber, normalize and delete work from any view, and Undo reverses them. Settings: \texttt{org-footnote-section} (the heading; \texttt{nil} keeps each definition at the end of its own section), \texttt{org-footnote-auto-label}, \texttt{org-footnote-define-inline} and \texttt{org-footnote-auto-adjust} (renumber and/or sort after adding or deleting). \texttt{\#+STARTUP:} accepts \texttt{fninline}, \texttt{fnlocal}, \texttt{fnauto}, \texttt{fnprompt}, \texttt{fnconfirm}, \texttt{fnplain}, \texttt{fnadjust} and \texttt{nofnadjust}.

\subsubsection{\LaTeX{} math fragments}
\label{sec:org5307a5d}
Math in a heading, paragraph or list item renders as typeset math with \href{https://katex.org}{KaTeX}, vendored locally (no CDN). It is display-only: the \texttt{.org} file's text is untouched, and editing shows the raw source.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
Delimiter & Kind & Restrictions\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{\textbackslash{}(...\textbackslash{})} & Inline & None — org's own recommended form\\[0pt]
\texttt{\textbackslash{}[...\textbackslash{}]} & Display & None\\[0pt]
\texttt{\$\$...\$\$} & Display & None\\[0pt]
\texttt{\$...\$} & Inline & One character is enough (\texttt{\$x\$}). No whitespace directly inside the delimiters; the closing \texttt{\$} must be followed by whitespace, the end of the line or punctuation\\[0pt]
\texttt{\textbackslash{}begin\{env\}...\textbackslash{}end\{env\}} & Display & \texttt{\textbackslash{}begin} must start a line, preceded by nothing but whitespace\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\texttt{\$...\$} follows Org's rules so that currency stays text: \texttt{costs \$5 and \$10 total} is not math, and neither are \texttt{\$a\$b} or \texttt{\$x\$-y}.

Fragments can span lines (\texttt{\$...\$} not across a blank line). A fragment KaTeX can't render shows its raw source with a dashed border.

Math renders in the outline, the Docs viewer and HTML export. \LaTeX{} export writes it unchanged, ASCII export passes the source through, and ODT export makes an embedded formula object of each fragment.

Example: \texttt{The quadratic formula is \textbackslash{}(x = \textbackslash{}frac\{-b \textbackslash{}pm \textbackslash{}sqrt\{b\textasciicircum{}2-4ac\}\}\{2a\}\textbackslash{}).} renders inline with a fraction bar and a radical. An \texttt{align} environment renders right-aligned, numbered equations, lined up at the \texttt{\&} marks (see \texttt{examples/inline-latex.org}):

\begin{verbatim}
\begin{align}
E &= mc^2 \\
F &= ma
\end{align}
\end{verbatim}

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Searching}
\label{sec:org83d8646}
Tap the \textbf{Search} button in the top bar (see \hyperref[sec:org90a63f9]{The Search button}), or open the command palette's \textbf{Search} (or god-mode's \texttt{s}, see \hyperref[sec:org956255c]{Keybindings}) to search the open document, case-insensitively: headings, tags, TODO keyword, priority, properties (key or value), SCHEDULED and DEADLINE timestamps, paragraphs, list items, table cells and block content. When any are configured it also searches every file in \texttt{org-agenda-files}.

Search also finds the text above the first heading and the file's \texttt{\#+KEY: value} lines (shown as \textbf{Top of the file}); tapping a result opens the Org view there. Tag, TODO, priority and property filters and Match queries describe headings, so they leave it out.

In View → Text, Find marks every match in the text and selects the first one from the cursor; Enter, ▼ or \texttt{C-s} goes to the next, Shift+Enter, ▲ or \texttt{C-r} to the previous, wrapping round, with "N of M matches" shown. Find searches from where you began, so deleting a letter of the query goes back to the earlier match. Closing Find leaves the last match selected. The Regex option works as elsewhere.

On the Agenda, TODO, Match and Keyword search screens Find works in place, as \texttt{C-s} does in an agenda buffer: every match in the rows on screen is highlighted and the current one is marked more strongly. Enter or ▼ (\texttt{C-s}) goes to the next, Shift+Enter or ▲ (\texttt{C-r}) to the previous, wrapping round. A lower-case query ignores case and a capital letter makes it exact; ⋯ has Regex. Closing the search clears the marks and leaves the row of the current match focused. On these screens \texttt{n} and \texttt{p} (or \texttt{j}, \texttt{k} and the arrow keys) move the focus, \texttt{t} changes the row's state, a comma sets its priority, Enter goes to its heading and Space opens its actions.

In the Org view, ▼ or Enter (\texttt{C-s}, Down) marks the next result and ▲ or Shift+Enter (\texttt{C-r}, Up) the previous, wrapping round, with "N of M results" and \textbf{Narrow} kept above the list; only the list scrolls, and tapping a result opens it and closes the search. ⋯ shows \textbf{Close} (✕) under it, which ends the search as Esc does.

Results update as you type, grouped under their heading with the match highlighted, and fill in as each agenda file loads; a result from another file shows its name. Search covers the whole document whatever the fold state, and tapping a result reveals it, switching file first if needed. The query box and its options live in the minibuffer (see \hyperref[sec:orgf259c86]{Modeline and minibuffer}). Examples with Emacs's results: \texttt{examples/search-filter.org} and \texttt{examples/match-queries.org}.

\subsubsection{Filter tokens}
\label{sec:org5fa7c3e}

Tokens in the query box combine as an implicit AND:

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{word} or \texttt{+word}: the entry (title, tags, TODO state, priority, properties, planning and body text) must contain it. \texttt{-word} excludes entries that contain it. \texttt{+computer +wifi -ethernet}, or just \texttt{computer wifi -ethernet}, finds entries with "computer" and "wifi" but not "ethernet", as in org's \texttt{org-search-view}. So a query like \texttt{-5} means "exclude entries containing 5", not the literal text; use Regex mode for that.
\item \texttt{tag:urgent}: the heading must have this tag, inherited tags included. \texttt{-tag:urgent} excludes it.
\item \texttt{todo:KEYWORD}: the TODO state must equal this (case-insensitive), as in \texttt{todo:WAITING}. \texttt{-todo:KEYWORD} excludes it; a heading with no keyword passes an exclude.
\item \texttt{priority:X}: the priority must equal this, as in \texttt{priority:A}. \texttt{-priority:X} excludes it.
\item \texttt{key:value}: any other \texttt{key:value} matches a property \texttt{key} whose value contains \texttt{value} (substring, case-insensitive), such as \texttt{spouse:Mary}. \texttt{-key:value} excludes it.
\item \texttt{|} inside \texttt{tag:}, \texttt{todo:}, \texttt{priority:} or \texttt{key:value} means "any of these": \texttt{tag:urgent|blocked}, \texttt{todo:TODO|WAITING}, \texttt{assignee:Bob|Alice}. Negated, it means "none of these". It combines alternatives only within one filter. There is no OR between filters and no grouping; Match mode has both.
\end{itemize}

A word shaped \texttt{word:word} (such as \texttt{mailto:}) can be read as a filter; URLs are not. Tag inheritance is on and property inheritance off, as in Org. A query of only filters (\texttt{tag:work -someday}) returns the matching headings directly.

Example: \texttt{+work todo:WAITING budget} finds entries tagged \texttt{work}, in WAITING state, containing "budget".

\subsubsection{Regex mode}
\label{sec:org5e115fc}

The \textbf{Regex} toggle in the minibuffer switches from plain substring matching to a regular expression, case-insensitive either way, in Emacs's syntax rather than JavaScript's. The biggest difference: an unescaped \texttt{(}, \texttt{)}, \texttt{\{}, \texttt{\}} or \texttt{|} is literal, and grouping needs \texttt{\textbackslash{}(} and \texttt{\textbackslash{})}, alternation \texttt{\textbackslash{}|}, and an interval \texttt{\textbackslash{}\{n,m\textbackslash{}\}}. With Regex off, a \texttt{.} or \texttt{(} in the query simply matches that character.

Backreferences (\texttt{\textbackslash{}1} to \texttt{\textbackslash{}9}), word and symbol boundaries (\texttt{\textbackslash{}<} \texttt{\textbackslash{}>} \texttt{\textbackslash{}\_<} \texttt{\textbackslash{}\_>} \texttt{\textbackslash{}b} \texttt{\textbackslash{}B}), POSIX classes (\texttt{[[:digit:]]}) and the whole-string anchors \texttt{\textbackslash{}`} and \texttt{\textbackslash{}'} work. A pattern that is invalid, or uses a syntax-table class such as \texttt{\textbackslash{}s<}, shows an error naming the problem, never "no matches".

Example: \texttt{\textasciicircum{}\textbackslash{}(Buy\textbackslash{}|Fix\textbackslash{})} finds headings whose title starts with "Buy" or "Fix".

\subsubsection{Match mode}
\label{sec:org0e7ecde}

\textbf{Match}, beside \textbf{Regex} in the options popover (the \texttt{⋯} button at the search bar's right edge, which shows a check mark by the active one and a dot when either is on), uses org's tag and property match grammar, the one behind \texttt{C-c / m}. Match and Regex are mutually exclusive.

The grammar is \texttt{org-make-tags-matcher}'s. \texttt{|} is the lowest-precedence operator and splits the query into OR'd groups. Within a group, \texttt{+family} (or a bare \texttt{family}) and \texttt{-work} combine as AND, so \texttt{family+work|urgent} means "(family AND work) OR urgent". \texttt{\{\textasciicircum{}w\}} matches a tag by regular expression. \texttt{LEVEL>1} compares the level. A condition can compare a property, \texttt{Effort<"1:00"} (text), \texttt{SIZE>3} (number), \texttt{NAME=\{\textasciicircum{}x\}} (regexp) or \texttt{DEADLINE<"<today>"} (time, also \texttt{<now>}, \texttt{<+2d>}, \texttt{<2026-10-20>}), with \texttt{=}, \texttt{<>}, \texttt{<}, \texttt{>}, \texttt{<=} or \texttt{>=}, combined freely with tags. \texttt{TODO}, \texttt{PRIORITY}, \texttt{CATEGORY}, \texttt{ITEM}, \texttt{TAGS}, \texttt{ALLTAGS}, \texttt{SCHEDULED}, \texttt{DEADLINE} and \texttt{CLOSED} work as pseudo-properties. After the last \texttt{/} come the keywords the heading must have: \texttt{work/TODO|NEXT}, and \texttt{/!} means any TODO item that is not done. Text the grammar does not read is left unread, as Emacs does, so nothing here gives an error. Replace is disabled in this mode. A property is looked up on the heading itself unless \texttt{org-use-property-inheritance} is on.

Example: \texttt{work+urgent|blocked} finds headings tagged both \texttt{work} and \texttt{urgent}, or tagged \texttt{blocked}.

\subsubsection{Search extra files}
\label{sec:org62bf069}
\texttt{org-agenda-text-search-extra-files} lists more files to search, in addition to the file you have open and your \hyperref[sec:orgffa4011]{Agenda Files}. It is a list of file names, as in Emacs, each starting with \texttt{github:}, \texttt{webdav:} or \texttt{local:}:

\begin{verbatim}
org-agenda-text-search-extra-files: ("github:notes/reference.org" "webdav:archive/2024.org")
\end{verbatim}

Set it in \textbf{Settings → Advanced → Advanced (raw syntax) → Search extra files}, or per document in Local Variables. These files are searched only: they stay out of the Agenda, TODO and tag views, so they suit notes that should be findable but not scheduled. A file that is loading or can't be loaded is named above the results. \textbf{Replace} works on the open file and your agenda files only.

\subsubsection{Search and replace}
\label{sec:org718f295}

The options button (\texttt{⋯}) also shows \textbf{Replace}, which starts an Emacs-style \texttt{query-replace} (or \texttt{query-replace-regexp}, following the Regex toggle) with the search text as the pattern. It walks every \hyperref[sec:orgffa4011]{Agenda Files} file that has a match, starting with the open one, and a file it enters opens as its own tab. It asks for the replacement text, then offers each match:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Key & Action\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{y} or Space & Replace this one and go on\\[0pt]
\texttt{n} or Delete & Skip it\\[0pt]
\texttt{q} or Return & Stop the walk (replacements already made stay; the rest is untouched)\\[0pt]
\texttt{.} & Replace this one and stop\\[0pt]
\texttt{!} & Replace all remaining matches in the current file, then go on to the next file with a match\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Buttons for all five sit beside the prompt. In a regexp replacement \texttt{\textbackslash{}1} to \texttt{\textbackslash{}9} fill from the match's groups, \texttt{\textbackslash{}\&} is the whole match and \texttt{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}} a backslash; a plain-text replacement is literal. A lowercase search keeps the case of what it replaces, as in Emacs. As in Emacs nothing is saved automatically: each touched file shows as modified. Open files and GitHub or WebDAV files can be walked.

Replace works on heading titles, paragraphs, list items and table cells. Tags, TODO state, priority, properties, planning and block content are left alone so the document's syntax can't break; when every match is inside a block, Replace says so, and \hyperref[sec:orge6ba82b]{Text view}'s own search and replace can change them.

\subsubsection{Narrow}
\label{sec:org7d12d07}

When the open document has a match, the results show \textbf{Narrow} with the count. It works in any search mode and restricts the outline to the matching headings plus their ancestors, with a banner and a \textbf{Widen} button. It composes with \hyperref[sec:org6838b46]{subtree narrowing} and survives a reload.

Org's search is several tools: the Search box finds as you type, \textbf{Narrow} is its sparse tree, Match mode takes the tag grammar, and the Agenda views below list results as rows.

\subsubsection{The Search button}
\label{sec:org90a63f9}
The magnifier in the top bar is the one place for every way to search. A tap opens the search you used last (Find the first time). Tap it again while a search is showing, or press and hold, for the chooser: \textbf{Find} (\texttt{C-s}), \textbf{Match tags and state} (\texttt{C-c a m}), \textbf{Keyword search} (\texttt{C-c a s}), and your saved queries as one-tap chips.

\subsubsection{Match and Keyword search views}
\label{sec:orgcada7ac}
Two Agenda views list a query's results as rows, with the Agenda's prefix format, filters, Effort chip, tap menu and \texttt{org-agenda-sorting-strategy}. Open them from the Search button in the top bar (see below), the command palette (\texttt{org-tags-view}, \texttt{org-search-view}), \texttt{C-c a m} and \texttt{C-c a s} in god-mode, or the search options (\texttt{⋯} → \textbf{Open as Agenda view}).

\textbf{Match} is Emacs's \texttt{m}: tags, properties and TODO state, such as \texttt{work+urgent|blocked} or \texttt{/NEXT}. \textbf{TODO only} is \texttt{M}, the unfinished TODO entries. Rows follow the \texttt{tags} sorting strategy.

\textbf{Keyword search} is Emacs's \texttt{s}. Without a leading \texttt{+}, \texttt{-} or \texttt{\{} the whole text is one phrase, and each space matches any run of whitespace. With one, the words are a Boolean list: \texttt{+budget -draft} needs "budget" and excludes "draft"; \texttt{"Q4 plan"} keeps its space; \texttt{\{regexp\}} is an Emacs regular expression. A leading \texttt{*} searches headlines only, then \texttt{!} limits to TODO entries, then \texttt{:} matches whole words. An entry is a heading with its own text, not its sub-headings. Rows follow the \texttt{search} strategy, and the matching words are marked.

\textbf{Agenda commands} (the button in either view, or the palette) lists the keys \texttt{a}, \texttt{t}, \texttt{m} and \texttt{s} and the commands of \texttt{org-agenda-custom-commands}. \textbf{Save…} adds the current query under a key you choose; for example \texttt{+budget -draft} in Keyword search, saved as \texttt{b}. A composite command, a \texttt{stuck} command and an \texttt{agenda} command with settings open as a screen of their own: each block under its own heading (or its \texttt{org-agenda-overriding-header}), a rule between blocks, rows in the prefix format with the Agenda's keys (\texttt{j} \texttt{k} move, \texttt{t} state, \texttt{,} priority, Enter opens the heading), and an agenda block's days with their own span buttons, \texttt{l} and \texttt{v c}. A single command shows Emacs's hint under its heading, such as \texttt{Press `C-u r' to search again}. The span and day of the Agenda itself are back when you leave the screen. A command's settings go over the variables, a composite's own over the variables and a block's over those; \texttt{org-agenda-files} in a command lists those files only, and the filter presets (tag, category, regexp, effort) of a command hide the rows that do not match. Custom commands, prefix formats and sort keys are in \texttt{examples/agenda-settings.org}.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Modeline and minibuffer}
\label{sec:orgf259c86}
A fixed two-row bar at the bottom of the screen, laid out like Emacs's frame: a dense modeline above a minibuffer.

\textbf{The modeline} is read-only, monospace and terse:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Modified indicator}: \texttt{-{}-{}} unmodified, \texttt{**} modified, \texttt{\%\%} read-only, \texttt{\%*} read-only and modified.
\item \textbf{Buffer name}: the document's name plus a suffix, \texttt{(GitHub)}, \texttt{(WebDAV)}, \texttt{(Local)} or \texttt{(Imported)}.
\item \textbf{Position}: \texttt{Top}, \texttt{Bot}, \texttt{All} or a percentage for how far down the visible area is, plus \texttt{L} and the line number when a heading is focused, and \texttt{C} and the column while a text field is being edited.
\item \textbf{Date and time}, when \texttt{display-time-mode} is on (it is off, as in Emacs, until you turn it on): formatted by \texttt{display-time-format} (default \texttt{nil}: \texttt{2:05PM}), using the same \texttt{format-time-string} as \hyperref[sec:orgab0be70]{Capture templates}. It updates at least every 30 seconds.
\item \textbf{Clock}, when a clock is running anywhere in the document: the elapsed time of this clock-in in brackets, then the heading's title, like \texttt{[⏱ 0:35] Write the quarterly report}. It shows the current session, not the task's lifetime total.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The minibuffer}, below it, is one strip for the search box (see \hyperref[sec:org83d8646]{Searching}), god-mode's chord echo (see \hyperref[sec:org24e47cb]{God-mode}) and the last status message, in that order of priority. A status message clears at your next keypress or tap.

Three variables control it, set in Global or Local Variables or the Lisp init; Settings → Editing and startup → \textbf{Modeline} has the first:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
Variable & Default & Effect\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{display-time-mode} & \texttt{nil} (off) & Emacs's minor-mode toggle, with its \texttt{1} and \texttt{0} convention instead of \texttt{t} and \texttt{nil}. \texttt{1} shows the date and time.\\[0pt]
\texttt{display-time-24hr-format} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} shows the clock as \texttt{14:05} when \texttt{display-time-format} is \texttt{nil}. Add \texttt{(setq display-time-24hr-format t)} to Global Variables.\\[0pt]
\texttt{display-time-format} & \texttt{nil} & Emacs's variable and default. \texttt{nil} shows \texttt{2:05PM}, or \texttt{14:05} when \texttt{display-time-24hr-format} is \texttt{t}; a string such as \texttt{"\%b\%d \%H:\%M"} is used as it is, with any \texttt{format-time-string} code that \hyperref[sec:orgab0be70]{Capture templates} list.\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Links and images}
\label{sec:org3674ada}
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{[[target][description]]} links render as tappable text. A backslash escapes a bracket inside the target (\texttt{[[a\textbackslash{}]b]]} is the target \texttt{a]b}).
\item \textbf{Bare URLs} link too, typed in a sentence or wrapped as \texttt{<https://example.com>}. The schemes are Org's link types (\texttt{org-link-types}) and \texttt{github}, \texttt{webdav} and \texttt{local}, so \texttt{10:30} is never a link. A URL ends at its last letter, digit, slash or closing parenthesis (a final period stays outside); wrap it in \texttt{<...>} or \texttt{[[...]]} to end it differently. \texttt{doi:10.1145/1327452.1327492} opens \texttt{https://doi.org/...}.
\item \textbf{Internal links} go to a heading by title (\texttt{[[*Some Heading]]}), by \texttt{CUSTOM\_ID} (\texttt{[[\#my-id]]}, case ignored) or by bare text (\texttt{[[some words]]}), expanding the ancestors and scrolling to the target. Bare text finds, in order, a \texttt{<{}<{}some words>{}>{}} target, a \texttt{\#+NAME: some words} line, then a heading with those words. Set a \texttt{CUSTOM\_ID} in the general editor (see \hyperref[sec:orge56f2ad]{Editing your outline}).
\item \textbf{Help links}: \texttt{[[help:name]]} opens this Help at the line that documents \texttt{name} (a setting, a command or a function), or says there is no help for it. \texttt{shell:}, \texttt{elisp:} and \texttt{news:} links are not run.
\item \textbf{Link abbreviations}: \texttt{\#+LINK: gh https://github.com/\%s} lets \texttt{[[gh:org/repo]]} stand for the full address. The first \texttt{\%s} in the value becomes the text after the colon, else the first \texttt{\%h} becomes that text percent-encoded, else the text is added to the end.
\item \textbf{ID links}: \texttt{[[id:3f2a-…][Meeting notes]]} go to the heading with that \texttt{:ID:} property wherever it now lives. Tapping one looks in the open file, the other tabs, your \hyperref[sec:orgffa4011]{Agenda Files}, then files you opened or saved here before (like \texttt{org-id-locations}); the back arrow comes back. \textbf{Copy link to heading} (\texttt{org-store-link}, \texttt{C-c l}) puts \texttt{[[id:…][Title]]} on the clipboard, adding an \texttt{:ID:} first if needed; \textbf{Add ID to heading} (\texttt{org-id-get-create}) only adds it; \textbf{Find links to this heading} searches this file and your Agenda Files.
\item \textbf{Targets}: \texttt{<{}<{}name>{}>{}} is a spot a link can go to. The same words in triple angle brackets, \texttt{<{}<{}<name>{}>{}>}, make a \textbf{radio target}: every plain use of those words in the file (any case, whole words) becomes a link to it. Code blocks are not read. HTML and \LaTeX{} export turn targets into anchors and links.
\item \textbf{The back arrow}: after you follow a link, a floating arrow at bottom-left goes back, one hop at a time, so a document with a table of contents is navigable on a touch device without a browser Back. It disappears when there is nowhere left to go.
\item \textbf{Images}: \texttt{http://} and \texttt{https://} image links, and paths relative to the document on GitHub and WebDAV (\texttt{[[images/photo.png]]}, \texttt{[[github:images/photo.png]]}), render inline with \texttt{\#+STARTUP: inlineimages}. Local files and iOS imports show an \texttt{[image: path]} placeholder.
\item \textbf{\texttt{file:}, \texttt{github:}, \texttt{webdav:} and \texttt{local:} links} use org's \texttt{::} convention: an absolute path (\texttt{file:/home/user/notes.org}), a relative one (\texttt{file:projects/todo.org}), a headline (\texttt{file:\textasciitilde{}/notes.org::*Project Alpha}), a custom ID (\texttt{::\#my-id}), a line number (\texttt{::120}, the heading that holds it) or a target, name or heading (\texttt{file:\textasciitilde{}/notes.org::exact phrase}), found as for internal links. Tapping one opens the document and jumps to the match. A path with no scheme uses the backend the current document came from (\texttt{local:} is a file on this device: see \hyperref[sec:orgd336588]{Android app}). The back button returns to the heading the link was in. Documents on GitHub or WebDAV open from a link; a local file or iOS import needs the file picker, and a message says so.
\item \textbf{\texttt{attachment:} links} are org-attach's link type, produced by \textbf{Attach} (see \hyperref[sec:orgc5944b1]{Attachments}). They are bracketed only (\texttt{[[attachment:photo.jpg]]}); a bare \texttt{attachment:photo.jpg} in text is not a link.
\end{itemize}

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Configuration}
\label{sec:org26a342a}
Three layers set variables (Emacs Lisp variables or org directives), in org's own precedence: \textbf{Local Variables beats \#+STARTUP beats Global Variables}. A variable left unset falls through to the next layer down.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Global Variables} (\hyperref[sec:orga253268]{below}): an app-wide baseline, set in Settings.
\item \textbf{\texttt{\#+STARTUP:}} (\hyperref[sec:org3339e1e]{below}): a file's own directive. Only some variables have a \texttt{\#+STARTUP:} shorthand, as in real org:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Variable & \texttt{\#+STARTUP:} keyword(s)\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{org-log-done} & \texttt{logdone} (→ \texttt{time}), \texttt{lognotedone} (→ \texttt{note}), \texttt{nologdone} (→ \texttt{nil})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-log-into-drawer} & \texttt{logdrawer} (→ \texttt{t}), \texttt{nologdrawer} (→ \texttt{nil})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-log-repeat} & \texttt{logrepeat} (→ \texttt{time}), \texttt{lognoterepeat} (→ \texttt{note}), \texttt{nologrepeat} (→ \texttt{nil})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-startup-indented} & \texttt{indent} (→ \texttt{t}), \texttt{noindent} (→ \texttt{nil})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-startup-folded} & \texttt{overview}, \texttt{content}, \texttt{showall}, \texttt{showeverything}, \texttt{show2levels}, \texttt{show3levels}, \texttt{show4levels}, \texttt{show5levels}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-startup-with-inline-images} & \texttt{inlineimages} (→ \texttt{t}), \texttt{noinlineimages} (→ \texttt{nil})\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Local Variables} (\hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{below}): a file's own \texttt{\# Local Variables:} block, a general Emacs mechanism processed last.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsubsection{Global Variables}
\label{sec:orga253268}
Set in \textbf{Settings → Global Variables}. This is the lowest layer, and the only one not stored in a \texttt{.org} file. It is written as an init file is, one \texttt{(setq NAME VALUE)} per variable (a \texttt{setq} may set several, and \texttt{;} starts a comment):

\begin{verbatim}
(setq org-log-done 'time
      org-agenda-start-on-weekday 1)
\end{verbatim}

Settings you change on the Settings screen are saved here as Lisp (a symbol as \texttt{'overview}, a toggle as \texttt{t} or \texttt{nil}, a string in quotes, a list quoted), so the text can be pasted into a Lisp init. Every Local Variables variable works here too, at app-wide precedence. Changes take effect on \textbf{Save}, with no reload, and they are part of \textbf{Export Settings} and \textbf{Import Settings…} (see \hyperref[sec:org8402fde]{File management}).

\textbf{A value that cannot be used}: a variable that is not set has its Emacs default. A variable that holds something the setting cannot use (text where a number belongs, a list with a missing parenthesis) shows a message naming the variable and its value, and the action that needed it is not done, as an Emacs command stops with an error.

\textbf{Smart quotes are normalized}: iOS and many Android keyboards turn a typed straight quote into a curly one, but quoted values here (\texttt{org-xx-extra-menu}, \texttt{org-xx-menu-aliases}) need straight quotes. The Settings controls and this text box convert them back on save; quotes in ordinary prose are untouched.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsubsection{Folding and \texttt{\#+STARTUP}}
\label{sec:org3339e1e}
org-pwa applies \texttt{\#+STARTUP:} directives, typically on the first line. They can share a line or be spread across several, and the last matching keyword wins.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
Category & Keywords & Default\\[0pt]
\hline
Heading visibility & \texttt{overview}, \texttt{content}, \texttt{showall}, \texttt{showeverything}, \texttt{show2levels}, \texttt{show3levels}, \texttt{show4levels}, \texttt{show5levels} & \texttt{showeverything}\\[0pt]
Indentation & \texttt{indent}, \texttt{noindent} & \texttt{noindent}\\[0pt]
Inline images & \texttt{inlineimages}, \texttt{noinlineimages} & \texttt{noinlineimages}\\[0pt]
Progress logging on DONE & \texttt{logdone}, \texttt{lognotedone}, \texttt{nologdone} & none\\[0pt]
Log into the drawer & \texttt{logdrawer}, \texttt{nologdrawer} & \texttt{nologdrawer}\\[0pt]
Log a repeat & \texttt{logrepeat}, \texttt{lognoterepeat}, \texttt{nologrepeat} & \texttt{logrepeat}\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{overview}: only top-level headings, everything else folded.
\item \texttt{show2levels} to \texttt{show5levels}: like \texttt{overview} with that cutoff depth. Headings are shown through that level with no body text at any visible level, and deeper levels are folded.
\item \texttt{content}: every heading line shown, but body text (paragraphs, lists, tables) and properties hidden until you open a heading.
\item \texttt{showall}: body text, lists and tables shown. Property drawers (\texttt{:PROPERTIES:}) and blocks (\texttt{\#+BEGIN\_SRC}, \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_QUOTE} and the like) stay folded, one line each.
\item \texttt{showeverything}: \texttt{showall} plus drawers and blocks fully expanded.
\item \texttt{indent}, \texttt{noindent}: set \texttt{org-startup-indented}; \texttt{indent} indents text and lists under their headings (tables too unless \texttt{org-xx-indent-tables} is \texttt{nil}), \texttt{noindent} draws everything at the left edge.
\item \texttt{logdone}, \texttt{lognotedone}, \texttt{nologdone}, \texttt{logdrawer}, \texttt{nologdrawer}, \texttt{logrepeat}, \texttt{lognoterepeat}, \texttt{nologrepeat}: set \texttt{org-log-done}, \texttt{org-log-into-drawer} and \texttt{org-log-repeat} (see \hyperref[sec:org08c2b92]{Progress logging}).
\end{itemize}

Cycling a heading to fully expanded always reveals its properties and blocks, whatever \texttt{\#+STARTUP:} says, and collapsing hides them again. With no \texttt{\#+STARTUP} line everything is shown, as in org.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsubsection{Local Variables}
\label{sec:orgcf34018}
Two forms, both general Emacs mechanisms: a first-line \texttt{-*- var: val; -*-} cookie, and a \texttt{\# Local Variables: ... \# End:} block, conventionally at the end of the file. Both can appear in one file, and the block wins a conflict. Every line of the block starts with the same prefix as the \texttt{Local Variables:} line; a block Emacs cannot read (a line without the prefix, a line that is not \texttt{name: value}, a value that is cut off, no \texttt{End:}) gives no variables, and the message shows in Emacs's words, such as \texttt{Local variables list is not properly terminated}. Most variables below also have a labeled control on the Settings screen (see \hyperref[sec:org5be3190]{Settings}) for the app-wide baseline.

\begin{verbatim}
# -*- buffer-read-only: t; -*-
\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}
# Local Variables:
# org-agenda-start-on-weekday: 1
# org-cycle-open-archived-trees: nil
# org-agenda-skip-comment-trees: t
# org-agenda-skip-archived-trees: t
# End:
\end{verbatim}

The recognized variables, alphabetically. Those marked "(own)" are this app's extensions, not real org variables. A boolean is \texttt{nil} (or \texttt{()}) for off and any other value for on, as in Emacs. \texttt{examples/settings.org} lists every variable below, and the ones with no control in Settings, in alphabetical order with its default, ready to copy into the Lisp init.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
Variable & Default & What it does\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{before-save-hook} & \texttt{nil} & Functions run before a file is saved; \texttt{org-encrypt-entries} in it (or \texttt{(org-crypt-use-before-save-magic)} in the Lisp init) encrypts the \texttt{crypt} entries first (see \hyperref[sec:orgcfad5dd]{Org Crypt})\\[0pt]
\texttt{buffer-read-only} & \texttt{nil} & Whether the buffer is read-only (see \hyperref[sec:org956255c]{Keybindings}: \texttt{C-x C-q}, or \textbf{Toggle read-only} in the command palette)\\[0pt]
\texttt{calendar-bahai-all-holidays-flag} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} adds the longer Bahá'í list (see \hyperref[sec:orgc740e73]{Holidays})\\[0pt]
\texttt{calendar-christian-all-holidays-flag} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} adds the longer Christian list (see \hyperref[sec:orgc740e73]{Holidays})\\[0pt]
\texttt{calendar-date-style} & \texttt{american} & Order of the date in \texttt{diary-anniversary}, \texttt{diary-cyclic}, \texttt{diary-block} and \texttt{diary-date}: \texttt{american} (month day year), \texttt{european} (day month year) or \texttt{iso} (year month day)\\[0pt]
\texttt{calendar-hebrew-all-holidays-flag} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} adds the longer Hebrew list (see \hyperref[sec:orgc740e73]{Holidays})\\[0pt]
\texttt{calendar-islamic-all-holidays-flag} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} adds the longer Islamic list (see \hyperref[sec:orgc740e73]{Holidays})\\[0pt]
\texttt{calendar-latitude} & \texttt{nil} & Latitude for sun times and \texttt{org-weather}, which need it and \texttt{calendar-longitude} set (a sun-time entry without them reports the error); also Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Diary}\\[0pt]
\texttt{calendar-longitude} & \texttt{nil} & Longitude for the same; also Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Diary}\\[0pt]
\texttt{calendar-time-display-form} & \texttt{(12-hours ":" minutes am-pm (if time-zone " (") time-zone (if time-zone ")"))} & How \texttt{solar-time-string} shows a time, as in Emacs: the default reads "6:30am (EDT)". \texttt{(24-hours ":" minutes)} gives "06:30". The checkbox in Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Diary} switches between the two (see \hyperref[sec:org82df7fe]{Sun times})\\[0pt]
\texttt{diary-abbreviated-year-flag} & \texttt{t} & \texttt{t} reads a two-digit year in a diary date as the year it ends: \texttt{4/20/27} is 2027 (see \hyperref[sec:org5dda1cf]{Diary file})\\[0pt]
\texttt{diary-date-forms} & unset (from \texttt{calendar-date-style}) & Which written dates a diary line may start with, as in Emacs: a list such as \texttt{((month "/" day "[\textasciicircum{}/0-9]") (dayname "\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}W"))} of the symbols \texttt{month}, \texttt{day}, \texttt{year}, \texttt{monthname}, \texttt{dayname} and regexp strings\\[0pt]
\texttt{diary-file} & unset & The diary: one \texttt{github:}, \texttt{webdav:} or \texttt{local:} file, shown in the Agenda when \texttt{org-agenda-include-diary} is \texttt{t}\\[0pt]
\texttt{diary-hebrew-sabbath-candles-minutes} & \texttt{18} & Minutes before sunset that \texttt{(diary-hebrew-sabbath-candles)} gives for lighting the Sabbath candles\\[0pt]
\texttt{diary-include-string} & \texttt{"\#include"} & The word that starts a line naming another diary file\\[0pt]
\texttt{diary-list-entries-hook} & unset & \texttt{diary-include-other-diary-files} in the list follows \texttt{\#include} lines; \texttt{diary-sort-entries} sorts a day's entries by time. Any other name is reported in a message, and the function does not run\\[0pt]
\texttt{diary-nongregorian-listing-hook} & unset & \texttt{diary-hebrew-list-entries}, \texttt{diary-islamic-list-entries} and \texttt{diary-bahai-list-entries} in the list show the diary's \texttt{H}, \texttt{I} and \texttt{B} entries (see \hyperref[sec:org5dda1cf]{Diary file})\\[0pt]
\texttt{diary-nonmarking-symbol} & \texttt{"\&"} & The character that may come before a date\\[0pt]
\texttt{diary-sexp-entry-symbol} & \texttt{"\%\%"} & What starts a sexp line\\[0pt]
\texttt{diary-show-holidays-flag} & \texttt{t} & \texttt{t} lists the day's holidays with its diary entries (see \hyperref[sec:org5dda1cf]{Diary file})\\[0pt]
\texttt{display-line-numbers-mode} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} shows each row's line number in the file beside it in the outline, and in the Text view (see \hyperref[sec:org6f1084d]{Line numbers})\\[0pt]
\texttt{display-line-numbers-type} & \texttt{t} & \texttt{t} numbers from the top of the file; \texttt{relative} counts file lines from the current line; \texttt{visual} counts the rows shown\\[0pt]
\texttt{display-line-numbers-widen} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} keeps the file's own line numbers in a narrowed outline; \texttt{nil} counts from 1 at the narrowed heading\\[0pt]
\texttt{display-time-24hr-format} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil indicates time should be displayed as hh:mm, 0 <= hh <= 23; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{large-file-warning-threshold} & \texttt{512000} & Ask before opening an Org file above this many bytes (500KB here; Emacs asks at 10000000); \texttt{nil} never asks; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-category-filter-preset} & unset & Agenda and TODO category chip to start with: a list like \texttt{("+Work" "-Home")}. A \texttt{-} hides that category; several \texttt{+} keep any of them\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-clock-consistency-checks} & Emacs's own list & Limits for the clock consistency checks, shown as a line above each Clocked row with an issue (white on dark red) in the Agenda's \textbf{ClkCk} log mode: \texttt{:max-duration}, \texttt{:min-duration}, \texttt{:max-gap} and \texttt{:gap-ok-around} of a property list; its face keys are not read. Set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-cmp-user-defined} & unset & A function of two agenda lines for the \texttt{user-defined-up} and \texttt{-down} sort keys: it returns \texttt{-1} (the first goes first), \texttt{1} or \texttt{nil} (no opinion), as \texttt{(lambda (a b) (cond ((string-match-p "URGENT" a) -1) ((string-match-p "URGENT" b) 1)))}. The lines are the category and headline as text, without Emacs's text properties\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-custom-commands} & unset & Saved queries that open from \textbf{Agenda commands}: \texttt{(("w" "Urgent work" tags "work+urgent") ("b" "Budget" search "+budget -draft" ((org-agenda-sorting-strategy '((search alpha-up))))))}. Types: \texttt{tags}, \texttt{tags-todo}, \texttt{search}, \texttt{todo}, \texttt{agenda}, \texttt{alltodo} and \texttt{stuck}; a list of blocks (\texttt{((agenda "") (todo "NEXT"))}, with settings for the whole command after it); or a Lisp function (a name or a \texttt{lambda}), as in \texttt{("x" "Mine" my-fn "match")}: it is called with the match and what it writes (\texttt{princ}, \texttt{insert}) or returns (a string, or a list of strings) is shown in an \textbf{Org Agenda} text buffer; a command's settings (any variable of the Agenda, \texttt{org-agenda-overriding-header}, \texttt{org-agenda-files} with \texttt{local:}, \texttt{github:} or \texttt{webdav:} names, the filter presets) apply to that command; the sorting strategy is read as in the views above (see \hyperref[sec:orgcada7ac]{Match and Keyword search views})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-effort-filter-preset} & unset & Effort filter to start with, such as \texttt{("+<2:00")} (at most 2 hours; \texttt{>} is at least, \texttt{=} exactly)\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-files} & unset (current file only) & A list of file names, such as \texttt{("github:notes.org" "webdav:work.org")}: more files for the Agenda and TODO views (see \hyperref[sec:orgffa4011]{Agenda Files})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-include-diary} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} adds the entries of \texttt{diary-file} to the Agenda (see \hyperref[sec:org5dda1cf]{Diary file})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-include-inactive-timestamps} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means include inactive time stamps in agenda; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-log-mode-add-notes} & \texttt{t} & Non-nil means add first line of notes to log entries in agenda views; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-log-mode-items} & \texttt{(closed clock)} & List of items that should be shown in agenda log mode; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-max-effort} & \texttt{nil} & Per-day effort limit the ⏱ panel starts with: minutes, such as \texttt{240}, or \texttt{((agenda . 240) (todo . 120))}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-prefer-last-repeat} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil sets date for repeated entries to their last repeat; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-prefix-format} & unset & Text before each row, such as \texttt{"  \%-12:c\%?-12t\% s"}, or an alist by view, \texttt{((agenda . "…") (todo . "…"))}: \texttt{\%c} category, \texttt{\%t} time, \texttt{\%s} Scheduled:/Deadline:, \texttt{\%e} effort, \texttt{\%l} a space for each outline level, \texttt{\%b} the parents' titles with \texttt{->} after each, \texttt{\%(form)} the text a Lisp form gives (it sees \texttt{category}, \texttt{time}, \texttt{extra}, \texttt{level}, \texttt{effort}, \texttt{tag} and \texttt{breadcrumbs}, and \texttt{org-entry-get} and the like work on the row's heading; an error stops the view and shows Emacs's message); \texttt{\%-12c} pads right, \texttt{\%12c} left, \texttt{\%?} leaves the part out when empty. Unset keeps the usual row\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-regexp-filter-preset} & unset & Search chip to start with: \texttt{("+rent" "-later")}; Emacs regular expressions; every \texttt{+} pattern must match, no \texttt{-} pattern may\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-remove-times-when-in-prefix} & \texttt{t} & Leave timestamps out of a heading's title in the agenda (\texttt{Do task <2026-10-11 Sun +14d>} shows as \texttt{Do task}; each day of a range shows \texttt{(day 2/3)}). \texttt{nil} shows the title as written. Emacs removes only a time of day; this removes the whole stamp\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-search-view-always-boolean} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} reads every Keyword search as a Boolean list of words, without needing a leading \texttt{+} or \texttt{-}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-search-view-force-full-words} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} makes the words of a Keyword search match whole words\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-search-view-max-outline-level} & \texttt{0} & A number above 0 limits Keyword search to headings down to that level; a heading at that level takes in the text below it\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-show-all-dates} & \texttt{t} & Whether days with nothing on them show in the Agenda; the \textbf{g} button toggles it for the session (see \hyperref[sec:org8b51351]{Agenda}); also Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Agenda}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-show-future-repeats} & \texttt{t} & Whether repeating items show in the future part of the Agenda; also Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Agenda}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-show-inherited-tags} & \texttt{t} & Whether Agenda and TODO list rows show inherited tags, dimmed after the title: \texttt{t} (when \texttt{org-agenda-use-tag-inheritance} covers the view), \texttt{always}, \texttt{nil}, or a list of views such as \texttt{(todo agenda)}. The tag filter sees inherited tags in the same views\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-skip-additional-timestamps-same-entry} & \texttt{nil} & When nil, multiple same-day timestamps in entry make multiple agenda lines; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-skip-archived-trees} & \texttt{t} & Exclude archived headings (tagged \texttt{:ARCHIVE:}) from the agenda; \texttt{nil} includes them\\[0pt]
