\texttt{org-agenda-skip-comment-trees} & \texttt{t} & Exclude commented headings (\texttt{** COMMENT draft}) from the agenda. They stay visible in the outline; \texttt{nil} includes them\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-skip-deadline-prewarning-if-scheduled} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means skip deadline prewarning when entry is also scheduled; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-skip-function} & \texttt{nil} & Function to be called at each match during agenda construction; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-skip-function-global} & \texttt{nil} & Function to be called at each match during agenda construction; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-skip-scheduled-delay-if-deadline} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means skip scheduled delay when entry also has a deadline; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-skip-scheduled-if-deadline-is-shown} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means skip scheduling line if same entry shows because of deadline; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-skip-timestamp-if-deadline-is-shown} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means skip timestamp line if same entry shows because of deadline; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-skip-timestamp-if-done} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means don't select item by timestamp or -range if it is DONE; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-sorting-strategy} & unset & The order of the rows, per view, as in Emacs: \texttt{((agenda habit-down time-up priority-down category-keep) (todo priority-down category-keep))}. Keys: \texttt{time}, \texttt{priority}, \texttt{category}, \texttt{tag}, \texttt{todo-state}, \texttt{effort}, \texttt{deadline}, \texttt{scheduled}, \texttt{timestamp}, \texttt{ts}, \texttt{habit} and \texttt{alpha}, each \texttt{-up} or \texttt{-down}, and \texttt{category-keep}. The \texttt{agenda} entry orders each day's rows, \texttt{todo} the TODO list, \texttt{tags} the Match view and \texttt{search} the Keyword search view (their defaults are \texttt{(tags priority-down category-keep)} and \texttt{(search category-keep)}). Unset is that default; a variable with no entry for a view keeps the rows as they are. \texttt{user-defined-up} and \texttt{-down} ask \texttt{org-agenda-cmp-user-defined} (no opinion while it is \texttt{nil})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-span} & \texttt{week} & Number of days to include in overview display; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-start-day} & \texttt{nil} & Start day for the agenda view; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-start-on-weekday} & \texttt{1} (Monday) & The Week view's first day: \texttt{0} is Sunday through \texttt{6} Saturday; other numbers count modulo 7, as in Emacs\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-start-with-log-mode} & \texttt{nil} & The initial value of log-mode in a newly created agenda window; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-tag-filter-preset} & unset & Tag chip to start with: \texttt{("+work" "-later")}. Several \texttt{+} tags must all be present; a \texttt{-} tag hides its headings\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-text-search-extra-files} & unset & More files for text search only, a list of file names like \texttt{org-agenda-files} (see \hyperref[sec:org62bf069]{Search extra files})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-todo-ignore-deadlines} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means ignore some deadline TODO items when making TODO list; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-todo-ignore-scheduled} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means, ignore some scheduled TODO items when making TODO list; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-todo-ignore-timestamp} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means don't show entries with a timestamp; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-todo-ignore-with-date} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means don't show entries with a date in the global todo list; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-todo-list-sublevels} & \texttt{t} & Non-nil means check also the sublevels of a TODO entry for TODO entries; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-agenda-use-tag-inheritance} & \texttt{(todo search agenda)} & The views that use tag inheritance: \texttt{t}, \texttt{nil}, or a list of \texttt{agenda}, \texttt{todo} and \texttt{search}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-ascii-charset} & \texttt{ascii} & Characters used by ASCII export: \texttt{ascii}, \texttt{latin1} or \texttt{utf-8}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-ascii-text-width} & \texttt{72} & Wrap width, in characters, for ASCII export\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-attach-method} & \texttt{cp} & What Attach does with a file you pick: \texttt{cp} copies it, \texttt{mv} asks to delete the original after copying, \texttt{ln} (or \texttt{lns}) keeps a link to it; \texttt{mv} and \texttt{ln} copy where the app cannot do them (see \hyperref[sec:orgc5944b1]{Attachments}); also Settings → Attachments\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-babel-load-languages} & \texttt{((emacs-lisp . t))} & \texttt{(js . t)} in the list lets \texttt{js} source blocks run (see \hyperref[sec:orgf955b76]{Source blocks}); read from Global Variables only, never from a file; also Settings → Editing and startup → \textbf{Editing}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-cite-basic-author-year-separator} & \texttt{", "} & Text between author and year in a citation, a string\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-cite-basic-sorting-field} & \texttt{author} & Field the reference list is sorted by\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-cite-global-bibliography} & unset & Bibliography files used by every document, as a Lisp list of paths (see \hyperref[sec:org78fb33b]{Citations})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-clock-idle-time} & \texttt{nil} & A whole number of minutes. While a clock runs, after that long without a tap, key press or scroll in the app you are asked whether to keep the time, subtract it and keep clocking, or subtract it and clock out\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-clock-into-drawer} & \texttt{t} & Where clock lines go: \texttt{t} the \texttt{:LOGBOOK:} drawer, a drawer name, a number (a drawer once the entry holds that many clock lines), or \texttt{nil} (bare lines under the heading); also a \texttt{CLOCK\_INTO\_DRAWER} property. Settings → Clocking\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-clock-out-remove-zero-time-clocks} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} removes a clock line that lasted zero minutes when you clock out\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-clock-out-switch-to-state} & \texttt{nil} & A TODO keyword to switch to when clocking out of an entry that has a state\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-clock-sound} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} beeps when a clocked task reaches its estimate. A file name plays that file in the Android app, which looks for it by name in the org-pwa folder (a folder part such as \texttt{\textasciitilde{}/sounds/} is ignored); a file that is not there plays nothing, as in Emacs, and so does the browser, which has no folder to look in. \texttt{t}, or a file that will not play, gives two beeps\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-closed-keep-when-no-todo} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} keeps a CLOSED timestamp when a DONE heading is cycled back to no keyword. Cycling to another keyword always removes it (see \hyperref[sec:org08c2b92]{Progress logging})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-columns-default-format} & \texttt{"\%25ITEM \%TODO \%3PRIORITY \%TAGS"} & The columns of column view (\texttt{C-c C-x C-c}) when neither a \texttt{COLUMNS} property nor a \texttt{\#+COLUMNS:} line gives them (see \hyperref[sec:org12113e9]{Column View})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-columns-ellipses} & \texttt{".."} & What column view puts at the end of a value cut to its column's width\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-contacts-birthday-property} & \texttt{"BIRTHDAY"} & The property \texttt{org-contacts-anniversaries} reads, as a string (\texttt{\# org-contacts-birthday-property: "EVENT"})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-contacts-files} & unset (current file only) & A list of file names like \texttt{org-agenda-files}: more files for \hyperref[sec:org8e45f5f]{Contacts (.vcf)} export (see \hyperref[sec:org4775bc5]{Contacts Files})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-crypt-disable-auto-save} & \texttt{ask} & What happens to the copy kept on this device while entries are decrypted: \texttt{ask}, \texttt{t} (keep none), \texttt{nil} (keep it), \texttt{encrypt} (see \hyperref[sec:orgcfad5dd]{Org Crypt})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-crypt-key} & \texttt{""} & The key entries are encrypted to: a key ID, or part of a name or address. \texttt{""} matches no key, and \texttt{nil} always uses a passphrase\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-crypt-tag-matcher} & \texttt{"crypt"} & The match (as in \texttt{C-c / m}) for the entries \textbf{Encrypt all crypt entries} and \textbf{Decrypt all crypt entries} use\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-cycle-open-archived-trees} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{nil}: an archived heading starts folded whatever \texttt{\#+STARTUP:} says, and the swipe gesture refuses to open it (the chevron still does, as org's force-open commands do). \texttt{t} makes archived headings behave like any other\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-deadline-past-days} & \texttt{10000} & Number of days to warn about missed deadlines; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-deadline-warning-days} & \texttt{14} & How many days before its date a DEADLINE with no warning suffix starts showing in the agenda\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-duration-units} & the Emacs list & An alist such as \texttt{(("min" . 1) ("h" . 60) ("d" . 480))}: the units a duration may use, and how many minutes each is. A value that is not an alist shows an error naming it. The units are used as given: \texttt{("min" . 1)} need not be in the list, \texttt{nil} means no units, and the first of two entries with the same name is used\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-export-with-broken-links} & \texttt{nil} & What export does with a link that leads nowhere (a heading, target, custom id or code reference that is not there): \texttt{nil} stops with "Unable to resolve link: …", \texttt{t} leaves the link out, \texttt{mark} writes \texttt{[BROKEN LINK: path]}; also Settings → Export. A file's \texttt{\#+OPTIONS: broken-links:} wins\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-footnote-auto-adjust} & \texttt{nil} & After adding or deleting a footnote: \texttt{renumber} fn:N, \texttt{sort} the definitions, both (\texttt{t}) or neither\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-footnote-auto-label} & \texttt{t} & Label for a new footnote: \texttt{t} next number, \texttt{confirm} next number you can edit, \texttt{nil} ask, \texttt{random}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-footnote-define-inline} & \texttt{nil} & Write new footnotes as \texttt{[fn:label:text]} at the reference\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-footnote-section} & \texttt{"Footnotes"} & Heading that holds footnote definitions; \texttt{nil} puts each at the end of its own section (see \hyperref[sec:org4659b10]{Footnote commands})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-global-properties} & unset & Properties that apply everywhere, as the alist Emacs takes. Only \texttt{Effort\_ALL} is used, as in \texttt{(("Effort\_ALL" . "0:15 0:30 1:00 2:00"))} (see \hyperref[sec:orgfca7aeb]{Effort\textsubscript{ALL}})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-habit-following-days} & \texttt{7} & Days shown after today in a habit's strip, today included (see \hyperref[sec:org5c8d2b4]{Habits}); also Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Agenda}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-habit-preceding-days} & \texttt{21} & Days before today in a habit's strip; also Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Agenda}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-habit-show-all-today} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} shows every habit today, even one not yet due; also Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Agenda}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-habit-show-habits-only-for-today} & \texttt{t} & Habits appear only in today's Agenda; also Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Agenda}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-html-checkbox-type} & \texttt{ascii} & How HTML export writes checklist boxes: \texttt{ascii} (\texttt{[X]}, \texttt{[ ]}, \texttt{[-]} as text), \texttt{unicode} (☑ and ☐) or \texttt{html} (checkbox inputs)\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-html-doctype} & \texttt{xhtml-strict} & The document type of HTML export: \texttt{xhtml-strict}, \texttt{xhtml-transitional}, \texttt{xhtml-frameset}, \texttt{xhtml-11}, \texttt{xhtml5}, \texttt{html5}, \texttt{html4-strict}, \texttt{html4-transitional} or \texttt{html4-frameset}; a file's \texttt{\#+HTML\_DOCTYPE:} wins\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-html-head} & unset & A quoted string added to the \texttt{<head>} of every HTML export; a file's own \texttt{\#+HTML\_HEAD:} is added after it. Settings → Export sets it\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-html-postamble} & \texttt{auto} & The foot of every HTML export: \texttt{auto} the date, author, email, "Created" time, creator and validation link (each in the document's \texttt{\#+LANGUAGE:}; the date, author, email and creator follow \texttt{\#+OPTIONS:} \texttt{date:}, \texttt{author:}, \texttt{email:} and \texttt{creator:}, the time \texttt{timestamp:}), \texttt{nil} nothing, \texttt{t} the \texttt{org-html-postamble-format} text for the language, a quoted format string, or a function like \texttt{org-html-preamble}'s. Nothing is written when the text is blank. A file's own \texttt{\#+OPTIONS: html-postamble:} wins\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-html-postamble-format} & see Emacs & The postamble text for each language, as \texttt{org-html-preamble-format} is; the default is the author, date, creator and validation lines\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-html-preamble} & \texttt{t} & What goes above the content of an HTML export: \texttt{nil} nothing, \texttt{t} the \texttt{org-html-preamble-format} text for the document's \texttt{\#+LANGUAGE:} (or \texttt{"en"}), a quoted format string, or a function (a symbol or a \texttt{lambda}) that gets the export options (\texttt{:title}, \texttt{:subtitle}, \texttt{:author}, \texttt{:date}, \texttt{:email}, \texttt{:language}, \texttt{:creator}) and returns the text. Nothing is written when the text is blank. A file's own \texttt{\#+OPTIONS: html-preamble:} wins\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-html-preamble-format} & \texttt{(("en" ""))} & The preamble text for each language, as an alist of a language and a format string: \texttt{\%t} title, \texttt{\%s} subtitle, \texttt{\%a} author, \texttt{\%e} email, \texttt{\%d} date, \texttt{\%c} creator, \texttt{\%v} validation link, \texttt{\%T} and \texttt{\%C} time, \texttt{\%\%} a percent sign; flags and widths work as in Emacs's \texttt{format-spec} (\texttt{\%-10t}, \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}a})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-html-validation-link} & \texttt{<a href="https://validator.w3.org/check?uri=referer">Validate</a>} & What \texttt{\%v} stands for in the preamble and the postamble, and the last line of an \texttt{auto} postamble; \texttt{nil} for none\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-alarm-time} & \texttt{0} & Minutes before a timed event that Calendar (.ics) export puts a display alarm; \texttt{0} for none (an \texttt{:APPT\_WARNTIME:} property sets one for one heading)\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-categories} & \texttt{(local-tags category)} & Items that should be entered into the "categories" field; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-combined-description} & \texttt{""} & Calendar description for the combined iCalendar (all agenda files); set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-combined-name} & \texttt{"OrgMode"} & Calendar name for the combined iCalendar representing all agenda files; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-date-time-format} & \texttt{":\%Y\%m\%dT\%H\%M\%S"} & Format-string for exporting icalendar DATE-TIME; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-deadline-summary-prefix} & \texttt{"DL: "} & String prepended to exported headlines with a deadline; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-exclude-tags} & \texttt{nil} & Tags that exclude a tree from export; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-force-alarm} & \texttt{nil} & Non-nil means alarm will be created even if is set to zero; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-include-todo} & \texttt{nil} & Whether Calendar (.ics) export also writes TODO items as tasks: \texttt{nil}, \texttt{t} (not done), \texttt{'unblocked} or \texttt{'all}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-scheduled-summary-prefix} & \texttt{"S: "} & String prepended to exported scheduled headlines; set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-timezone} & the system zone & The time zone string for iCalendar export (the system zone by default); set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-use-deadline} & \texttt{(event-if-not-todo todo-due)} & Which DEADLINEs become events (\texttt{event-if-todo}, \texttt{event-if-todo-not-done}, \texttt{event-if-not-todo}) and whether a task's deadline is its due date (\texttt{todo-due})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-use-scheduled} & \texttt{(todo-start)} & Which SCHEDULED dates become events (\texttt{event-if-todo}, \texttt{event-if-todo-not-done}, \texttt{event-if-not-todo}) and whether a task's scheduled date is its start (\texttt{todo-start})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-icalendar-with-timestamps} & \texttt{'active} & Which timestamps in a heading's title and text become events: \texttt{'active}, \texttt{'inactive}, \texttt{t} or \texttt{nil}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-inlinetask-min-level} & \texttt{15} & With \texttt{org-inlinetask} in \texttt{org-modules}: the number of stars from which a headline is an inline task (see Inline tasks under Export)\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-latex-compiler} & \texttt{pdflatex} & \texttt{pdflatex}, \texttt{xelatex} or \texttt{lualatex}, for files with no \texttt{\#+LATEX\_COMPILER:}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-latex-default-class} & \texttt{article} & \texttt{article}, \texttt{report}, \texttt{book} or a class the Lisp init adds to \texttt{org-latex-classes}: the class of every \LaTeX{} export whose file has no \texttt{\#+LATEX\_CLASS:}. Settings → Export sets it\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-log-done} & \texttt{nil} (no logging) & \texttt{'time} inserts a \texttt{CLOSED:} timestamp when a heading becomes DONE; \texttt{'note} also asks for a closing note. Its \texttt{\#+STARTUP:} shorthands are \texttt{logdone} and \texttt{lognotedone} (see \hyperref[sec:org08c2b92]{Progress logging} for the per-keyword \texttt{!} and \texttt{@} forms)\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-log-into-drawer} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} or a drawer name writes log items into \texttt{:LOGBOOK:} (any name is written as \texttt{LOGBOOK}). \texttt{\#+STARTUP: logdrawer}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-log-repeat} & \texttt{'time} & \texttt{'time} logs a repeating task's completion and sets \texttt{LAST\_REPEAT}; \texttt{'note} asks for a note; \texttt{nil} does neither. \texttt{\#+STARTUP: logrepeat}, \texttt{lognoterepeat}, \texttt{nologrepeat}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-modules} & unset & Add \texttt{org-inlinetask} to read long headlines as inline tasks in exports. A Lisp init does the same with \texttt{(add-to-list 'org-modules 'org-inlinetask)} or \texttt{(require 'org-inlinetask)}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-priority-default} & \texttt{?B} & The priority of a heading without a cookie when rows are ordered by priority\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-priority-faces} & unset & Colors for the priority badges: \texttt{((?A . error) (?B . "orange"))}\\[0pt]

\texttt{org-startup-truncated} & \texttt{t} & \texttt{t} scrolls long lines of the Text view sideways; \texttt{nil} wraps them; also Settings → Editing and startup → \textbf{Editing}\\[0pt]

\texttt{org-tag-alist} & unset & Tags to offer when you tag a heading, written as in Emacs: \texttt{(("work" . ?w) "home")}. A file's own value replaces it\\[0pt]

\texttt{org-tags-exclude-from-inheritance} & (none) & Tags that never inherit, as a list (\texttt{'("private" "archive")})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-timer-default-timer} & \texttt{"0"} & The countdown asked for by \textbf{Set countdown timer}, in minutes or \texttt{h:mm:ss}; \texttt{"0"} asks with nothing filled in\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-timer-display} & \texttt{mode-line} & Where a running timer shows: \texttt{mode-line}, \texttt{frame-title} (the title of the page), \texttt{both} or \texttt{nil}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-timer-format} & \texttt{"\%s "} & What \texttt{org-timer} and \texttt{org-timer-item} insert; \texttt{\%s} is the time\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-use-property-inheritance} & \texttt{nil} & \texttt{t} lets a \texttt{key:value} search filter and an attachment folder use a value inherited from an ancestor (a heading's own value wins). A list of property names, or a regexp in quotes, limits inheritance to those properties\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-use-sub-superscripts} & \texttt{t} & \texttt{t}, \texttt{\{\}} or \texttt{nil} (three values, as in org; any other value counts as \texttt{t}); see \hyperref[sec:orgc52a359]{Inline text markup}\\[0pt]

\texttt{org-xx-size-limit-attachment-warn} & \texttt{"20MB"} & (own) Ask before attaching a file above this size; \texttt{nil} never asks; a string such as \texttt{"20MB"}, set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-xx-size-limit-bibliography} & \texttt{"5MB"} & (own) Refuse a \texttt{\#+BIBLIOGRAPHY:} file above this size; \texttt{nil} sets no limit; a string such as \texttt{"5MB"}, set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-xx-size-limit-image} & \texttt{"3MB"} & (own) An inline image above this size shows its size and a \textbf{Load} link instead; \texttt{nil} shows every image; a string such as \texttt{"3MB"}, set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-xx-size-limit-include} & \texttt{"2MB"} & (own) Skip an \texttt{\#+INCLUDE:} file above this size; \texttt{nil} sets no limit; a string such as \texttt{"2MB"}, set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-xx-size-limit-org-file} & \texttt{"2MB"} & (own) Refuse to open an Org file above this size; \texttt{nil} sets no limit; a string such as \texttt{"2MB"}, set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-xx-size-limit-setupfile} & \texttt{"1MB"} & (own) Refuse a \texttt{\#+SETUPFILE:} above this size; \texttt{nil} sets no limit; a string such as \texttt{"1MB"}, set in Global Variables or the Lisp init\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-xx-startup-with-show-photos} & \texttt{nil} & (own) \texttt{t} shows a contact's photo as a thumbnail beside its field when a file opens: next to \texttt{:PHOTO:} in Flat style, in the "Photo" sub-heading's drawer in Tree style. It follows that field's visibility, so a collapsed contact or folded drawer shows no photo. It has no \texttt{\#+STARTUP:} keyword (see \hyperref[sec:org8e45f5f]{Contacts (.vcf) export})\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-xx-text-font-size} & \texttt{13} & (own) The Text view's text size in pixels, 9 to 28\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-xx-windowing-threshold} & \texttt{400} & (own) Above this many rows an outline or agenda draws only the rows near the screen; \texttt{0} always draws every row\\[0pt]
\texttt{recentf-max-saved-items} & \texttt{20} & How many files \textbf{Recently opened} keeps, as in Emacs (\texttt{nil}, 0 or a negative number keeps them all); also Settings → Editing and startup → \textbf{Startup}\\[0pt]

\end{center}

A variable the app does not read is kept with the file's variables and has no effect here, as in Emacs.

\subsubsection{Lisp init}
\label{sec:orgc928c7c}
Settings → Advanced → \textbf{Lisp init} takes Emacs Lisp, run as Emacs runs an init file. \texttt{setq} gives any setting in the table above a value, written as in Emacs:

\begin{verbatim}
(setq org-agenda-files '("github:home.org" "github:journal.org")
      org-deadline-warning-days (* 2 7)
      org-log-done 'time)
(add-to-list 'org-modules 'org-habit)
\end{verbatim}

All of Lisp is there to compute a value: \texttt{let}, \texttt{defun}, loops, \texttt{append}, \texttt{format}. What the init defines is available to diary entries and holiday lists too: after \texttt{(defun my-plus (x) (+ x 1))} an entry can use \texttt{\%\%(= (my-plus 1) 2)}. A setting the init sets shows in Settings marked \textbf{Set by the Lisp init} and wins over the saved value, as \texttt{init.el} wins over customized values; the saved value returns when the line is removed. \texttt{org-xx-extensions} is always your own choice in Settings.

A form that fails shows Emacs's message in the status line (\texttt{Symbol’s function definition is void: foo}) and the forms after it still run. \texttt{(load "github:file.el")} reads another file as part of the init, and the Agenda's \textbf{Refresh} reads it again. More forms, with the values Emacs gives, are in \texttt{examples/lisp-init.org}.

\textbf{Limits.} A program stops after 5 seconds or about a million steps with \texttt{Lisp evaluation stopped: too many steps (possible infinite loop)}; nothing in the program can catch it. As in Emacs, nesting deeper than \texttt{max-lisp-eval-depth} (1600) signals \texttt{excessive-lisp-nesting}, and a number of more than \texttt{integer-width} bits (65536) signals \texttt{overflow-error}. A list or vector of more than 16 million elements, or a string or bool-vector of more than 134 million characters or bits, is refused with Emacs's \texttt{Memory exhausted} message. A regexp that would backtrack without end, or a loop that runs through a string of tens of thousands of characters (such as \texttt{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}(a\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}|b\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{})*c} on 100,000 characters), signals \texttt{Stack overflow in regexp matcher}, at about the same length as Emacs 29.3. A size that is negative or not an integer signals \texttt{wrong-type-argument} and a shift or power too large for memory \texttt{overflow-error}, as in Emacs.

\subsection{Progress logging}
\label{sec:org08c2b92}
Changing a heading's TODO state follows Emacs's \texttt{org-todo}. \texttt{examples/todo-states.org} and \texttt{examples/logging.org} show the results, as Emacs wrote them.

\subsubsection{\texttt{org-log-done}}
\label{sec:orgf3668a6}

Set by \texttt{\#+STARTUP: logdone} or \texttt{lognotedone} (see \hyperref[sec:org3339e1e]{Folding and \#+STARTUP}); it controls what happens when a heading becomes DONE:

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{logdone} (\texttt{time}) inserts \texttt{CLOSED: [timestamp]}. Cycling to an open keyword removes it, and so does cycling to no keyword unless \texttt{org-closed-keep-when-no-todo} is set. Switching between two done keywords leaves it alone.
\item \texttt{lognotedone} (\texttt{note}) also asks for a note, saved as \texttt{- CLOSING NOTE [timestamp]}. \textbf{Skip} declines only the note.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Where log items go}
\label{sec:org86ca9ad}

A log item is written under the planning line and properties, newest first. With \texttt{\#+STARTUP: logdrawer} (\texttt{org-log-into-drawer} \texttt{t}), or a \texttt{:LOG\_INTO\_DRAWER:} property on the heading or an ancestor, it goes into the \texttt{:LOGBOOK:} drawer. A state item reads \texttt{- State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [timestamp]}.

\subsubsection{Repeating tasks and \texttt{org-log-repeat}}
\label{sec:orgc884e28}

Marking a task with a repeating timestamp done moves every repeating active timestamp forward (\texttt{+}, \texttt{++} and \texttt{.+} as in Org), removes a \texttt{SCHEDULED} without a repeater, drops \texttt{CLOSED} and sets the state to \texttt{:REPEAT\_TO\_STATE:} if it names a keyword of the file, else to the first keyword. \texttt{LAST\_REPEAT} and a \texttt{- State "DONE" from "TODO"} item are written unless \texttt{\#+STARTUP: nologrepeat}; \texttt{lognoterepeat} asks for a note.

\subsubsection{The per-keyword logging spec}
\label{sec:org8add711}

The spec overrides \texttt{org-log-done} for any keyword. It uses the fast-key syntax of \texttt{\#+TODO:}:

\begin{verbatim}
#+TODO: TODO(t) WAIT(w@/!) | DONE(d!) KILL(k@)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Marker & Meaning\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{!} & Log a timestamp when \textbf{entering} the state\\[0pt]
\texttt{@} & Log a note when \textbf{entering}\\[0pt]
\texttt{@/!} & A note when entering, and a timestamp when \textbf{leaving}\\[0pt]
\texttt{/!} & A timestamp when \textbf{leaving} only\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

A leaving-log fires only if the target state doesn't already log on entry. Above, WAIT to DONE adds nothing from WAIT's \texttt{/!} because DONE logs on entry (\texttt{d!}); WAIT to TODO does, since TODO logs nothing. A \texttt{CLOSED} timestamp and a state item can both fire for one transition.

A \texttt{\#+TODO:} line with no \texttt{|} treats its last keyword as the only done state. Several \texttt{\#+TODO:} lines define coexisting workflows: the badge cycles within a heading's own sequence, and for a heading with no state the badge, the \textbf{TODO} button and \texttt{C-c C-t} open a picker of every state of every workflow (first states green, done states red). \texttt{\#+SEQ\_TODO:} and \texttt{\#+TYP\_TODO:} read like \texttt{\#+TODO:}.

\subsubsection{The \texttt{:LOGBOOK:} drawer}
\label{sec:org2e6dfef}

Shown under a heading like \texttt{:PROPERTIES:}, with the same visibility rule. A state change shows the transition and timestamp (\texttt{WAIT → DONE   [timestamp]}) with any note beneath; \texttt{CLOCK:} lines show as \texttt{Clock: start–end ⇒ duration}, or \texttt{Clock: start (running)} while open (see \hyperref[sec:org2e62d01]{Clocking}).

\subsubsection{Agenda: Log}
\label{sec:orgb4c73db}

The Agenda's date-range line has a \textbf{Log} choice (\texttt{org-agenda-log-mode}; it starts as \texttt{org-agenda-start-with-log-mode} says, off by default): \textbf{Off}, \textbf{On} (the items of \texttt{org-agenda-log-mode-items}), \textbf{LogAll} (closed, clock and state changes), \textbf{Only} (nothing but log items) and \textbf{ClkCk} (the clock lines, with a line above each one that has a clocking issue). They are Emacs's \texttt{l}, \texttt{C-u l}, \texttt{C-u C-u l} and \texttt{v c}. The keys are Emacs's: \texttt{l} toggles Off/On, \texttt{C-u l} is LogAll, \texttt{C-u C-u l} is Only and \texttt{v c} toggles ClkCk. They work from a hardware keyboard, from the floating keyboard (god-mode: \texttt{u} is \texttt{C-u}, and Space then \texttt{l} types a literal \texttt{l}) and from the palette, and keep the choice in step.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Archiving}
\label{sec:org2712015}
Tap a heading's title, then \textbf{Archive}, to move its subtree to the archive location (\texttt{org-archive-subtree}, \texttt{C-c C-x C-s}). A panel shows the destination and what will be added, and places to refile to instead (see \hyperref[sec:org183621b]{Refile}); \textbf{Cancel} has focus, so a stray tap does nothing. The moved heading gets \texttt{ARCHIVE\_TIME}, \texttt{ARCHIVE\_FILE}, \texttt{ARCHIVE\_OLPATH}, \texttt{ARCHIVE\_CATEGORY}, \texttt{ARCHIVE\_TODO} and \texttt{ARCHIVE\_ITAGS} properties. The original is removed only after the copy is written. Examples with Emacs's results: \texttt{examples/archive-refile.org}.

The location is \texttt{org-archive-location}: the heading's \texttt{ARCHIVE} property, else the file's \texttt{\#+ARCHIVE:}, else \texttt{\%s\_archive::}. It is a file (\texttt{\%s} is the current file's name; empty means the current file) and an optional heading, joined by \texttt{::}:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Location & Behavior\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{\%s\_archive::} (default) & Sibling file \texttt{notes.org\_archive}, top-level entries\\[0pt]
\texttt{::* Archived Tasks} & Same file, under a top-level \texttt{* Archived Tasks} heading (created if missing)\\[0pt]
\texttt{\textasciitilde{}/org/archive.org::} & One central file, top-level entries\\[0pt]
\texttt{\textasciitilde{}/org/archive.org::* \%s} & One central file, under a heading named after the source file\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Archiving to another file works on GitHub and WebDAV (a local or iOS-imported file needs a file picker); within the current file it works everywhere.

\subsubsection{Restoring (unarchive)}
\label{sec:org8b637ce}
Open the archive file (\textbf{File → Open} lists \texttt{\_archive} files), tap the archived heading, then \textbf{Unarchive} (\texttt{org-unarchive-subtree}). The same panel opens with \textbf{Restore}: the heading moves back to its original file and place, loses the \texttt{ARCHIVE\_*} properties, and gets its state back from \texttt{ARCHIVE\_TODO}. A heading tagged \texttt{:ARCHIVE:} by hand, with no \texttt{ARCHIVE\_FILE}, just has the tag stripped in place.

\subsubsection{Refile}
\label{sec:org183621b}
\textbf{Archive}, then pick a target in the lower part of the panel and tap \textbf{Refile} (\texttt{org-refile}, also in the palette) to move the subtree elsewhere in the outline or into another file. Targets show their outline path, with a search box (every word must match), your last five under \textbf{RECENT} and the rest under \textbf{ALL TARGETS}. The subtree becomes the target's last child with its levels adjusted.

Targets come from \texttt{org-refile-targets}, written as in Emacs; the default, also for \texttt{nil}, is the current file's top-level headings. A value that cannot be read as a list names the variable. Each entry is \texttt{(FILES :KEY . VALUE)}:

\begin{verbatim}
(setq org-refile-targets
      '((nil :maxlevel . 3)
        ("notes.org" :tag . "work")
        (org-agenda-files :todo . "NEXT")))
\end{verbatim}

In a \texttt{\# org-refile-targets:} line of a Local Variables block, write the list without the quote.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{FILES}: \texttt{nil} (this file), \texttt{org-agenda-files}, a file name (a bare name is a sibling of the current file, optionally with a \texttt{github:}, \texttt{webdav:} or \texttt{local:} prefix), or a list of file names.
\item \textbf{Key}: \texttt{:level N}, \texttt{:maxlevel N}, \texttt{:tag "NAME"} (the heading's own tag), \texttt{:todo "KEYWORD"} or \texttt{:regexp "RE"} (matched against the whole heading line). One key per entry, as in Emacs.
\end{itemize}

An entry the app can't understand is skipped and listed with the reason at the top of the picker. Refiling to another file works on GitHub and WebDAV; a local file must have been opened once, except in the \hyperref[sec:orgd336588]{Android app}, where a file in the org-pwa folder works.

With \texttt{org-refile-allow-creating-parent-nodes} set to \texttt{t} (or \texttt{confirm}, which asks first), choose a parent as usual, then type the new heading's name in the box under the details; it is made as the parent's last child and the subtree goes under it.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Extensions}
\label{sec:orgaf1b952}
An init script can add your own diary functions. Set \textbf{Run extension scripts} to \texttt{On} in Settings → Editing and startup → \textbf{Editing}, paste the script under Settings → Advanced → \textbf{Extensions}, and tap \textbf{Approve and run}. The script stays on this device (it is not synced, exported or read from any file), and editing it withdraws the approval.

\texttt{org.sexp(name, fn)}: makes \texttt{\%\%(name args)} work in an agenda file. \texttt{fn} is called once per day with \texttt{ctx} (\texttt{date}, \texttt{year}, \texttt{month}, \texttt{day}, \texttt{weekday} with 0 for Sunday, \texttt{today}, \texttt{calendarLatitude}, \texttt{calendarLongitude}) and then your arguments as plain values. Return \texttt{true} for an entry with the line's own text, a string for an entry with that text, anything else for none.

\begin{verbatim}
org.sexp("every-other-friday", (ctx, start) => {
  const days = (Date.parse(ctx.date) - Date.parse(start)) / 86400000;
  return days >= 0 && days % 14 === 0;
});
\end{verbatim}

\begin{verbatim}
* Pay day
%%(every-other-friday "2026-01-02") Pay day
\end{verbatim}

\texttt{org.command(id, label, fn)}: adds \textbf{label} to the command palette. \texttt{fn(ctx)} gets \texttt{ctx.heading}, the heading the command was run on (or null), and can read the whole file through \texttt{org.document}: its \texttt{name} and its \texttt{headings}, each with \texttt{index}, \texttt{level}, \texttt{title}, \texttt{todo}, \texttt{priority}, \texttt{tags}, \texttt{properties}, \texttt{scheduled}, \texttt{deadline}, \texttt{closed}, \texttt{body} and \texttt{path}. It changes the file with \texttt{org.edit}: \texttt{setTitle}, \texttt{setTodo}, \texttt{setTags}, \texttt{setProperty}, \texttt{deleteProperty} and \texttt{appendBody}, each taking a heading's \texttt{index}. The edits are checked, then applied together as one undo step; none is applied if one is invalid, the buffer is read-only or the file changed while the command ran. \texttt{org.notify(text)}, or a string returned from \texttt{fn}, shows a message in the status line.

\begin{verbatim}
org.command("tag-urgent", "Tag as urgent", (ctx) => {
  if (!ctx.heading) return "Put the cursor on a heading first";
  org.edit.setTags(ctx.heading.index, [...ctx.heading.tags, "urgent"]);
});
\end{verbatim}

\texttt{org.on(event, fn)}: runs \texttt{fn(ctx)} when something happens. The events are \texttt{open} (a file finished loading), \texttt{save} (a save succeeded), \texttt{todo-change} (a heading's TODO state changed; \texttt{ctx.heading}, \texttt{ctx.from} and \texttt{ctx.to}) and \texttt{capture} (a capture was filed; \texttt{ctx.description}, \texttt{ctx.file}). A hook can use \texttt{org.notify} in any event, and \texttt{org.edit} after \texttt{todo-change} and \texttt{capture} (one separate undo step; edits after \texttt{save} or \texttt{open} are ignored). A hook that fails is logged and never blocks saving or opening.

\begin{verbatim}
org.on("todo-change", (ctx) => {
  if (ctx.to === "DONE") org.edit.setProperty(ctx.heading.index, "FINISHED", new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10));
});
\end{verbatim}

A name is letters, digits and dashes, and \texttt{org.sexp} cannot take a standard form such as \texttt{diary-float}. The script runs in the same sandbox as \texttt{js} blocks; a diary function that takes longer than 3 seconds, a command longer than 5, or a hook longer than 2 stops it. A file that uses your function needs it defined in Emacs Lisp to work in Emacs.

\subsubsection{Table functions, link types and exports}
\label{sec:org668d61c}
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{org.tableFunction(name, fn)}: use \texttt{name(...)} in a \texttt{\#+TBLFM:} formula. Arguments are numbers or text; return a number or text. Run with the table's Calc button or \emph{Recalculate all tables}.
\item \texttt{org.linkType(prefix, fn)}: makes \texttt{[[prefix:path][label]]} clickable. \texttt{fn(path)} returns an address (https, mailto, tel or geo) that is opened.
\item \texttt{org.exportBackend(id, label, fn)}: adds \emph{Export: label} to the palette. \texttt{fn(ctx)} gets \texttt{ctx.document} and returns text, or \texttt{\{ text, filename, mime \}} (up to 2 MB).
\end{itemize}

\begin{verbatim}
org.tableFunction("twice", (n) => n * 2);
org.linkType("weather", (place) => "https://wttr.in/" + encodeURIComponent(place));
org.exportBackend("titles", "Titles only", (ctx) => ctx.document.headings.map((h) => h.title).join("\n"));
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Agenda sources and header lines}
\label{sec:org58cde37}
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{org.agenda.source(name, fn)}: \texttt{fn(\{ from, to \})} returns items for the agenda, each \texttt{\{ title, start, end, repeat \}} with \texttt{start} as \texttt{"2026-12-25"} or \texttt{"2026-12-25 09:30"} and \texttt{repeat} such as \texttt{"+1w"}. Asked again after ten minutes.
\item \texttt{await org.ics.parse(text)}: the events of a calendar feed as \texttt{\{ summary, start, end, allDay, location, repeat, cancelled \}}. Complex recurrences are not expanded.
\item \texttt{org.ui.line(id, fn)}: \texttt{fn()} returns one line of text shown above the agenda.
\end{itemize}

\begin{verbatim}
org.agenda.source("holidays", async () => {
  const r = await org.fetch("https://example.org/us-holidays.ics");
  return org.ics.parse(await r.text());
});
org.ui.line("mood", () => "Have a good day");
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Network, position and cache}
\label{sec:orgb6ff74b}
The sandbox has no network, but a script or a \texttt{js} block can ask the page:
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{await org.fetch(url, \{ method, headers, body \})} returns \texttt{\{ status, ok, url, text(), json() \}}. Only https (or http to this device), GET or POST, the headers Accept, Content-Type, Authorization and X-Api-Key, a body up to 100 KB, no cookies, 8 seconds, up to 1 MB back, 30 requests per run. A redirect to a host you did not allow is refused.
\item \texttt{await org.location.get()} returns \texttt{\{ lat, lon, accuracy, time \}}, rounded to about 10 m.
\item \texttt{await org.cache.get(key, maxAgeMs)} returns a stored value or \texttt{null}; \texttt{await org.cache.set(key, value)} stores one (200 KB each, 1 MB and 100 keys per script or document) and returns it.
\end{itemize}
You are asked before the first use. A block lists what it needs: \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_SRC js :net api.open-meteo.com :location yes} (several hosts separated by spaces; \texttt{*.example.org} covers subdomains) and you are asked once per document. The init script is asked per host and for the position when it first uses them. The question warns that the code can send anything it can read, including the open file, to the site, so allow only code you trust.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Source blocks}
\label{sec:orgf955b76}
\texttt{emacs-lisp} (or \texttt{elisp}) blocks run in place, as in Org Babel, on the app's own Lisp interpreter (no files, buffers or network; a loop that never ends stops with a message). \texttt{:var}, \texttt{:results}, \texttt{:wrap}, \texttt{:cache} and \texttt{:noweb} work as for \texttt{js}, \texttt{:lexical yes} turns on lexical binding, and leaving \texttt{(emacs-lisp . t)} out of \texttt{org-babel-load-languages} switches them off. As in Emacs, the app asks before running a document's code.

\begin{verbatim}
#+BEGIN_SRC emacs-lisp :var n=3
(mapcar (lambda (x) (* x n)) '(1 2 3))
#+END_SRC
\end{verbatim}

\texttt{js} blocks are off until \textbf{Run JavaScript source blocks} is \texttt{On} in Settings → Editing and startup → \textbf{Editing}. The setting comes from Global Variables, never from a file, so a document cannot turn it on. Each block then has a \textbf{Run} button (or \texttt{C-c C-c}, or \textbf{Run source block} in the palette). The result is written under it as \texttt{\#+RESULTS:} and replaced on the next run; one Undo removes it. The first run in a saved document asks for confirmation; an unsaved one asks every time. Code runs in a sandbox with no access to the page, your files or your accounts, and no network unless the header asks and you allow it (see Network, position and cache). Examples with Emacs's results: \texttt{examples/babel-js.org}.

\begin{verbatim}
#+NAME: sales
| q  |  n |
|----+----|
| Q1 | 10 |
| Q2 | 20 |

#+BEGIN_SRC js :var data=sales
return data.map(([q, n]) => [q, n * 2]);
#+END_SRC

#+RESULTS:
| Q1 | 20 |
| Q2 | 40 |
\end{verbatim}

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{:results}: \texttt{value} (default, what the block \texttt{return\textasciitilde{}s) or \textasciitilde{}output} (the \texttt{console.log} lines), with \texttt{table}, \texttt{list}, \texttt{scalar}, \texttt{verbatim}, \texttt{raw}, \texttt{org}, \texttt{html}, \texttt{latex}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{pp}, \texttt{drawer} or \texttt{silent}, and \texttt{replace}, \texttt{append} or \texttt{prepend}. Results are laid out as \texttt{org-babel-insert-result} does: a list of lists is a table, a list a bullet list, a scalar a \textasciitilde{}: \textasciitilde{} line, and ten or more lines an example block.
\item \texttt{:var name=value}: a number, a quoted string, a quoted list such as \texttt{'(1 2 3)}, or the name (\texttt{\#+NAME:}) of a table, a list, a result or a source block, found anywhere in the file; a table arrives as an array of rows, and a block is run first (an \texttt{emacs-lisp} block; \texttt{name(n=4)} or \texttt{name(4)} gives its variables). \texttt{name[1,2]} picks a cell and \texttt{name[0:1,*]} a range. \texttt{:colnames yes} drops the first row, \texttt{:rownames yes} the first column, \texttt{:hlines yes} keeps the rules (the script sees \texttt{"hline"}).
\item \texttt{:prologue} and \texttt{:epilogue}: text before and after the code when it runs or is tangled.
\item \texttt{:timeout N}: seconds, 5 by default, 60 at most.
\item \texttt{:wrap NAME}: wraps the result in a \texttt{\#+begin\_NAME} block.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Literate programming: header arguments, Noweb and Tangle}
\label{sec:org65d5d93}
Header arguments are inherited as in Org: \texttt{\#+PROPERTY: header-args :results output} applies to the file, \texttt{header-args:js} to \texttt{js} blocks, and a \texttt{:header-args:} property to a subtree (\texttt{header-args+} adds). A block's own arguments and \texttt{\#+HEADER:} lines win.

\textbf{Noweb}: with \texttt{:noweb yes}, \texttt{<{}<{}name>{}>{}} is replaced by the block \texttt{\#+NAME: name}, by all blocks with \texttt{:noweb-ref name} (joined with \texttt{:noweb-sep}), or by the text of the heading whose \texttt{CUSTOM\_ID} is \texttt{name}. Text before the reference on its line goes before every line of the expansion. \texttt{:noweb} also takes \texttt{tangle}, \texttt{no-export}, \texttt{strip-export} and \texttt{strip-tangle}. A reference that matches nothing expands to nothing; one that goes round in a circle is an error.

\textbf{Tangle}: \textbf{Tangle this file} (\texttt{org-babel-tangle}) writes the blocks with \texttt{:tangle} to files: \texttt{yes} names the file after the document, \texttt{path/file.js} names it, \texttt{no} skips it. Blocks for one file are joined in order with a blank line (\texttt{:padline no} removes it). \texttt{:shebang}, \texttt{:tangle-mode}, \texttt{:comments link}, \texttt{org}, \texttt{both} and \texttt{noweb}, \texttt{:prologue}, \texttt{:epilogue}, \texttt{:no-expand} and \texttt{:var} (a JavaScript block gets \texttt{var x=3;} lines, an emacs-lisp block is wrapped in \texttt{let}) work. \texttt{COMMENT} and \texttt{:ARCHIVE:} subtrees are skipped. One file is saved as it is; several, or one in a folder, come as a zip. Paths may not be absolute or climb out with \texttt{..}.

\textbf{Cache}: \texttt{:cache yes} skips a block whose code, variables and \texttt{:results} are unchanged since its last run (the hash sits in \texttt{\#+RESULTS[hash]:}). Delete the results to force a run; without \texttt{:cache yes} an old hash stays in the results line.

\textbf{Export} follows \texttt{:exports}: \texttt{code} (default), \texttt{results}, \texttt{both} or \texttt{none}. Nothing is run on export; \texttt{results} shows what \texttt{\#+RESULTS:} already holds.

\textbf{The init script from an Org file}: Settings → Extensions → \textbf{Use an Org file…} takes \texttt{github:path}, \texttt{webdav:path} or \texttt{local:name}, then \texttt{::target} (default \texttt{::init.js}). The blocks that tangle to the target become the init script, Noweb included; the approval covers the assembled text, so a change asks again.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Attachments}
\label{sec:orgc5944b1}
Files kept with a heading, as in \texttt{org-attach}. Press \texttt{C-c C-a} on a heading, or tap \textbf{Attach} in 📋 Edit details, for a grid of buttons. Examples: \texttt{examples/attachments.org}.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Attach} (\texttt{a}): the system chooser for files or photos, or a photo or video from the camera; the file is copied into the heading's folder. On ChromeOS and desktop it first asks \textbf{Choose a file}, \textbf{Take a photo} or \textbf{Record a video}.
\item \textbf{Attach a copy} (\texttt{c}), \textbf{Attach and move} (\texttt{m}), \textbf{Attach a link} (\texttt{l}): \texttt{a} follows \texttt{org-attach-method} (Settings → Attachments): \texttt{cp} copies, \texttt{mv} copies then asks before deleting the original, \texttt{ln} keeps a link. Where the app cannot move or link a picked file it copies.
\item \textbf{Attach from URL} (\texttt{u}), \textbf{Record audio} (\texttt{r}), \textbf{Attach open document} (\texttt{b}, as text), \textbf{New text file} (\texttt{n}).
\item \textbf{Open} (\texttt{o}) shows a picture, recording, video or text file in the app; anything else opens in the browser's viewer or downloads.
\item \textbf{Folder} (\texttt{f}): the files as a list with checkboxes, then \texttt{O} (open), \texttt{S} (save to disk) and \texttt{D} (delete). \textbf{Copy to heading…} and \textbf{Move to heading…} put the selected files in another heading's folder.
\item \textbf{Delete one} (\texttt{d}) and \textbf{Delete all} (\texttt{D}), after a confirmation.
\item \textbf{Set DIR} (\texttt{s}) and \textbf{Unset DIR} (\texttt{S}): keep a heading's files in a folder of your choosing. Unset asks whether to move the files to the ID folder, delete them, or leave them.
\item \textbf{Sync} (\texttt{z}): sets the \texttt{:ATTACH:} tag to match the folder.
\end{itemize}

Each heading's files live in \texttt{data/<first 2 characters of its ID>/<rest of the ID>/} beside the document; the heading gets an \texttt{ID} and an \texttt{:ATTACH:} tag the first time. A \texttt{DIR} property names another folder and wins over the ID. It is relative to the document, and \texttt{.}, \texttt{..} and doubled slashes mean what they do in Emacs (\texttt{../shared} is the folder beside the document's); a leading \texttt{/} starts at the root of the storage. A \texttt{DIR} that is empty, starts with \texttt{\textasciitilde{}}, has a backslash or is the root itself cannot hold attachments: a message names it. Attaching a name that already exists in the folder is refused ("File already exists").

\textbf{Links in the body}: Settings → Attachments chooses whether attaching also adds an \texttt{[[attachment:name]]} link: for pictures, audio and video (default), always, or never. A link to a picture shows it inline, audio gets a play button, and tapping a link does what \textbf{Open} does.

\textbf{Names}: an \texttt{:ID:} or an \texttt{attachment:} name stays inside the heading's folder, so one with \texttt{..}, a backslash or a control character is refused (a name may include sub-folders such as \texttt{attachment:scans/a.png}). Attaching a file named \texttt{..}, \texttt{.git} or \texttt{CON} saves it under a safe name.

\textbf{Requirements}: GitHub or WebDAV must be connected; the \hyperref[sec:orgd336588]{Android app} keeps a local file's attachments in the org-pwa folder you choose once. A file over 20MB asks first and one over 95MB is refused (use WebDAV for long videos); see \hyperref[sec:orgfe6fddc]{Size limits}.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Clocking}
\label{sec:org2e62d01}
Clocking actions are \hyperref[sec:org9fe54f3]{command palette} commands, found by name or by Org name: \textbf{Clock in}, \textbf{Clock out}, \textbf{Cancel clock}, \textbf{Continue last clock}, \textbf{Go to clocked task} and \textbf{Set effort estimate}. One clock runs at a time.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{org-clock-in} inserts a bare \texttt{CLOCK: [timestamp]} line on the heading whose action menu is open, else the focused one. Clocking in elsewhere clocks the running one out at the same moment.
\item \textbf{org-clock-out} turns the line into \texttt{CLOCK: [start]-{}-{}[end] =>  H:MM} (one space before HH:MM from ten hours); \textbf{org-clock-cancel} removes it and records nothing. Clocking out also follows \texttt{org-clock-out-switch-to-state} and \texttt{org-clock-out-remove-zero-time-clocks}; the lines go where \texttt{org-clock-into-drawer} says.
\item \textbf{org-clock-in-last} (\texttt{C-c C-x C-x}, god-mode \texttt{c x x}) resumes the most recently clocked heading.
\item \textbf{org-clock-goto} (\texttt{C-c C-x C-j}, \texttt{c x j}) jumps to the clocked heading from any tab. With \texttt{C-u} (\texttt{u c x j}, or \textbf{Go to a recently clocked task}, \texttt{org-clock-select-task}) it lists recently clocked tasks from every open tab.
\end{itemize}

Clock lines live in a \texttt{:LOGBOOK:} drawer from the first one (see \hyperref[sec:org08c2b92]{Progress logging}).

\textbf{Showing clocked time}: the \textbf{Clock} checkbox on \textbf{View → TODO} (\texttt{org-clock-display}) shows each item's total clocked time, running clock included. A \texttt{\#+BEGIN: clocktable} block (\texttt{org-clock-report}) is computed for a date range and shown under \textbf{View → TODO}'s \textbf{Clock report} (see \hyperref[sec:org809ff20]{The TODO view}); \texttt{examples/clock-tables.org} has reports with Emacs's results. While a clock runs, the modeline shows \texttt{[⏱ H:MM] Heading title}.

\textbf{Effort estimates}: \textbf{Set effort estimate} (\texttt{C-c C-x e}, \texttt{org-set-effort}) prompts for the \texttt{EFFORT} of the open or focused heading. Any \texttt{org-duration} form works, stored as typed: \texttt{1:30}, \texttt{2h}, \texttt{45min}, \texttt{1d 3h}, \texttt{2.35h}, or a bare number of minutes. Units are Emacs's: \texttt{min}, \texttt{h}, \texttt{d} (24 h), \texttt{w}, \texttt{m} (a month of 30 days) and \texttt{y}; \texttt{org-duration-units} changes them, for example \texttt{(("min" . 1) ("h" . 60) ("d" . 480))} for an eight-hour day. A blank value clears it; an invalid one is refused. The \texttt{EFFORT} shows beside the title as a \texttt{⏱} badge, and tapping it opens the same prompt. While that heading is clocked in, the modeline shows \texttt{[⏱ 0:45 / 2:00] Heading title}, with a trailing \texttt{!} once the estimate is passed.

\textbf{Reminder}: when a running clock first passes its estimate, the status line says "Task ‘Title’ should be finished by now. (2:00)", with a notification if you allowed them. \texttt{org-clock-sound} adds a sound: two beeps, or a file in the org-pwa folder in the Android app.

\textbf{Idle time}: with \texttt{org-clock-idle-time} set, a clock that has seen no activity in the app for that many minutes asks "Clocked in \& idle for N mins" and offers Org's keys: \texttt{i} ignore, \texttt{k} keep some minutes, \texttt{t} keep until a time, \texttt{g} got back some minutes ago, \texttt{s} subtract the idle time, \texttt{C} cancel the clock, \texttt{j} jump to it; a capital (\texttt{K} \texttt{T} \texttt{G} \texttt{S} \texttt{J}) also clocks out.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsubsection{Effort\textsubscript{ALL}: allowed effort values}
\label{sec:orgfca7aeb}
The effort prompt completes against \texttt{Effort\_ALL}. The first source with a usable value wins (an \texttt{Effort\_ALL+} property adds to the list above it):

\begin{enumerate}
\item an \texttt{Effort\_ALL} property on the heading or its nearest ancestor that has one;
\item the file's \texttt{\#+PROPERTY: Effort\_ALL 0 0:10 0:30 1:00 2:00};
\item \texttt{org-global-properties} (Settings → Advanced or Local Variables), such as \texttt{(("Effort\_ALL" . "0:15 0:30 1:00 2:00 4:00"))}.
\end{enumerate}

Values are space-separated \texttt{org-duration} forms. When a list applies, \textbf{Set effort estimate} shows its values as buttons and the box still takes any other duration. The same list supplies the Agenda's effort filter; with none, the filter uses Org's \texttt{0 0:10 0:30 1:00 2:00 3:00 4:00 5:00 6:00 7:00}.

\subsection{Column View}
\label{sec:org12113e9}
\textbf{Column view} (\texttt{C-c C-x C-c}, \texttt{org-columns}) shows the headings of the subtree you are in, or of the whole file when the cursor is above the first heading, as a table with a column for each entry of the format. Tap a cell to edit the value, to pick one of its allowed values (\texttt{Effort\_ALL}, \texttt{Cost\_ALL}, \ldots{}), or to change the column: wider, narrower, move, add, delete, edit its title and summary. The format comes from the \texttt{COLUMNS} property of the nearest heading that has one, then the first \texttt{\#+COLUMNS:} line, then \texttt{org-columns-default-format}. A column is written \texttt{\%25ITEM(Task)\{+;\%.2f\}}: an optional width, the property, a title in parentheses, and a summary type with an optional \texttt{printf} format in braces. Changing the format stores it where it came from (the \texttt{COLUMNS} property of the heading, or the \texttt{\#+COLUMNS:} line).

The special properties are \texttt{ITEM}, \texttt{TODO}, \texttt{PRIORITY}, \texttt{TAGS}, \texttt{ALLTAGS}, \texttt{CATEGORY}, \texttt{FILE}, \texttt{DEADLINE}, \texttt{SCHEDULED}, \texttt{CLOSED}, \texttt{TIMESTAMP}, \texttt{TIMESTAMP\_IA}, \texttt{BLOCKED} and \texttt{CLOCKSUM}; any other name is a property, taken from the heading itself (or from the ancestors, as \texttt{org-use-property-inheritance} says).

\textbf{Summaries} are computed from the children up and written into the property of each parent that has one, as Emacs does. Types: \texttt{+} sum, \texttt{\$} currency, \texttt{min}, \texttt{max}, \texttt{mean}, \texttt{X} \texttt{X/} \texttt{X\%} check boxes, \texttt{:} \texttt{:min} \texttt{:max} \texttt{:mean} times, \texttt{@min} \texttt{@max} \texttt{@mean} ages, \texttt{est+} ranges such as \texttt{3-5}. A \texttt{printf} format after the type (\texttt{\{+;\%.1f\}}) shapes the numbers, including those of rows with no summary.

\textbf{Dynamic block}: \texttt{\#+BEGIN: columnview} \ldots{} \texttt{\#+END:} holds the same table as text. \textbf{Insert column view block} (\texttt{org-columns-insert-dblock}) adds one to the focused heading; \textbf{Update dynamic block} (\texttt{C-c C-x C-u}, \texttt{org-dblock-update}) writes the blocks under the focused heading again, and \textbf{Update all dynamic blocks} (\texttt{org-update-all-dblocks}) those of the file. Parameters: \texttt{:id} (\texttt{local}, \texttt{global}, or the \texttt{ID} of an entry in this file), \texttt{:format}, \texttt{:maxlevel}, \texttt{:match}, \texttt{:skip-empty-rows}, \texttt{:exclude-tags}, \texttt{:hlines}, \texttt{:indent}, \texttt{:vlines}; a \texttt{\#+TBLFM:} line inside the block is recalculated.

Example, in \texttt{examples/column-view.org}: with \texttt{\#+COLUMNS: \%30ITEM(Task) \%10Effort(Estimate)\{:\} \%Cost(Cost)\{+;\%.2f\}} at the top, a heading with children that have \texttt{:Effort: 6:00} and \texttt{:Cost: 1200} shows a row of its own whose \texttt{Estimate} is the total of theirs and whose \texttt{Cost} reads \texttt{1200.00}. A heading with \texttt{:COLUMNS: \%25ITEM \%Cost(Cost)\{min\}} shows the cheapest of its children instead. The block

\begin{verbatim}
#+BEGIN: columnview :id global :maxlevel 2 :hlines 1
#+END:
\end{verbatim}

is filled with the table, and written again by \textbf{Update all dynamic blocks}.

\subsection{Org Crypt}
\label{sec:orgcfad5dd}
\textbf{Org Crypt} keeps the text of an entry secret in the file. The text below the heading and its properties, sub-headings included, becomes an ASCII-armored PGP message, the same text Emacs's \texttt{org-crypt} and \texttt{gpg} write and read, so a file can be opened in either. The heading, tags and properties stay readable.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Encrypt entry}, \textbf{Decrypt entry} (\texttt{org-encrypt-entry}, \texttt{org-decrypt-entry}): the focused entry.
\item \textbf{Encrypt all crypt entries}, \textbf{Decrypt all crypt entries} (\texttt{org-encrypt-entries}, \texttt{org-decrypt-entries}): every entry matching \texttt{org-crypt-tag-matcher}, the \texttt{crypt} tag by default.
\end{itemize}

An entry is encrypted with a passphrase, asked for twice. With \texttt{org-crypt-key} set to a key ID, or part of a name or address, it is encrypted to the matching keys in \textbf{Settings → Encryption keys} instead, and a \texttt{:CRYPTKEY:} property on the entry names its own key (\texttt{nil} for a passphrase). Decrypting an entry encrypted to a key asks for the passphrase of its secret key. A passphrase typed is kept in memory for ten minutes after its last use, and two hours at most, as gpg-agent keeps it. Decrypted text that did not change is encrypted to the same message again, so the file does not change for nothing.

While entries are decrypted, \texttt{org-crypt-disable-auto-save} says what happens to the copy of the file kept on this device after each edit: \texttt{ask} (the default) asks when you decrypt, \texttt{t} keeps no copy until the file is read again, \texttt{nil} keeps it (decrypted text may then be stored), \texttt{encrypt} stores the entries encrypted. The undo history is not kept either, except with \texttt{nil}. Saving the file writes what is on screen; \texttt{(org-crypt-use-before-save-magic)} in the Lisp init encrypts the \texttt{crypt} entries first.

Example, in \texttt{examples/crypt.org}: the heading \texttt{* Waiting to be encrypted :crypt:} has plain text under its properties. \textbf{Encrypt all crypt entries} asks for a passphrase and puts a \texttt{-{}-{}-{}-{}-BEGIN PGP MESSAGE-{}-{}-{}-{}-} block there; the passphrase of the other entries in the file is \texttt{example}. Import \texttt{crypt-example-key.asc} under \textbf{Encryption keys} to open the entry encrypted to a key.

\subsection{Org Timer}
\label{sec:org8708a1b}
\textbf{Org Timer} is a relative timer that counts up, and a countdown. While one runs, \texttt{<0:12:03>} shows in the modeline (\texttt{org-timer-display}).

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Start timer} (\texttt{C-c C-x 0}, \texttt{org-timer-start}), \textbf{Start timer with an offset} (\texttt{C-u C-c C-x 0}; an offset such as \texttt{0:08:26}, for a timer started late).
\item \textbf{Pause or continue timer} (\texttt{C-c C-x ,}), \textbf{Stop timer} (\texttt{C-c C-x \_}).
\item \textbf{Insert timer list item} (\texttt{C-c C-x -}, \texttt{org-timer-item}) adds \texttt{- 0:12:03 ::} at the end of the text of the focused heading; the next one goes under it. The \textbf{Timer} button in the text editors (\texttt{org-timer}) inserts the time at the cursor.
\item \textbf{Set countdown timer} (\texttt{C-c C-x ;}, \texttt{org-timer-set-timer}): minutes or \texttt{h:mm:ss}; with an \texttt{Effort} on the focused heading, that effort, without asking (\textbf{Set countdown timer, ignoring the effort}, \texttt{C-u C-c C-x ;}, asks). At zero, a reminder with the sound of \texttt{org-clock-sound}. \textbf{Show time left on the countdown} is \texttt{org-timer-show-remaining-time}.
\item \textbf{Shift timer stamps in the text} (\texttt{org-timer-change-times-in-region}): every \texttt{H:MM:SS} in the text of the focused heading moves by an amount such as \texttt{-0:08:26}; empty makes the first one \texttt{0:00:00}.
\end{itemize}

Example, in \texttt{examples/timer.org}: start the timer when a meeting starts and choose \textbf{Insert timer list item} at each topic to get \texttt{- 0:03:40 :: Release status}.

\subsection{Line numbers}
\label{sec:org6f1084d}
As in Emacs, \texttt{display-line-numbers-mode} shows the file's own line numbers; \texttt{-n} on a source block numbers only the exported block (see \hyperref[sec:org1f139d4]{Line numbers and references in source blocks}). Set \texttt{display-line-numbers-mode} to \texttt{t} (Settings → Editing) and every file line the outline shows gets a number; a wrapped line keeps one. Lines that are not drawn (the \texttt{\#+end} line, planning and drawer lines, a folded body) are skipped. A narrowed outline counts from 1 at the narrowed heading unless \texttt{display-line-numbers-widen} is \texttt{t}. The Text view shows them too.

\texttt{display-line-numbers-type} is \texttt{t} (numbers from the top), \texttt{relative} (file lines away from the current row) or \texttt{visual} (rows shown away from it); the current row keeps its absolute number.

\subsection{Narrowing}
\label{sec:org6838b46}
\textbf{🔽 Narrow} in a heading's action menu restricts the outline to that heading and its subtree (\texttt{C-x n s}, god-mode \texttt{x SPC n s}). On the narrowed heading it becomes \textbf{🔼 Widen} (\texttt{C-x n w}), and a banner \textbf{Narrowed to: TITLE — Widen} stays at the top. Narrowing elsewhere replaces the restriction.

Only the display is restricted: Save, Export, Agenda and Search use the whole document. Narrowing follows its heading through promote, demote, move and rename, and persists across tabs and restarts. The Text view shows only the narrowed subtree (see \hyperref[sec:orge6ba82b]{The plain-text editor}).

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{The plain-text editor}
\label{sec:orge6ba82b}
Tap \textbf{View → Text} to replace the outline with one textarea holding the raw org text, including \texttt{\#+STARTUP:}, \texttt{\#+TODO:}, a \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables} block and syntax the outline has no UI for. Tap \textbf{View → Org} to switch back; the text is reparsed then, so changes take effect at once and count as edits.

Switching in lands near your last navigation (a search result, link or agenda item). While \hyperref[sec:org6838b46]{narrowed}, only the narrowed subtree is editable and switching back splices it into place.

The text is colored (headings, TODO words, tags, timestamps, \texttt{\#+} lines, drawers, links, emphasis, and JavaScript or Lisp in source blocks). A row of tools sits above it: \textbf{Undo} and \textbf{Redo}, line numbers, wrap, \textbf{A−} and \textbf{A+} for the text size, \textbf{Line…} and \textbf{Find}. \textbf{Line…} goes to a line number, duplicates, deletes, moves, indents or outdents the selected lines, and has \textbf{Select all} and \textbf{Copy all}. Enter keeps the line's indentation, and a row of keys above the keyboard types \texttt{Tab * / \% ( ) \& - : < >}. Line numbers follow \texttt{display-line-numbers-mode} (see \hyperref[sec:org6f1084d]{Line numbers}), wrapping follows \texttt{org-startup-truncated}, and \texttt{org-xx-text-font-size} is the size; all three are at the end of Editing in \hyperref[sec:org5be3190]{Settings}.

\textbf{Other files}: \textbf{File → Open} lists every file; filter by extension to narrow it. One that is not Org (a \texttt{notes.txt}, a \texttt{README.md}, a \texttt{diary}) opens in Text view only; \texttt{.md}, \texttt{.js}, \texttt{.json} and \texttt{.el} are colored.

\textbf{Search} works on the live raw text, so it finds and replaces inside property drawers and blocks. \textbf{Regex} and \textbf{Replace} work as in Org view; replacements stay in the textarea until you leave or Save.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Agenda}
\label{sec:org8b51351}
Tap \textbf{View → Agenda} for everything with a date, in Day, Week or Month view. One button cycles the three views. \textbf{‹} and \textbf{›} step back or forward by the current unit, \textbf{Today} jumps to today, and a horizontal swipe does the same as ‹ and ›. Tapping an item returns to the Org view at that item.

\textbf{Row actions}: press and hold an item for \textbf{Mark done}, \textbf{Set state}, \textbf{Reschedule}, \textbf{Priority}, \textbf{Refile} and \textbf{Open heading}. Swipe an item to the right to mark it done; \textbf{Undo} stays for a few seconds, and a repeating item moves to its next date. They change the open file only: an item from another agenda file offers \textbf{Open heading} alone.

\textbf{Filter chips} under the controls narrow the list; a chip shows its choice and an ✕ clears it. They last for the session and combine with \textbf{and}:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Tag}, \textbf{State}, \textbf{Category}: pick values, then say what they do: show only items with \textbf{any} of them, with \textbf{all} of them (tags), or hide items with any (Emacs's \texttt{-} prefix). Tags include inherited ones (\texttt{org-use-tag-inheritance}).
\item \textbf{Search}: an Emacs regular expression (\texttt{\textbackslash{}(} \texttt{\textbackslash{})} group, \texttt{\textbackslash{}|} alternates), not case sensitive, matched against the keyword, title and tags (Emacs's \texttt{=} filter). A box can hide the matching rows instead.
\item \textbf{Top heading}: only items under the chosen top-level headings (Emacs's \texttt{\textasciicircum{}}).
\item \textbf{Effort} (TODO view): at most, at least or exactly a duration, as in the ⏱ panel.
\end{itemize}

The chips start from \texttt{org-agenda-tag-filter-preset}, \texttt{org-agenda-category-filter-preset}, \texttt{org-agenda-regexp-filter-preset} and \texttt{org-agenda-effort-filter-preset}, and the ⏱ panel from \texttt{org-agenda-sorting-strategy} and \texttt{org-agenda-max-effort} (see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables}).

\textbf{Order and prefix}: \texttt{org-agenda-sorting-strategy} orders the rows per view and \texttt{org-agenda-prefix-format} builds the text before each row, as in Emacs; the Lisp init can also use functions for both (see \texttt{examples/agenda-settings.org}):

\begin{verbatim}
# Local Variables:
# org-agenda-sorting-strategy: ((agenda time-up priority-down category-keep) (todo priority-down))
# org-agenda-prefix-format: ((agenda . "%-10:c%b") (todo . "%l%c "))
# End:
\end{verbatim}

By default each Agenda day orders habits last, then time, then priority with \texttt{[\#A]} first, then category. With that prefix, \texttt{** Call bank} under \texttt{* Errands} in a file with category \texttt{home} starts with \texttt{home:     Errands->}.

\textbf{Priorities}: the range is \texttt{org-priority-highest} to \texttt{org-priority-lowest} (letters, or numbers for \texttt{[\#1]} cookies), with \texttt{org-priority-default} for a heading without a cookie. A file can set all three with \texttt{\#+PRIORITIES: 1 5 3}. The priority buttons, the cycle and the Agenda's Priority menu offer that range. Tapping a priority badge steps down as \texttt{org-priority-down} does: none, the highest priority, then each lower one, then none. \texttt{org-priority-faces} colors the badges: \texttt{((?A . error) (?B . "orange"))}.

\textbf{Inherited tags}: \texttt{org-agenda-show-inherited-tags} chooses where rows show them: \texttt{(todo)} for the TODO list only, \texttt{always}, or \texttt{nil}.

\textbf{Titles}: a timestamp in a heading's title is left out of its row, since the day and time column say it; \texttt{org-agenda-remove-times-when-in-prefix} \texttt{nil} shows titles as written.

\textbf{Empty days}: every day shows by default. The \textbf{g} button toggles \texttt{org-agenda-show-all-dates} for the session; it is bold while empty days are hidden.

\textbf{Weeks}: Week view shows a full week, Monday to Sunday by default (\texttt{org-agenda-start-on-weekday}), with the ISO week number on each week's first day and in the range label (\texttt{(W31-W36)}).

\textbf{Categories}: every item shows a category prefix: the file's \texttt{\#+CATEGORY:}, else its file name without directory or \texttt{.org}.

\textbf{Times}: a timestamp can carry a range, like \texttt{SCHEDULED: <2026-08-31 Mon 08:00-09:00>}, shown as \texttt{08:00-09:00} in Week and Month; a single time shows as \texttt{08:00 ……}; an untimed SCHEDULED or DEADLINE shows its \texttt{Scheduled:} or \texttt{Deadline:} label.

\textbf{Time grid}: Day view adds Org's default hour grid (dashed lines every two hours, 8am to 8pm). Untimed items come first; timed items sit at their time.

\textbf{Effort}: an item with an \texttt{EFFORT} property (any \texttt{org-duration} form, see \hyperref[sec:org2e62d01]{Clocking}) shows it after its title (\texttt{⏱ 1:30}). Each day header shows the day's total (\texttt{⏱ 3:30}), with a trailing \texttt{+2?} for TODOs that have no estimate. A heading shown twice in a day counts once; an overdue task carried forward counts toward today; appointments count when they have an effort; logged entries and diary lines never do.

The \texttt{⏱} button opens a panel, the touch version of \texttt{effort-up} and \texttt{effort-down}, \texttt{org-agenda-filter-by-effort} and \texttt{org-agenda-max-effort}: \textbf{Sort} by least or most effort within each day, \textbf{Filter} to effort at most, at least or exactly a value from the \hyperref[sec:orgfca7aeb]{Effort\textsubscript{ALL}} list, \textbf{Max per day} to keep tasks while the running total stays within, say, \texttt{4:00}, and \textbf{Reset}. The rules are Org's: \textbf{at most} and \textbf{at least} are inclusive, a task with no effort counts as high effort, and the order is sort, limit, filter. These last for the session.

\subsubsection{Dated entry sources}
\label{sec:orgf08c5b9}
Five kinds of entry show up; they carry forward as in org:

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{SCHEDULED:} shows on its date and, on today as overdue ("3 days overdue") until the heading is done; a done heading shows only on its own date, and not at all with \texttt{org-agenda-skip-scheduled-if-done}. A delay suffix (\texttt{SCHEDULED: <2026-01-10 Sat -2d>}) hides it on its own date and shows it on today once the delay has passed.
\item \texttt{DEADLINE:} shows on its date, and on today when overdue or inside its warning period ("due in 3 days"). A suffix (\texttt{DEADLINE: <2026-01-10 Sat -3d>}) sets the period; otherwise it is \texttt{org-deadline-warning-days} (default 14; see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables}). Overdue and upcoming entries show on today only, and a repeating one counts from its first date. A done heading shows only on its own date; \texttt{org-agenda-skip-deadline-if-done} hides it.
\item \textbf{Plain active timestamps} anywhere in a heading's entry (title, body, property values, drawers), such as \texttt{**** Jane Doe <2000-01-01 Sat +1y>}, are listed beside its SCHEDULED or DEADLINE and never carry forward. Inactive \texttt{[...]} timestamps, comment lines, \texttt{\#+} lines and source, example, export and comment blocks are ignored. A timestamp inside \texttt{code}, \texttt{verbatim} markup or a link's text is not a reminder, so an example in your notes does not clutter the agenda or your calendar.
\item A \textbf{general sexp timestamp} \texttt{<\%\%(sexp)>} in the title follows the same rules; see \hyperref[sec:orgb6164b5]{General sexp timestamps}.
\item \texttt{org-contacts-anniversaries} reads yearly events (birthdays, anniversaries) from contact headings, as Emacs's org-contacts does: the headings of your \hyperref[sec:org4775bc5]{Contacts Files} (\texttt{org-contacts-files}), else the files you are looking at. A contact's date is a property written \texttt{YYYY-MM-DD} with an optional description:
\end{itemize}

\begin{verbatim}
* Mary Doe
:PROPERTIES:
:BIRTHDAY: 2000-01-01
:ANNIVERSARY: 2015-06-15
:SPOUSE: John Doe
:END:
\end{verbatim}

A line \texttt{\%\%(org-contacts-anniversaries FIELD FORMAT)} in any agenda file switches a scan on. \texttt{FIELD} is the property to read as a quoted string (\texttt{BIRTHDAY} by default, or \texttt{org-contacts-birthday-property}) and \texttt{FORMAT} says how each entry reads; either may be left out or \texttt{nil}. Each distinct line is its own scan: \texttt{\%\%(org-contacts-anniversaries "ANNIVERSARY" "Anniversary: \%h \& \%s (\%Y)")}.

Entries read \texttt{Birthday: John Doe (26th)}, with the age worked out for each year. In a \texttt{FORMAT}, \texttt{\%h} and \texttt{\%l} are the name, \texttt{\%y} the age, \texttt{\%Y} the age as an ordinal, \texttt{\%s} the spouse, \texttt{\%n} the name with the spouse and \texttt{\%\%} a percent sign. A year of \texttt{nil} shows as \texttt{(??)}, and text after the date replaces the label. This works with \hyperref[sec:orgdb5a142]{vCard import}: in Flat style the properties are bare dates; in Tree style they are descendant headings (\texttt{:FIELDTYPE: birthday}, \texttt{anniversary} and \texttt{spouse}).

\subsubsection{Diary-sexp forms}
\label{sec:orgf15187b}
Self-contained lines anywhere in a heading's body, with no switch line needed; they show with a 🔁 icon. \texttt{examples/diary.org} has each form with its days.

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{\%\%(org-anniversary YEAR MONTH DAY) text}: years after YEAR. In the text \texttt{\%d} is the elapsed years and \texttt{\%s} its ordinal suffix: \texttt{\%\%(org-anniversary 2001 6 12) \%d\%s wedding anniversary} shows "25th wedding anniversary" in 2026. February 29 counts as March 1 in non-leap years.
\item \texttt{\%\%(org-cyclic N YEAR MONTH DAY) text}: every N days from that date.
\item \texttt{\%\%(diary-float MONTH DAYNAME N [DAY] [MARK]) text}: the Nth weekday of a month. MONTH is 1 to 12, a list like \texttt{(1 4 7 10)}, or \texttt{t} for every month; DAYNAME is 0 (Sunday) to 6; a negative N counts from the end. \texttt{\%\%(diary-float 11 4 4) Thanksgiving} is the 4th Thursday of November. DAY moves where scanning starts, as in Emacs.
\item \texttt{\%\%(org-block Y1 M1 D1 Y2 M2 D2) text}: every day from the first date to the second, inclusive; a range written end date first matches nothing, as in Emacs.
\item Lines built from \texttt{and}, \texttt{or}, \texttt{not}, \texttt{when}, \texttt{if}, \texttt{cond}, \texttt{let}, \texttt{org-class} or \texttt{org-date} use the evaluator under \hyperref[sec:orgb6164b5]{General sexp timestamps}. The text after the closing parenthesis is the entry, and a string result replaces it.
\item \texttt{\%\%(org-weather)} shows current conditions and today's forecast from \href{https://open-meteo.com/}{Open-Meteo} (free, no key) for \texttt{calendar-latitude} and \texttt{calendar-longitude} (Settings → Weather says when they are not set): one entry, on today only, from the last-fetched snapshot.
\end{itemize}

\texttt{org-weather-format} (default \texttt{"Weather: \%desc, \%tcur(\%tmin-\%tmax)\%tu, \%p\%pu, \%h\%hu, \%s\%su, \%a\%au"}) controls the text:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Placeholder & Meaning\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{\%desc}, \texttt{\%icon}, \texttt{\%main} & Description, emoji and weather group (\texttt{Clear}, \texttt{Clouds}, \texttt{Fog}, \texttt{Drizzle}, \texttt{Rain}, \texttt{Snow} or \texttt{Thunderstorm}) for the current weather\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%tmorn}, \texttt{\%tday}, \texttt{\%teve}, \texttt{\%tnight} & Today's temperature at 6:00, 12:00, 18:00 and 0:00\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%tcur}, \texttt{\%tmin}, \texttt{\%tmax}, \texttt{\%tamin}, \texttt{\%tamax} & Current, low and high temperature, and the "feels like" low and high\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%tu}, \texttt{\%hu}, \texttt{\%pu}, \texttt{\%su}, \texttt{\%au} & Units: temperature (\texttt{org-weather-temperature-unit}), humidity, pressure (\texttt{hPa}), wind (\texttt{org-weather-speed-unit}: \texttt{mph}, \texttt{km/h}, \texttt{m/s} or \texttt{Knots}), snapshot age\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%h}, \texttt{\%p}, \texttt{\%s}, \texttt{\%a} & Humidity, surface pressure, wind speed, age of the snapshot (\texttt{m}, \texttt{h} or \texttt{d})\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Settings → Weather} shows the last refresh and has \textbf{Refresh weather now}; \texttt{org-weather-refresh-interval} refreshes automatically (\texttt{never}, or every 1, 2, 4, 6, 12 or 24 hours) while \texttt{\%\%(org-weather)} is in use. A failed refresh keeps the cached data.

\texttt{diary-anniversary}, \texttt{diary-cyclic}, \texttt{diary-block} and \texttt{diary-date} read their dates in the order of \texttt{calendar-date-style} (month day year by default, \texttt{european} day month year, \texttt{iso} year month day), so \texttt{\%\%(diary-anniversary 10 31 1948) \%d years} equals \texttt{\%\%(org-anniversary 1948 10 31)}, whose dates are always year month day.

\subsubsection{Sun times}
\label{sec:org82df7fe}
Sunrise, sunset, the twilights and the day's length are computed as Emacs's \texttt{solar.el} does, to the minute, from \texttt{calendar-latitude} and \texttt{calendar-longitude} (both \texttt{nil} until set; set them in Local Variables or Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Diary}, which has \textbf{Use device location}).

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{(solar-sunrise-sunset DATE)} returns \texttt{((RISE ZONE) (SET ZONE) "H:MM")}: local times as decimal hours with the zone name, then the daylight length. A time the day doesn't have is \texttt{nil}.
