An optional second argument, the sun's height in degrees (\texttt{-6} civil, \texttt{-12} nautical, \texttt{-18} astronomical), gives dawn and dusk; the default is \texttt{-0.61}, as in Emacs.
\item \texttt{(solar-time-string TIME ZONE)} turns decimal hours into text through \texttt{calendar-time-display-form}: "6:30am (EDT)" by default, "06:30" with \texttt{(24-hours ":" minutes)} (also a checkbox in Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Diary}).
\item \texttt{(apply 'F ARGS... LIST)} calls F with the arguments followed by the items of LIST.
\end{itemize}

This entry shows today's sun times; leave out \texttt{when} and \texttt{today-p} to show them every day:

\begin{verbatim}
*** <%%(when (today-p) (let ((l (solar-sunrise-sunset date))) (format "Sun times: 🌅 %s | 🌇 %s | ⌛ %s" (apply 'solar-time-string (car l)) (apply 'solar-time-string (cadr l)) (nth 2 l))))>
\end{verbatim}

Single values: sunrise is \texttt{(apply 'solar-time-string (car (solar-sunrise-sunset date)))}, sunset the same with \texttt{cadr}, day length \texttt{(nth 2 (solar-sunrise-sunset date))}, and twilight the same with \texttt{-6}, \texttt{-12} or \texttt{-18} as the second argument. A day without the event gives \texttt{nil}; wrap the entry in \texttt{(when (car l) ...)} to leave it out.

\subsubsection{Hebrew diary functions}
\label{sec:org4664190}
Emacs's \texttt{cal-hebrew.el} functions, giving the same days and text; dates follow \texttt{calendar-date-style}.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Function & Shows\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{(diary-hebrew-birthday MONTH DAY YEAR)} & "ENTRY's Nth Hebrew birthday" on each Hebrew anniversary of the Gregorian date\\[0pt]
\texttt{(diary-hebrew-yahrzeit MONTH DAY YEAR)} & "Yahrzeit of ENTRY: Nth anniversary"; add \texttt{nil t} for a death after sunset\\[0pt]
\texttt{(diary-hebrew-omer)} & "Day N of the omer" from Passover to Shavuot\\[0pt]
\texttt{(diary-hebrew-rosh-hodesh)} & The new Hebrew month, on the days it begins\\[0pt]
\texttt{(diary-hebrew-parasha)} & The Torah portion, on Saturdays\\[0pt]
\texttt{(diary-hebrew-sabbath-candles)} & The time to light candles on Fridays: sunset less \texttt{diary-hebrew-sabbath-candles-minutes}\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsubsection{Diary file}
\label{sec:org5dda1cf}
Set \texttt{org-agenda-include-diary} to \texttt{t} (Settings → Agenda, diary and weather → \textbf{Diary}) and name your Emacs diary in \texttt{diary-file} (\texttt{github:diary}, \texttt{webdav:diary} or \texttt{local:diary}). The Agenda then shows its entries under the category \textbf{Diary}, with the day's holidays. A diary row offers \textbf{Open entry}, \textbf{Add entry on this day} and \textbf{Delete entry…}. \texttt{examples/diary.org} and its \texttt{diary} file are a working example.

A diary line starts with a date in the order of \texttt{calendar-date-style}; the rest of the line and the indented lines after it are the entry:

\begin{verbatim}
4/20/27  Switch-over to the new system
*/25     The 25th of every month
Friday   Back up files
10/24/2026
  9:30am Coffee break
  12:00pm Lunch with engineering team
&thu 4:00pm Weekly squash game
%%(diary-float 11 4 4) Thanksgiving
\end{verbatim}

\texttt{*} stands for any month, day or year, and names may be abbreviated. A time at the start of an entry (\texttt{10:00am}, \texttt{14:30}) puts it in the day's timeline. A weekday name is every week, a full date one day, and a \texttt{\&} before the date, \texttt{\%\%(…)} lines and indented continuation lines work as in Emacs.

Rows are as Emacs's Org agenda shows them: each indented line that starts with a time is its own row, and a line without a time joins the row before it; \texttt{org-xx-diary-merge-rows} \texttt{nil} gives each date and its indented lines one row. \texttt{diary-show-holidays-flag} \texttt{nil} leaves the holidays out. \texttt{diary-list-entries-hook} may name \texttt{diary-include-other-diary-files} (follow \texttt{\#include "file"} lines) and \texttt{diary-sort-entries}. \textbf{Refresh} reads the file again.

Hebrew, Islamic and Bahá'í dates: a line starting \texttt{H}, \texttt{I} or \texttt{B} before a date in that calendar (\texttt{HHeshvan 10, 5787 Anniversary}) is listed once \texttt{diary-nongregorian-listing-hook} names \texttt{diary-hebrew-list-entries}, \texttt{diary-islamic-list-entries} or \texttt{diary-bahai-list-entries}. \texttt{\%\%(diary-hebrew-date)}, \texttt{\%\%(diary-islamic-date)} and \texttt{\%\%(diary-bahai-date)} show the day's date in each calendar.

In the diary's Text view, \textbf{Insert entry} writes a date, weekly, monthly, yearly, anniversary, cyclic or block entry at the end of the file, as \texttt{diary-insert-*} does, and saves it. \textbf{Check this line} says whether the line under the cursor is an entry, by which form, and on which days it falls next. \textbf{Date…} puts a date at the cursor.

\subsubsection{Holidays}
\label{sec:orgc740e73}
The Agenda, the diary, \texttt{org-class} and \texttt{calendar-check-holidays} use Emacs's \texttt{calendar-holidays}: \texttt{holiday-general-holidays} (US), \texttt{holiday-christian-holidays}, \texttt{holiday-hebrew-holidays}, \texttt{holiday-islamic-holidays}, \texttt{holiday-bahai-holidays}, \texttt{holiday-oriental-holidays} (Chinese New Year, and with \texttt{calendar-chinese-all-holidays-flag} the other Chinese festivals) and \texttt{holiday-solar-holidays} (equinoxes, solstices, daylight saving changes), plus your own \texttt{holiday-local-holidays} and \texttt{holiday-other-holidays}. The forms are Emacs's: see \href{https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/manual/html\_node/emacs/Holidays.html}{Holidays} in the Emacs manual.

\textbf{Apropos variable…} (palette, \texttt{apropos-variable}) asks for a word, a list of words (names with at least two of them) or an Emacs regexp, and opens a read-only buffer named \texttt{*Apropos*} with a heading for each matching variable: its description, its value now and a link. Search, filter and fold work on it as on any document. Example: \texttt{\textasciicircum{}org-agenda-skip} lists the agenda skip variables.

The link is Org's \texttt{[[elisp:(customize-variable 'NAME)]]}. It opens the variable's field in Settings, highlighted; a variable that has no control on a Settings page opens Global Variables with a \texttt{(setq NAME VALUE)} line ready to add. The Settings search box searches the same list as you type. Any variable can be set from Global Variables or the Lisp init, with or without a control.

\textbf{List holidays…} (palette, \texttt{list-holidays}) asks for a first and last year and lists the holidays in a new buffer, one to a line.

Change them in Settings → Advanced → \textbf{Lisp init}; \texttt{remove} and \texttt{delete} take one entry out of a group. \texttt{examples/holidays.org} shows the default entries, every flag turned on, how to switch groups and single entries off, how to add each kind of entry, and a description link for every holiday. This switches the built-in groups off and keeps three days of your own:

\begin{verbatim}
(setq holiday-general-holidays nil
      holiday-christian-holidays nil
      holiday-hebrew-holidays nil
      holiday-islamic-holidays nil
      holiday-bahai-holidays nil
      holiday-solar-holidays nil)
(setq holiday-local-holidays
      '((holiday-fixed 3 14 "Pi Day")
        (holiday-fixed 6 19 "Juneteenth")
        (holiday-easter-etc 1 "Easter Monday")))
\end{verbatim}

\textbf{Shorter and longer lists}: each of the Christian, Hebrew, Islamic and Bahá'í groups has a short list of widely observed days; \texttt{calendar-christian-all-holidays-flag}, \texttt{calendar-hebrew-all-holidays-flag}, \texttt{calendar-islamic-all-holidays-flag} or \texttt{calendar-bahai-all-holidays-flag} \texttt{t} adds the rest.

\textbf{Sharing}: \texttt{(load "github:org/holidays.el")} reads that file in place of the line, so one file can serve every device (written like an agenda file; a file can load others). The last copy read is kept on the device, and the Agenda's refresh reads the files again.

Each entry is Lisp, evaluated for the month shown, so \texttt{if}, \texttt{let}, \texttt{mapcar} and your own \texttt{defun} work. The functions are Emacs's: \texttt{holiday-fixed}, \texttt{holiday-float}, \texttt{holiday-easter-etc}, \texttt{holiday-greek-orthodox-easter}, \texttt{holiday-advent}, \texttt{holiday-julian}, \texttt{holiday-hebrew}, \texttt{holiday-islamic}, \texttt{holiday-bahai}, \texttt{holiday-chinese}, \texttt{holiday-sexp}, the named \texttt{holiday-hebrew-passover} family, \texttt{holiday-islamic-new-year}, \texttt{holiday-bahai-new-year} and \texttt{solar-equinoxes-solstices}, and the \texttt{calendar-*} date functions also work in diary sexps. An entry that fails is skipped and shows as \emph{Holiday list error: ..} on the first of the month. Solar holidays use this device's time zone and \texttt{calendar-latitude}.

\subsubsection{General \texttt{<\%\%(sexp)>} timestamps}
\label{sec:orgb6164b5}
A \texttt{<\%\%(expression)>} goes where a plain timestamp would, in a heading's title. The expression is evaluated for each day shown, and every day it is non-nil is an occurrence. It is a matcher, not a repeater: marking the heading DONE has no effect. It is skipped when the heading has SCHEDULED or DEADLINE, and never carries forward.

\begin{verbatim}
* Weekly Sync <%%(when (org-cyclic 7 2026 8 9) "Weekly sync")>
* TODO Team Sync <%%(diary-float t 6 1)>
\end{verbatim}

The expression is Emacs Lisp (\texttt{setq}, \texttt{defun}, \texttt{lambda}, \texttt{let}, loops, lists, strings, regexps, \texttt{condition-case}, \texttt{format}). Each day is evaluated on its own with \texttt{date} set to that day (as \texttt{(month day year)}) and \texttt{entry} the text of the line.

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{when}, \texttt{and}, \texttt{or}, \texttt{not}, \texttt{let}, \texttt{let*}, \texttt{if}, \texttt{unless}, \texttt{cond}, \texttt{progn}; arithmetic, comparisons, \texttt{zerop}, \texttt{equal}, \texttt{list}, \texttt{car}, \texttt{cdr}, \texttt{cadr}, \texttt{nth}, \texttt{length}, \texttt{memq}, \texttt{member}, \texttt{min}, \texttt{max}, \texttt{abs}. \texttt{and} yields its last value, so a string survives.
\item Calendar: \texttt{calendar-day-of-week} (0 is Sunday), \texttt{calendar-last-day-of-month}, \texttt{calendar-leap-year-p}, \texttt{calendar-extract-month} (and \texttt{-day}, \texttt{-year}), \texttt{calendar-current-date}, \texttt{calendar-absolute-from-gregorian} and \texttt{calendar-gregorian-from-absolute}. A day count makes "N days until" rules easy: \texttt{<\%\%(let ((n (- (calendar-absolute-from-gregorian '(12 25 2026)) (calendar-absolute-from-gregorian date)))) (and (>= n 0) (<= n 30) (format "\%d days until Christmas" n)))>}.
\item \texttt{(diary-remind SEXP DAYS)} shows the entry on the day SEXP matches and "Reminder: Only 3 days until \ldots{}" on the DAYS before it (a number, a list like \texttt{'(1 3 7)}, or a negative number for every day up to it). \texttt{(diary-offset SEXP DAYS)} matches DAYS days after SEXP; \texttt{(diary-ordinal-suffix N)} gives \texttt{st}, \texttt{nd}, \texttt{rd} or \texttt{th}; \texttt{(calendar-nth-named-day N DAYNAME MONTH YEAR [DAY])} gives a date.
\item \texttt{(today-p)} is shorthand for \texttt{(equal date (calendar-current-date))}.
\item \texttt{(org-block Y M D Y M D)}; \texttt{(org-date Y M D)} takes an integer, a list or \texttt{t} per field (\texttt{(org-date t '(10 11 12) 22)} is the 22nd of October, November and December); \texttt{(org-class Y1 M1 D1 Y2 M2 D2 DAYNAME [SKIP-WEEK...])} is DAYNAME every week between the dates, skipping the listed ISO weeks. Add \texttt{'holidays} to the list to skip holidays too: \texttt{<\%\%(org-class 2026 9 1 2026 12 15 1 'holidays)> Class meets}. \texttt{(calendar-check-holidays date)} gives a day's holiday names.
\item Day descriptions, worded as Emacs words them: \texttt{(diary-day-of-year)}, \texttt{(diary-iso-date)}, \texttt{(diary-julian-date)}, \texttt{(diary-hebrew-date)}, \texttt{(diary-islamic-date)}, \texttt{(diary-bahai-date)}, \texttt{(diary-chinese-date)}, \texttt{(diary-astro-day-number)}, \texttt{(diary-lunar-phases)} (on the days of a quarter, in this device's time zone) and \texttt{(diary-sunrise-sunset)} (the place is \texttt{calendar-location-name} when it is a string). \texttt{(diary-entry-time "9:30am x")} gives 930, or -9999 with no time.
\item \texttt{(org-cyclic ...)}, \texttt{(org-anniversary ...)}, \texttt{(diary-float ...)}, \texttt{(solar-sunrise-sunset)}, \texttt{(solar-time-string)}, \texttt{(apply)} and \texttt{(org-weather)} work as sub-expressions; a string result becomes the displayed text, and a title that is only the timestamp shows it exactly. The \texttt{diary-hebrew-*} functions are in \hyperref[sec:org4664190]{Hebrew diary functions}.
\item \texttt{(format FORMAT-STRING ARG...)} takes \texttt{\%s}, \texttt{\%S}, \texttt{\%d}, \texttt{\%o}, \texttt{\%x}, \texttt{\%X}, \texttt{\%c}, \texttt{\%e}, \texttt{\%f}, \texttt{\%g} and \texttt{\%\%} with flags, a width and a precision (\texttt{\%02d}, \texttt{\%-5s}, \texttt{\%5.2f}); extra arguments are ignored and too few signal Emacs's \emph{Not enough arguments for format string} error.
\item A program that fails shows Emacs's message in the agenda in place of the entry, once for the sexp (\texttt{Symbol’s function definition is void: no-such-function}). A program that loops forever or nests too deeply (\texttt{max-lisp-eval-depth}) stops with a message; \texttt{condition-case} cannot catch that stop. A bare value, such as a number, is a match.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Other agenda behavior}
\label{sec:org60e5da7}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Completed items are excluded}, using the done keywords of the file's own \texttt{\#+TODO:} sequence.
\item \textbf{Repeating timestamps expand} for SCHEDULED, DEADLINE and title timestamps (\texttt{<2000-01-01 Sat +1y>} shows every year in the range). A repeating SCHEDULED or DEADLINE shows only on its repeat dates.
\item \textbf{Marking a repeating task done shifts it}: its date moves forward, \texttt{LAST\_REPEAT} is stamped, and the state returns to the first keyword (or \texttt{REPEAT\_TO\_STATE}). \texttt{+N} adds one interval to the previous date, even if still in the past; \texttt{++N} adds intervals until the date is later than now, keeping weekday and time; \texttt{.+N} counts from today. Every repeating timestamp in the entry moves, \texttt{CLOSED} is removed, and the completion is logged as \texttt{org-log-repeat} says.
\item \textbf{Archived and commented headings are excluded} (a commented heading starts with \texttt{COMMENT}), by \texttt{org-agenda-skip-archived-trees} and \texttt{org-agenda-skip-comment-trees}.
\end{itemize}

A trailing tag needs a space before it (\texttt{<2000-01-01 Sat +1y> :BDAY:}), as in Org.

\subsubsection{Habits}
\label{sec:org5c8d2b4}
A habit is an open TODO with \texttt{:STYLE: habit} and a repeating SCHEDULED date, as in Emacs's \texttt{org-habit}. The agenda row gets a strip of days: 21 before today, today (outlined, \texttt{!}) and 6 after, 28 in all. Blue: not yet due. Green: can be done. Yellow: last chance. Red: overdue. A \texttt{*} is a day it was done.

\begin{verbatim}
* TODO Shave
SCHEDULED: <2026-10-13 Tue .+2d/4d>
:PROPERTIES:
:STYLE: habit
:END:
\end{verbatim}

\texttt{.+2d/4d} means every 2 days, no later than every 4. Set the second number under Details > Dates > "No later than". Marking the habit done records a \texttt{State "DONE"} line in its \texttt{:LOGBOOK:}; the strip is drawn from those lines. A habit shows in today's agenda once it is due. Settings > Agenda has \texttt{org-habit-preceding-days}, \texttt{org-habit-following-days}, \texttt{org-habit-show-habits-only-for-today} and \texttt{org-habit-show-all-today}. The ⏱ panel hides habits for the session.

\texttt{examples/habits.org} shows strips with Emacs's colors.

Tap a habit's strip for its history: how many times in a row it was done on time (each no later than the last-chance day after the one before), the best run, the last 12 weeks as a grid, and the latest completions. Details > Props has a \textbf{Habit} switch that sets \texttt{STYLE: habit}.

\subsubsection{Agenda Files}
\label{sec:orgffa4011}
Add files in \textbf{Settings → Advanced → Advanced (raw syntax) → Agenda files}, or in a document's own \texttt{\# Local Variables:} block to override that for the one file (see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables}). The value is a list of file names, as in Emacs, each starting with \texttt{github:}, \texttt{webdav:} or \texttt{local:}: \texttt{("github:journal.org" "webdav:notes/todo.org")}, with or without the leading quote. The Agenda and TODO views then scan all of them. \texttt{github} and \texttt{webdav} files are fetched; \texttt{local:name.org} reads a file on this device: one you have opened with \textbf{File → Open → Local file} or, in the \hyperref[sec:orgd336588]{Android app}, one in the org-pwa folder. An entry with another prefix is skipped, and a value that is not a list is reported. If the open file is in the list, its live in-memory version is used.

The Agenda, TODO list, Match, Search and the calendar read these files only, as in Emacs: the file you have open counts when it is one of them. To look at one file or subtree instead, use \textbf{<} in \textbf{Agenda commands} (pressed again: the subtree you are on, then nothing; \texttt{C-c a <} starts it), or lock every agenda command with \texttt{C-c C-x <} and lift the lock with \texttt{C-c C-x >}. A line under the title says what the view is restricted to. With no agenda files, the views say so.

Files are fetched once per session; a \textbf{↻} button in the agenda controls refetches them, and a file that fails to load is reported above the list. A local file feeds the Agenda, TODO, Search and Export, and loads only if the browser already allows access; otherwise the agenda says it "needs permission" and \textbf{↻} asks. In a browser it is read-only here; in the \hyperref[sec:orgd336588]{Android app}, Refile and Replace also write into it. Export's \textbf{This file + Agenda Files} scope always fetches fresh. Two entries with the same file name (\texttt{github:notes.org} and \texttt{local:notes.org}) can't both be used; the agenda names the one it skipped.

\subsubsection{Contacts Files}
\label{sec:org4775bc5}
Set in \textbf{Settings → Advanced → Advanced (raw syntax) → Contacts files}, or per document in Local Variables, exactly like \hyperref[sec:orgffa4011]{Agenda Files} (real org-contacts' \texttt{org-contacts-files}; \texttt{github}, \texttt{webdav} and \texttt{local}). \hyperref[sec:org8e45f5f]{Contacts (.vcf)} export's \textbf{This file + Contacts Files} scope scans them. The list is independent of Agenda Files, because the two commonly differ.

\subsubsection{Calendar and contacts sync (CalDAV, CardDAV)}
\label{sec:orgac99be7}
Mirror your agenda files into a calendar on your own server, so its items appear, with alarms, in your phone's calendar app. Create a calendar on the server first (a Radicale or Nextcloud calendar), then set it in \textbf{Settings → Calendar (CalDAV) / Contacts (CardDAV)}: the calendar's address, and a username and password (blank means the WebDAV ones). Leave the address blank to turn it off.

Only your agenda files (\texttt{org-agenda-files}) go to the calendar, as in Emacs; a file you merely have open does not. It is one-way: the calendar follows them, and edits made in a calendar app are overwritten, so give it a calendar of its own. The app removes only events it created: those of a file that is no longer an agenda file go on the next sync, while those of an agenda file that failed to load stay until it loads.

What goes in is what \textbf{View → Agenda} shows from your \hyperref[sec:orgffa4011]{Agenda Files}: SCHEDULED, DEADLINE, plain timestamps, diary entries, and birthdays and anniversaries from your Contacts Files. Each event has its title, start and end, the heading's tags as categories, its \texttt{:LOCATION:}, the first 400 characters of its body, and a deadline's warning delay (\texttt{-3d}) as an alarm. Every event with a time of day also gets an alarm \texttt{appt-message-warning-time} minutes before it. A repeating item is one event with a repeat rule; a birthday is one event for each year in the window, with that year's age. Completed items and the agenda's overdue and warning entries are not sent. Items run from a month back to six months ahead.

A \texttt{<\%\%(…)>} timestamp in a heading title becomes one all-day event for each day it matches; \texttt{<\%\%(when (today-p) (org-weather))>} is a single event for today, updated whenever the weather refreshes. Script-defined functions are asked first (see \hyperref[sec:orgaf1b952]{Extensions}). Plain \texttt{\%\%(org-weather)} and sun-time lines in a body are Agenda-only.

It syncs after a save, when you return to the app, and at launch. \textbf{Sync} in Settings does it now, and \textbf{Rebuild calendar} removes the app's events and sends them all again. After a wrong address or password, automatic syncing stops until you change the settings or sync by hand.

\textbf{Contacts} work the same way: create an address book on the server and set its address as the \textbf{Contacts address} (same username and password; either address can be blank). Your \hyperref[sec:org4775bc5]{Contacts Files} are mirrored into it, one vCard per contact, in Flat or Tree style. \textbf{Sync} does both and says how each went; \textbf{Rebuild contacts} sends them all again; \textbf{Sync agenda to calendar} and \textbf{Sync contacts to the address book} do one each.

Example addresses: \texttt{https://dav.example.com/radicale/me/calendar/} and \texttt{.../me/contacts/}. As with WebDAV, the server must allow CORS requests, including \texttt{PUT}, \texttt{DELETE} and \texttt{PROPFIND} with the \texttt{Authorization}, \texttt{Content-Type} and \texttt{Depth} headers.

\subsubsection{Agenda notifications}
\label{sec:org3415eb2}
Get a reminder shortly before an appointment, as Emacs's \texttt{appt} does. Turn it on in \textbf{Settings → Agenda notifications}; the settings use Emacs's names and belong to this device.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Agenda notifications} (\texttt{appt-activate}): on or off.
\item \textbf{Warn this many minutes before} (\texttt{appt-message-warning-time}): 12 by default, as in Emacs, adjustable in 1-minute steps.
\item \textbf{Remind again every} (\texttt{appt-display-interval}): 3 minutes by default. Once an appointment is within its warning time, it is announced again at this interval, as in Emacs: 10 minutes warned every 3 reads 10, 7, 4 and 1. A warning time that is a multiple of the interval also ends with a reminder at the start.
\item \textbf{Scan agenda files every} (\texttt{appt-agenda-scan-interval}): 5 minutes by default. The app also looks again at launch, when you return to it, and after a save.
\item \textbf{Countdown in the mode line} (\texttt{appt-display-mode-line}): shows \texttt{Appt: 10m} while an appointment is inside its warning time.
\item \textbf{Show reminders as} (\texttt{appt-display-format}): \textbf{window} is a system notification plus a banner in the app; \textbf{echo} is the status line only.
\end{itemize}

An appointment is an item with a time of day, from your \hyperref[sec:orgffa4011]{Agenda Files}: SCHEDULED, DEADLINE or a plain timestamp, repeats included. A reminder is titled by the appointment with the time left below (\texttt{Dentist}, \texttt{in 10 min · 09:30–10:15}), then the start of its body. The banner stays until you tap \textbf{Open day} or \textbf{Dismiss}; the next reminder replaces it, and tapping one opens that day in the Agenda.

The first time, tap \textbf{Allow notifications}; if blocked, reminders still show in the app. In the browser they appear while the app is open; in the \hyperref[sec:orgd336588]{Android app} they are scheduled with the system and arrive when it is closed (allow \textbf{Exact timing} to keep them on the minute).

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{The TODO view}
\label{sec:org809ff20}
Tap \textbf{View → TODO} for every active TODO-state heading in the file, whatever its dates (org's \texttt{C-c a t}). A TODO with no date never shows in the Agenda, so this is where it lives.

It is a flat list in document order showing each item's keyword, title, category and SCHEDULED or DEADLINE date (overdue in red). The filter chips work as in the Agenda, and \textbf{Sort} cycles document order, date order (undated last), least effort and most effort. Tap an item to jump to it; press and hold or swipe as in the \hyperref[sec:org8b51351]{Agenda}. The Agenda's exclusions apply (completed, archived and commented headings).

\textbf{Clock report}: a checkbox beside \textbf{Clock} shows \texttt{org-clock-report} read-only instead of writing a \texttt{clocktable} block into the document. It asks for a start and end date (the last 7 days at first) and a \textbf{Parameters} field that takes the clocktable parameters of Org (\texttt{:scope}, \texttt{:block}, \texttt{:maxlevel}, \texttt{:tags}, \texttt{:step}, \texttt{:narrow}, \texttt{:formula}, \texttt{:link}, \texttt{:compact}, \texttt{:properties} and the rest); \texttt{:maxlevel} is 2 at first. The table is Org's: a time column per level, a total first, rows that include their descendants, titles cut at 40 characters. Headings with no clocked time are omitted and a running clock is excluded. \textbf{Copy} gives dynamic-block syntax to paste into a file.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Capture Templates}
\label{sec:orgab0be70}
The palette's \textbf{Capture} command (or \texttt{C-c c}) opens the templates of \texttt{org-capture-templates}: file a note, task or table row at a set place without navigating there. Tap a template; if it has \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}\{Prompt\}} or \texttt{\%?} fields, a form asks for each, with a live preview of the result. A template with no prompts captures at once.

Templates are set in the Lisp init (\texttt{org-xx-lisp-init}), exactly as in Emacs: \texttt{(setq org-capture-templates '(…))} and \texttt{(add-to-list 'org-capture-templates '(…))}, also when they are in a file the init loads with \texttt{(load …)}. With none, the Capture list says so. Examples with Emacs's results: \texttt{examples/capture-templates.org}, \texttt{examples/capture-datetree.org}.

\begin{verbatim}
(add-to-list 'org-capture-templates
  '("b" "Bullet List" item (file+olp "notes.org" "Lists" "Shopping")
    "%?" :empty-lines 1))
\end{verbatim}

In Text view the list has \textbf{Insert at the cursor} (\texttt{C-0 C-c c}): the capture goes in at the cursor instead of at the target; an entry gets the level of the heading above it.

If a capture fails (network error, sync conflict) the form keeps your text. Every template is also a palette command, \textbf{Capture: <description>}, and the Extras menu (see \hyperref[sec:org17e454c]{Extras Menu}) can jump to one by key. A capture into the open file scrolls to the new row, item or heading. A capture into a different file goes into that file's buffer, as in Emacs: a background tab, modified until you save it (see \hyperref[sec:org8402fde]{File management}). A template or keyword the app cannot use is named in a message when the Capture list opens, and so is an error in the Lisp init. A template of a type other than \texttt{entry}, \texttt{item}, \texttt{checkitem}, \texttt{table-line} or \texttt{plain} is refused with a message naming the type, so the text is not lost (Emacs files nothing).

\textbf{A template} is \texttt{("key" "description" type target "text" keyword value …)}:

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{key}: must be unique. It is the hotkey in a god-mode picker and shows beside the description on the capture form.
\item \texttt{type}: \texttt{item} (a bullet), \texttt{checkitem} (a bullet too: Org 9.6 inserts no box), \texttt{plain} (the text as it is, headings included, put where point would be), \texttt{entry} (a heading; its level follows the target, and so do the sub-headings of the text) or \texttt{table-line} (a row added to the first table under the target; with none, a new table starts with an empty header row and a rule, as in Emacs).
\item target, where the text goes: \texttt{(file "f")} the top level of a file; \texttt{(file+headline "f" "H")} and \texttt{(file+olp "f" "H1" "H2")} the outline path. \texttt{file+headline} makes its heading when the file lacks it; \texttt{file+olp} stops with \texttt{Heading not found on level N: NAME}, as Emacs does.
\item \texttt{(file+regexp "f" "REGEXP")} goes where the first match of an Emacs regular expression ends (where it starts, with \texttt{:prepend}): under the heading when the match is on a heading line, otherwise as for a target function that leaves point there. \texttt{(id "ID")} is the entry with that \texttt{:ID:} (in this file, an open tab, an agenda file, or the file it was last seen in), and \texttt{(clock)} the entry with the running clock; the capture goes under it as for \texttt{file+headline}. With none of them, Emacs's message is shown and nothing is filed.
\item The file \texttt{"f"} may be \texttt{""} for the open file. A bare name is a sibling of the open file, a path containing \texttt{/} is used as is, and a \texttt{github:}, \texttt{webdav:} or \texttt{local:} prefix names the backend (one that doesn't match the open document's is refused). GitHub and WebDAV targets work directly; a local or iOS-imported target must have been opened or saved once, except in the \hyperref[sec:orgd336588]{Android app}, where a file in the org-pwa folder works and is created if missing.
\item \texttt{(file+olp+datetree "f" "H" …)} files under today's date. After the headings (which may be none, for the top of the file), the year, month and day headings (\texttt{2026}, \texttt{2026-11 November}, \texttt{2026-11-07 Saturday}) are found or created in date order, and the capture goes into the day. \texttt{:tree-type week} files under the year, the ISO week (\texttt{2026-W45}) and the day; \texttt{:tree-type month} files directly under the month. \texttt{file+datetree} and \texttt{file+weektree} work too.
\item \texttt{:jump-to-captured t}: after filing, go to the new text: the headings above it open and the view scrolls to it, a table row included. For a template that files into another file, that file's buffer is shown. Without it the screen stays where it was, as in Emacs.
\item \texttt{:immediate-finish t}: file without offering the text to edit. The \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}\{…\}} questions are still asked; \texttt{\%?} is not, so a template with no question is filed at once.
\item \texttt{:time-prompt t} (\texttt{file+olp+datetree} only): the form asks for a date and time first, and the capture is filed for them: the day in the tree, \texttt{\%U}, \texttt{\%<…>}. It takes \texttt{2026-12-01 9:05}, a date alone (00:00 of that day, or the time of day if it is today), \texttt{+2d}, \texttt{-1w}, \texttt{+1m}, \texttt{+1y} or a weekday name (the next one); empty is now.
\item \texttt{:clock-in t}: clock in the new entry (for \texttt{item}, \texttt{checkitem}, \texttt{plain} and \texttt{table-line}, the heading it went under); a running clock is stopped first. \texttt{:clock-keep t} leaves the new clock running; otherwise it is stopped again at once, as when you finish a capture buffer in Emacs. \texttt{:clock-resume t} then starts the clock that was interrupted. \texttt{:clock-keep} wins over \texttt{:clock-resume}.
\item \texttt{:after-finalize FN}: a function, a \texttt{(lambda () …)} or a list of them, run once the entry is filed, in a buffer with no text (the capture buffer is gone, as in Emacs); an error is shown and the entry stays filed.
\item \texttt{:prepare-finalize FN} and \texttt{:before-finalize FN}: a function, a \texttt{(lambda () …)} or a list of them, run on the text of the capture once every \texttt{\%} escape and prompt is filled in, with point at its start; what is in the buffer afterwards is filed. \texttt{:before-finalize} runs after \texttt{:prepare-finalize}.
\item \texttt{:prepend t}: put the new entry at the top instead of the bottom. A new list item goes before the first item, and a new table row goes right after the header row and rule. For \texttt{item}, \texttt{checkitem} and \texttt{plain} it also puts any auto-created heading of the path first among its siblings.
\item \texttt{:empty-lines N}, \texttt{:empty-lines-before N}, \texttt{:empty-lines-after N} (default 0): the blank lines left before and after the new text. The blank lines around the place it goes are replaced by that many. A new item in a list changes only the separation of items, by at most one line; a table row ignores them.
\item \texttt{:table-line-pos "I+1"} (\texttt{table-line} only): where the row goes: \texttt{"I+1"} is the line after the first rule, \texttt{"II-1"} the line before the second.
\end{itemize}

A target can also be a function: \texttt{(file+function "f" FN)} or \texttt{(function FN)} runs FN, a name or a \texttt{(lambda () …)}, in a text buffer that holds the file, with point at its start; it may insert whole lines (a year heading, a table with its \texttt{\#+TBLFM}) and leaves point where the capture goes. With point on a heading an entry is filed as its last child (its first with \texttt{:prepend}), and an item or a table row in its text. Off a heading an entry goes to the top level of the file, and an item or a row is looked for from point to the end of that text; plain text goes where point is. \texttt{:prepare-finalize} takes a function, a lambda or a list of them, and runs them on the text of the capture once every \texttt{\%} escape and prompt is filled in, with point at its start; what is in the buffer afterwards is filed (see \emph{Text buffers} in the list of Lisp functions). A target function or \texttt{:prepare-finalize} function can read the template with \texttt{(org-capture-get :prepend)} (also \texttt{:key}, \texttt{:description}, \texttt{:type}, \texttt{:template} and any other keyword the template gives) and change it with \texttt{org-capture-put}, for example to make a new month heading first or last as \texttt{:prepend} says. An error in a function shows Emacs's message and files nothing. Templates that use a function call \texttt{(format-time-string "\%Y")} for the moment of the capture.

\textbf{Template text, the \%-escape language} (local time):

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{\%<FORMAT>} is \texttt{format-time-string} in full. The examples use Wednesday, March 5, 2025, 14:30:07 (Eastern time, so \texttt{\%z} is \texttt{-0500}):
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
Specifier & Meaning & Example output\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{\%a} \texttt{\%A} & Weekday name, short and full & \texttt{Wed} \texttt{Wednesday}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%b} \texttt{\%h} \texttt{\%B} & Month name, short and full & \texttt{Mar} \texttt{March}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%c} & Date and time as Emacs's default locale prints it & \texttt{Wed Mar  5 14:30:07 2025}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%C} & Century & \texttt{20}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%d} \texttt{\%e} & Day of month, zero-padded and space-padded & \texttt{05} \texttt{␣5}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%D} \texttt{\%x} & \texttt{\%m/\%d/\%y} & \texttt{03/05/25}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%F} & \texttt{\%Y-\%m-\%d} & \texttt{2025-03-05}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%g} \texttt{\%G} & ISO week-numbering year, two and four digits & \texttt{25} \texttt{2025}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%H} \texttt{\%k} & Hour 00–23, zero-padded and space-padded & \texttt{14} \texttt{14}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%I} \texttt{\%l} & Hour 01–12, zero-padded and space-padded & \texttt{02} \texttt{␣2}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%j} & Day of the year (001–366) & \texttt{064}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%m} & Month (01–12) & \texttt{03}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%M} \texttt{\%S} & Minute, second & \texttt{30} \texttt{07}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%n} \texttt{\%t} & Newline, tab & \\[0pt]
\texttt{\%N} & Nanoseconds; \texttt{\%3N} is milliseconds, \texttt{\%6N} microseconds & \texttt{000000000}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%p} \texttt{\%P} & \texttt{AM} or \texttt{PM}; \texttt{am} or \texttt{pm} & \texttt{PM} \texttt{pm}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%q} & Quarter of the year & \texttt{1}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%r} & \texttt{\%I:\%M:\%S \%p} & \texttt{02:30:07 PM}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%R} \texttt{\%T} \texttt{\%X} & \texttt{\%H:\%M}, \texttt{\%H:\%M:\%S} & \texttt{14:30} \texttt{14:30:07}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%s} & Seconds since 1970 & \texttt{1741203007}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%u} \texttt{\%w} & Weekday number, Monday is 1; Sunday is 0 & \texttt{3} \texttt{3}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%U} \texttt{\%W} \texttt{\%V} & Week of the year, Sunday first; Monday first; ISO & \texttt{09} \texttt{09} \texttt{10}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%y} \texttt{\%Y} & Year, two and four digits & \texttt{25} \texttt{2025}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%z} \texttt{\%:z} \texttt{\%::z} \texttt{\%:::z} & UTC offset: \texttt{-0500}, \texttt{-05:00}, \texttt{-05:00:00}, \texttt{-05} & \texttt{-0500}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%Z} & Time zone abbreviation; device-dependent & \texttt{EST}\\[0pt]
\texttt{\%\%} & A percent sign (inside \texttt{\%<...>} only) & \texttt{\%}\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Between \texttt{\%} and the letter go the flags \texttt{-} (no padding), \texttt{\_} (spaces), \texttt{0} (zeros), \texttt{\textasciicircum{}} (upper case) and \texttt{\#} (the other case), then a width: \texttt{\%-d} is \texttt{5}, \texttt{\%\_5H} is \texttt{␣␣␣14}, \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}a} is \texttt{WED}. Names are English, and text that is not a conversion stays as written. \texttt{\%Z} comes from the browser (\texttt{GMT+1} where Emacs writes \texttt{CET}).

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{\%t}, \texttt{\%T}: an active timestamp, date only or date and time. \texttt{\%u}, \texttt{\%U}: the same, inactive (\texttt{[...]} instead of \texttt{<...>}).
\item \texttt{\%i} is content shared in from another app (see \hyperref[sec:orgaef253e]{Capturing from other apps}), and \texttt{\%a} is a link to the shared page, \texttt{[[url][title]]}. Text before \texttt{\%i} on its line is added before every later line, so a \texttt{\%i} that follows indentation keeps every line indented. A shared line that would start a heading or a \texttt{\#+} line gets a leading comma, so shared text can never change the document's structure, and only web and mail addresses become links. Both are empty when nothing was shared.
\item \texttt{\%A} is the link with a prompt for its description, \texttt{\%l} the link without a description, \texttt{\%L} the bare address. \texttt{\%:link}, \texttt{\%:description} and \texttt{\%:type} are parts of the shared link.
\item \texttt{\%x} and \texttt{\%c} are the clipboard. It is read only for a template that uses it (\texttt{\%x}, \texttt{\%c}, \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}C} or \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}L}), the browser may ask permission (iOS shows a Paste confirmation), and a refusal leaves it empty while the capture still goes ahead.
\item \texttt{\%n} is the value of \texttt{user-full-name} from the global variables (empty when unset). \texttt{\%k} is the heading of the running clock and \texttt{\%K} a link to it, \texttt{[[file::*heading][heading]]}. \texttt{\%f} and \texttt{\%F} are the open file's name and full path.
\item \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}\{Prompt\}} asks a question on the in-app form. \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}\{Prompt|default\}} pre-fills an answer, and \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}\{Prompt|default|choice1|choice2\}} also lists the choices as a hint under the field (there is no dropdown). An empty answer is the default. Several prompts share one form, and cancelling discards the whole capture.
\item \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}\{Name\}p} asks for a value and sets the property \texttt{Name} on the entry the placeholder is in (the text of the placeholder is removed); \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}\{Name|default\}p} pre-fills it. Where there is no heading in the template the properties drawer is put at its start.
\item \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}g} and \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}G} ask for tags, written as \texttt{work:home}, and insert \texttt{:work:home:}. On a heading line the tags are placed where \texttt{org-tags-column} says.
\item \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}C} asks for a clipboard value (pre-filled with the shared text, when there is any) and inserts it; \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}L} inserts it as \texttt{[[value]]}.
\item \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}t}, \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}T}, \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}u}, \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}U} (and \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}\{Prompt\}t} and the other letters, to name the field) are interactive timestamps: active date (\texttt{<2026-09-22 Tue>}), active date and time, inactive date (\texttt{[2026-09-22 Tue]}), inactive date and time. Active timestamps show in the \hyperref[sec:org8b51351]{Agenda}; inactive ones don't. Each is a text field with a \textbf{📅 Pick date} (or \textbf{📅 Pick date \& time}) button. In the popup, \textbf{OK} writes the timestamp into the field, where it stays editable, and \textbf{Cancel} leaves the field as it was. The date \& time popup also has an \textbf{End time}, which follows the start by 30 minutes until you change it (\textbf{No end} removes it) and writes a range such as \texttt{<2026-09-22 Tue 09:00-10:30>}: an appointment with a start and an end, exported with both. A date typed into the field (\texttt{2026-09-22} or \texttt{2026-09-22 14:30}) becomes a timestamp; \texttt{T} and \texttt{U} add the current time when none is given, and an empty field is now.
\item \texttt{\%\textbackslash{}N} (\texttt{\%\textbackslash{}1}, \texttt{\%\textbackslash{}2}, \ldots{}) re-inserts the answer already given to the Nth \texttt{\%\textasciicircum{}\{Prompt\}} (1-based) instead of asking again; tag, clipboard, timestamp and \texttt{\%?} prompts are not counted. A number past the last prompt is an error and the capture does not run. In a Lisp string the backslash is doubled: \texttt{"\%\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}1"}.
\item A backslash before \texttt{\%} escapes it: \texttt{\textbackslash{}\%t} stays \texttt{\%t}. With several backslashes, half of them (rounded up) are removed and the \texttt{\%} is literal when their number is odd, so \texttt{\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}\%t} is a backslash and a timestamp.
\item \texttt{@\#} is the table-formula row number, for \texttt{table-line} captures only (empty otherwise). It takes an offset, \texttt{@\# + n} or \texttt{@\# - n}, with n a non-negative integer.
\item \texttt{\%?} is org's cursor marker, treated as one more prompt: labeled "Text", asked on the form, and focused with the keyboard up when it is the first or only field.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Worked example}, \textbf{Tracking}, logs a value with its date and time into a monthly table and plots it. A target function finds or makes the month's heading, its table with the plot line and the formulas, and leaves point on the heading; \texttt{:jump-to-captured t} then shows the new row:

\begin{verbatim}
(add-to-list 'org-capture-templates
  '("t" "Tracking" table-line (file+function "github:home.org" my-tracking-target)
    "| | %<%Y-%m-%d> | %<%H%M> ||" :jump-to-captured t))
\end{verbatim}

The row has a trailing \texttt{||} that leaves the 4th cell to the table's formula, and the first cell is numbered by \texttt{\$1=@\#-1}. \texttt{examples/capture-templates.org} has the function (\texttt{my-tracking-target}), the formulas and the file as Emacs files it.

\textbf{Worked example}, \textbf{Journal}, files an entry under the journal heading, the month and the day, making the month and day headings when they are not there yet. The function reads \texttt{:prepend} with \texttt{org-capture-get}: a new month or day heading goes first among its siblings (newest on top) when it is \texttt{t}, else last. The item follows the template's own \texttt{:prepend}, so \texttt{:prepend nil} keeps the entries of a day in time order. To have newest-first headings with items in time order, set \texttt{(prepend t)} in the function and \texttt{:prepend nil} on the template.

\begin{verbatim}
(defun my-olp-target (names)
  (let ((level 1) (start (point-min)) (end (point-max)) (prepend (org-capture-get :prepend)))
    (dolist (name names)
      (goto-char start)
      (if (re-search-forward (format "^\\*\\{%d\\} %s[ \t]*$" level (regexp-quote name)) end t)
          (setq start (1+ (match-end 0)))
        (goto-char start)
        (goto-char (if (and prepend (re-search-forward "^\\*+ " end t)) (match-beginning 0) end))
        (unless (bolp) (insert "\n"))
        (insert (make-string level ?*) " " name "\n")
        (setq start (point)))
      (goto-char start)
      (setq end (if (re-search-forward (format "^\\*\\{1,%d\\} " level) nil t) (match-beginning 0) (point-max)))
      (setq level (1+ level)))
    (goto-char start) (forward-line -1) (beginning-of-line)))
(defun my-journal-target ()
  (my-olp-target (list "Journal" (format-time-string "%Y-%m %b") (format-time-string "%Y-%m-%d"))))
(add-to-list 'org-capture-templates
  '("j" "Journal" item (file+function "github:home.org" my-journal-target) "%<%H:%M> - %?" :prepend nil))
\end{verbatim}

\subsubsection{Capturing from other apps}
\label{sec:orgaef253e}
On Android, the installed app is a share target: choose \textbf{org-pwa} in another app's Share sheet and the shared title, text and link open the share template (below); its \texttt{\%i} and \texttt{\%a} take the content. Long-press the app icon for a \textbf{Capture} shortcut.

Shared content goes to the template with the key \texttt{w} in the Lisp init, or, when the init has none, to one that files a web page under \textbf{Inbox}. A web page becomes a heading that is a link to it, titled as the page is (leave the title prompt blank); shared text goes under the heading with the title you type. The second prompt takes your own note, and \texttt{:CREATED:} records when. To choose where shares go, define \texttt{w} yourself:

\begin{verbatim}
(add-to-list 'org-capture-templates
  '("w" "Web page or text" entry (file+olp "inbox.org" "Inbox")
    "* %a%^{Title (leave blank for a web page)}\n:PROPERTIES:\n:CREATED: %U\n:END:\n  %i\n  %?"
    :empty-lines 1))
\end{verbatim}

Any link or bookmark can do the same: \texttt{index.html?capture=KEY\&text=Buy\%20milk} runs the template with that key and carries the content (a bare \texttt{?capture} shows the list; \texttt{\&title=} and \texttt{\&url=} also work). The address is cleaned afterwards, so reloading never captures twice, and it works offline. A template that files into another file needs a document from the same backend open.

\textbf{iPhone}: iOS can't share to installed web apps. Copy the text (a Shortcut can do it), open the app and run a template that contains \texttt{\%x}.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Extras menu}
\label{sec:org17e454c}
A floating ☰ button at bottom-right opens a configurable list of quick actions. It is this app's own feature, set with \texttt{org-xx-extra-menu} (see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables}); the button is hidden while the variable is unset. The sibling \texttt{org-xx-menu-aliases} relabels or hides buttons in the File, More, Export and View menus (see \hyperref[sec:orgdebc8db]{Menu customization}).

\textbf{Syntax}: a sequence of double-quoted \texttt{"SPEC;LABEL"} entries, spread over several lines with a trailing \texttt{\textbackslash{}} (see \hyperref[sec:org26a342a]{Configuration} for line continuation). Settings → Advanced → \textbf{Global Variables} takes it in this one-entry-per-line form (see \hyperref[sec:org5be3190]{Settings}):

\begin{verbatim}
org-xx-extra-menu: "j;📔 Journal" \
                   "c;✅ Checklist" \
                   "m;👥 Meeting" \
                   "-----" \
                   "t;⭐ Tracking" \
                   "["🛍️ Bag - lists and notes", "❤️ Health", "🏩 Tracking", "%<%Y-%m>"];👁 Current" \
                   "-----" \
                   "'calendar;📅 Calendar"
\end{verbatim}

In Settings → Global Variables the entries are a quoted list of strings, as in an init file, with a quote inside an entry written \texttt{\textbackslash{}"}:

\begin{verbatim}
(setq org-xx-extra-menu
      '("j;📔 Journal"
        "-----"
        "[\"Bag\", \"%<%Y-%m>\"];👁 Current"
        "'calendar;📅 Calendar"))
\end{verbatim}

\textbf{LABEL} is the text shown, exactly as written (icon and all). \textbf{SPEC} is one of three shapes:

\begin{itemize}
\item A bare \textbf{capture-template key} (\texttt{t}, \texttt{j}, \texttt{c}, \texttt{m} above) runs that template, as if picked from the Capture menu (see \hyperref[sec:orgab0be70]{Capture Templates}). A key with no template shows a status message.
\item A bracketed \textbf{OLP path}: an array of double-quoted heading titles, like the path of a \texttt{file+olp} target, each segment written \texttt{\%<FORMAT>} standing for the time when the item is tapped (\texttt{"\%<\%Y-\%m>"} gives the current year and month). It navigates to that heading. It never creates a missing heading, because browsing a menu shouldn't write to the file: a path that doesn't fully exist creates nothing and says so.
\item A \textbf{quoted function reference} (\texttt{'calendar} above) runs the command palette command with that real Emacs or Org function name, as if chosen from the palette. It acts on the heading whose action menu is open, else the keyboard-focused one. A command that can't run says why in the status line (\texttt{Clock out: no clock is running.}), and no confirmation is asked, since choosing the item is the confirmation. The names are the ones the palette shows and searches (\texttt{org-clock-out}, \texttt{org-clock-in}, \texttt{org-refile}, \texttt{org-todo}, \texttt{org-agenda}, \texttt{save-buffer}, \texttt{isearch-forward}, \texttt{calendar}, \texttt{org-html-export-to-html} and the rest), so type a function name into the palette to find the command, and quote the same name here.

A name that no command has shows \texttt{'name is not a recognized function.} when tapped; the entry stays so a typo is visible. \textbf{New document}, \textbf{Undo history}, \textbf{Undo settings change} and \textbf{Redo settings change} have no Emacs function to name. \textbf{Recalculate all tables} is \texttt{org-table-recalculate-buffer-tables} and \textbf{Export as an Org buffer} is \texttt{org-org-export-as-org}.

\textbf{The calendar} (\texttt{'calendar}, the palette's \textbf{Calendar}) is a single-month overview with year and month navigation and a Today jump (today is bold with a halo ring). Each day is color-coded from the Agenda's data: green for a contact's birthday, blue for any other event (SCHEDULED, DEADLINE, a plain timestamp or a diary-sexp entry), burnt orange for both; weather and logbook entries don't count. Tapping a date opens Agenda's Day view on it, and the displayed month is remembered for the session. \texttt{examples/calendar.org} builds one from \texttt{js} blocks.
\end{itemize}

Five hyphens (\texttt{"-{}-{}-{}-{}-"}) on their own are a visual separator rather than an item, for grouping related actions.

An entry with no label, or whose spec is not a template key, an OLP path or a quoted function, is left out of the menu and named in a message; the other entries stay. A quoted name that no command has is shown when it is tapped.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Menu customization}
\label{sec:orgdebc8db}
\texttt{org-xx-menu-aliases} (a Global or Local Variable; this app's own) relabels or hides buttons in the File, More, Export, Import and View menus. \texttt{org-xx-extra-menu} adds a quick-access menu instead (see \hyperref[sec:org17e454c]{Extras menu}).

\textbf{Syntax}: double-quoted \texttt{"menu:Label;alias"} entries, space-separated and spread over several lines with a trailing \texttt{\textbackslash{}}. \texttt{menu} is \texttt{file}, \texttt{more}, \texttt{export}, \texttt{import} or \texttt{view}. Settings → Advanced → \textbf{Global Variables} takes it one entry per line (see \hyperref[sec:org5be3190]{Settings}):

\begin{verbatim}
org-xx-menu-aliases: "more:Commands;💲 Commands" \
                     "more:Export;📤 Export" \
                     "more:Import;📥 Import" \
                     "more:Settings;⚙️ Settings"
\end{verbatim}

In Settings → Global Variables, a quoted list of strings:

\begin{verbatim}
(setq org-xx-menu-aliases
      '("more:Commands;💲 Commands"
        "more:Settings;⚙️ Settings"))
\end{verbatim}

Export and Import are steps within the More menu with their own namespaces, \texttt{export:} and \texttt{import:}. \texttt{Label} is a built-in button label (table below); an entry with no \texttt{menu:}, no \texttt{;}, no label or a menu that does not exist is named in a message; a label no button has changes nothing, and a label never mentioned keeps its default.

\textbf{\texttt{alias}}, after the semicolon: non-empty text replaces the button's visible text (the original label becomes its accessible name); empty (\texttt{"export:HTML;"}) hides the button. \texttt{more:Settings} can never be hidden, because GitHub and WebDAV setup is reachable only from there.

\textbf{Order}: once every label of a menu is listed, buttons follow the order written; a partial list leaves the order alone. To keep a button visible in a full list, repeat its text (\texttt{"more:Settings;Settings"}). Showing More as Settings, Commands, Import, Export:

\begin{verbatim}
org-xx-menu-aliases: "more:Settings;Settings" "more:Commands;Commands" \
                     "more:Import;Import" "more:Export;Export"
\end{verbatim}

\textbf{Popup menus}: File, View, More and Extras open as popups next to their button and share Settings → Appearance → \textbf{Menu Size}. Export is a step within More; \textbf{‹ Back} returns to the list.

The real labels of each menu, as used in \texttt{"menu:Label;alias"}:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\texttt{menu} & Labels\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{file} & \texttt{Export}, \texttt{New}, \texttt{Open}, \texttt{Save}, \texttt{Save As}, \texttt{Save Some Buffers}\\[0pt]
\texttt{more} & \texttt{Commands}, \texttt{Export}, \texttt{Import}, \texttt{Settings}\\[0pt]
\texttt{export} & \texttt{ASCII}, \texttt{Beamer}, \texttt{HTML}, \texttt{LaTeX}, \texttt{Slides (HTML)}\\[0pt]
\texttt{import} & \texttt{Contacts (.vcf)}, \texttt{iCalendar (.ics)}\\[0pt]
\texttt{view} & \texttt{Agenda}, \texttt{Org}, \texttt{Text}, \texttt{TODO}\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\texttt{Save Some Buffers} always comes last and is not part of a reordering list.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{File management}
\label{sec:org8402fde}
\textbf{File menu}: New, Open, Save, Save As, Save Some Buffers. The 💾 button beside it is a one-tap \textbf{Save}, disabled when there is no document or nowhere to save yet.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{New} creates a document in memory. The tab shows \texttt{*scratch*} in the red unsaved style until the first heading gets a title, which becomes the label. \textbf{Save} stays disabled until \textbf{Save As} picks a destination. Handy as a scratch pad for a capture template or table formula.
\item \textbf{Open} and \textbf{Save As} share the Files list: a place bar (\textbf{GitHub}, \textbf{WebDAV}, \textbf{This device}; \textbf{Import file} / \textbf{Download} where a file is read once) and the folder below it. Each place remembers its folder. The palette's \texttt{dired} opens the list in the folder of the current file. See \hyperref[sec:org97bb9ee]{Files view}.
\item \textbf{GitHub and WebDAV show a folder listing}: tap a folder to enter it, \textbf{↑ Up} to go back. WebDAV needs \texttt{PROPFIND} (Nextcloud, ownCloud and Apache \texttt{mod\_dav} have it). \textbf{Enter path…} opens a path the listing doesn't show.
\item \textbf{Save} writes back to the backend the file came from, without asking again.
\item \textbf{Save Some Buffers} (\texttt{save-some-buffers}, \texttt{C-x s}) asks about each modified tab in the minibuffer: \texttt{y} or Space saves, \texttt{n} or Backspace skips, \texttt{!} saves this and the rest, \texttt{.} saves this and stops, \texttt{q} or Escape stops, \texttt{d} shows what changed. Each save is the same as \textbf{Save}. \textbf{File → Save Some Buffers} saves them all without asking; it is dimmed when nothing is modified and skips new unsaved documents.
\item \textbf{Revert Buffer} (palette, \texttt{revert-buffer}) reads the open file again and drops the buffer's unsaved changes, after asking if there are any. \textbf{Undo} brings them back.
\item \textbf{Capture, Refile, Archive and Replace edit buffers, not files}: an entry sent to another file goes into that file's tab (opened in the background if needed), modified until you save. Nothing is written behind your back, and modified buffers are kept on the device.
\item \textbf{Line endings} are kept: a CRLF file is saved back with CRLF.
\item \textbf{Encoding}: files are read as UTF-8. A file that is not valid UTF-8 (a Latin-1 file, say) opens read-only, with the odd bytes shown as \texttt{�}, and cannot be saved, so it is not damaged. A banner at the top offers \textbf{Convert to UTF-8…} (also in the command palette) and \textbf{Dismiss}; it asks which encoding it is in (Latin-1, UTF-16, or another name), makes the buffer editable, and the next save writes UTF-8.
\item \textbf{Save As} may pick another backend; an existing file asks before it is replaced, and again if someone else saved it meanwhile.
\item A file with unsaved local edits asks to \textbf{resume} or \textbf{discard} them when opened. \textbf{Settings → Pending Local Changes} lists every file with unsynced edits.
\item \textbf{Conflicts}: if the stored version changed since the last sync, Save merges the two where it safely can and asks only about the parts that clash (see \hyperref[sec:org8e03395]{Offline behavior and sync}).
\item \textbf{Recently opened} lists the files you opened or saved, newest first, up to \texttt{recentf-max-saved-items} (20; \texttt{nil} or a number below 1 keeps them all). Closing a file leaves the list as it is, and opening a file that is already open just switches to it, kept across sessions in a list that scrolls. A file you are looking at is marked \emph{current} and another open file \emph{open}; tap an open file to switch to it. A closed file on GitHub or WebDAV is marked \emph{view}: if the server can't be reached, tapping it offers the saved version, read-only. Long-press an entry to remove it from the list (the file is not deleted). \textbf{Clear recents} empties the list and the saved versions.
\end{itemize}

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Files view}
\label{sec:org97bb9ee}
The Files list manages files the way Dired does. It shows every file. \textbf{Sort} by name, date (newest first) or size (largest first); \textbf{Reverse the order} flips it. Folders are sorted in with the files, as Dired does; put \texttt{-{}-{}group-directories-first} in \texttt{dired-listing-switches} (Lisp init) to list them first (that is the only switch read).

\textbf{Find…} (\texttt{find-lisp-find-dired}) asks for an Emacs regexp and lists the files below the folder whose \emph{name} matches, folders searched and not listed, with the case folded as Emacs does by default. \texttt{\textbackslash{}.org\$} finds the Org files, \texttt{\textbackslash{}.\textbackslash{}(org\textbackslash{}|el\textbackslash{})\$} Org and Elisp files; a bare \texttt{(} or \texttt{|} is text, as in Emacs. Each row shows its path. \textbf{Change filter…} (\texttt{find-lisp-find-dired-filter}) matches the same files against another regexp, \textbf{Search again} looks again, \textbf{Close} returns to the folder. GitHub is searched with one request; WebDAV and a device folder one folder at a time, with \textbf{Cancel}, and the search stops after 5000 files and says so.

\textbf{Marks}: the box at the left of a row marks it. \textbf{Marks…} marks by Emacs regexp (matched against the file name, case-folded; \texttt{\textbackslash{}.\textbackslash{}(org\textbackslash{}|el\textbackslash{})\$} marks Org and Elisp files), marks all shown, inverts, or unmarks. With files marked, \textbf{Copy to…}, \textbf{Move to…} and \textbf{Delete…} act on them; with none, a row's \textbf{⋯} menu acts on that row.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Copy to…} / \textbf{Move to…}: open the folder to copy into (in any place) and tap \textbf{Copy here}. A name that is already there asks \textbf{Yes / No / Yes to all / Quit}. A move deletes the original only after the copy is written.
\item \textbf{Rename…} (Dired's \texttt{R}) takes a new name or a path: \texttt{sub/a.org} is relative to this folder, \texttt{/x/a.org} to the top of the place, a folder you name takes the file, and the parent must exist. It copies, then deletes the original, so it works across folders. \textbf{Flag for deletion} and \textbf{Delete the flagged} are \texttt{d} and \texttt{x} of Dired; \textbf{Delete…} asks once, and names a folder as such.
\item \textbf{New…} makes a file (opened for editing) or a folder. A new folder is a real empty folder in WebDAV and in a browser's device folder; GitHub and the Android folder cannot hold an empty one, so there it holds an empty \texttt{.gitkeep}.
\item \textbf{Info} shows the path, size and modified time, where the place gives them.
\end{itemize}

A file open with unsaved changes is never deleted, moved or replaced. One that is open and saved is asked about, its tab closes with a delete and follows a move.

\textbf{Attach from Files}: in the Attach menu (\texttt{C-c C-a}), \textbf{Attach from Files} (\texttt{p}) lists a place; mark files and tap \textbf{Attach}. \texttt{org-attach-method} decides copy, move or link.

\subsection{Tabs}
\label{sec:orgb31a5d3}
\textbf{Several documents can be open at once.} Opening a file (New, Open, Recently opened, a \texttt{file:}, \texttt{github:} or \texttt{webdav:} link, or an Agenda or Search result) adds a tab; opening one already open switches to it. Each tab keeps its own content, cursor, scroll position, view mode and undo history (see \hyperref[sec:org10b54c5]{Undo/redo and History}).

Each tab shows the filename (or the first heading's title for an unsaved document) and a red dot when it has unsaved changes. The × closes a tab, asking first if it is modified, as \texttt{kill-buffer} does. Open tabs persist across restarts. \textbf{Help} has its own tab (see \hyperref[sec:org43084b9]{Help}), always last, and does not survive a restart.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Citations}
\label{sec:org78fb33b}
\textbf{Org-cite citations} work as in Emacs's default (\texttt{basic}) processor. Write \texttt{[cite:@knuth84]}, \texttt{[cite/t:@knuth84 p. 5]} or \texttt{[cite:see @a; @b, ch. 2]} and point at your references with \texttt{\#+BIBLIOGRAPHY: refs.bib} (BibTeX or CSL-JSON, read from the same place as the document, one line per file). In the outline a citation stays as typed, dimmed; tapping a key shows its entry. Examples with Emacs's results: \texttt{examples/citations.org}.

\begin{itemize}
\item Styles: default (author, year), \texttt{/t} (text), \texttt{/a} (author), \texttt{/na} (no author), \texttt{/n} (nothing printed), \texttt{/b} (numeric), with \texttt{/c} and \texttt{/b} variants for capitals and bare form.
\item \texttt{\#+PRINT\_BIBLIOGRAPHY:} marks where the reference list goes in HTML, ASCII, ODT and \LaTeX{} exports. \texttt{\#+CITE\_EXPORT: basic plain} (or \texttt{numeric}) picks the list style.
\item Settings (see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables}): \texttt{org-cite-global-bibliography} (files used by every document), \texttt{org-cite-basic-sorting-field} and \texttt{org-cite-basic-author-year-separator}.
\end{itemize}

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Export}
\label{sec:org8e45f5f}
\textbf{More → Export} lists ASCII, As-org, Beamer, HTML, \LaTeX{} and Slides (HTML). The other formats are palette commands (\textbf{Commands}): ODT (\texttt{org-odt-export-to-odt}), Calendar (.ics) (\texttt{org-icalendar-export-to-ics}) and Contacts (.vcf) (\texttt{org-vcard-export}); the last two open their own scope choice, and C-c C-e opens the menu. File keywords such as \texttt{\#+TITLE} and \texttt{\#+OPTIONS:} match case-insensitively, as in org.

\textbf{Scope}: \textbf{Choose a heading…} exports just that heading and its descendants, and every heading is listed, even folded ones. The chosen heading becomes the top level of the output. \textbf{This file} exports everything. Calendar and Contacts also offer \textbf{This file + Agenda Files} or \textbf{This file + Contacts Files} once those are configured, fetched fresh at export time. In Tree style, Contacts lists only contacts (headings with \texttt{:KIND:}).

\subsubsection{Document settings}
\label{sec:orgd9f1675}

\texttt{\#+TITLE}, \texttt{\#+AUTHOR} and \texttt{\#+DATE} appear in a whole-document export in ASCII, HTML and ODT: a visible title with the author and date beneath it (in HTML, the date and author close the page, as in Emacs), and the format's own metadata where it has some. A subtree export starts at its heading instead.

\texttt{\#+OPTIONS:} takes these keys, chained on one line or split across several (a later value wins):

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Key & Effect\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{toc:} & An integer depth limit, or \texttt{nil} for no table of contents. Independent of \texttt{num:}\\[0pt]
\texttt{num:} & Heading numbers on or off\\[0pt]
\texttt{\textasciicircum{}:} & Sub/superscript strictness, as \texttt{org-use-sub-superscripts} (see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables}); overrides it for this export\\[0pt]
\texttt{author:}, \texttt{date:} & Show each field or not\\[0pt]
\texttt{creator:} & A "Generated by org-pwa" notice, off by default\\[0pt]
\texttt{broken-links:} & What to do with a link that leads nowhere: \texttt{nil} stops the export, \texttt{t} leaves the link out, \texttt{mark} writes \texttt{[BROKEN LINK: path]}. Overrides \texttt{org-export-with-broken-links}\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

HTML export also takes these, with Org's defaults:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Key & Effect\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{H:} & How many heading levels are headings (3); deeper ones become list items\\[0pt]
\texttt{num:N} & Number only the first N levels\\[0pt]
\texttt{tags:}, \texttt{todo:}, \texttt{pri:} & Show tags (\texttt{not-in-toc} leaves them out of the contents), TODO keywords, priorities (off)\\[0pt]
\texttt{p:} & Show SCHEDULED, DEADLINE and CLOSED (off)\\[0pt]
\texttt{\textbackslash{}n:t} & Every line break in a paragraph is kept\\[0pt]
\texttt{-:}, \texttt{*:}, \texttt{e:}, \texttt{f:}, \texttt{stat:} & Special strings (\texttt{-{}-{}}, \texttt{...}), emphasis, entities, footnotes and \texttt{[1/3]} cookies\\[0pt]
\texttt{d:} & Drawers: \texttt{t}, \texttt{nil}, or a list such as \texttt{("NOTES")} (all but LOGBOOK)\\[0pt]
\texttt{arch:}, \texttt{tasks:} & Archived subtrees (title only), TODO headings (\texttt{nil}, \texttt{todo}, \texttt{done})\\[0pt]
\texttt{<:}, \texttt{title:}, \texttt{email:} & Timestamps, the title, the author's address\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\texttt{\#+EXCLUDE\_TAGS:} (default \texttt{noexport}), \texttt{\#+SELECT\_TAGS:}, COMMENT headings, \texttt{\#+SUBTITLE:}, \texttt{\#+DESCRIPTION:}, \texttt{\#+KEYWORDS:}, \texttt{\#+LANGUAGE:} and \texttt{\#+MACRO:} are honored. Other formats ignore these HTML-only keys.

\texttt{\#+INCLUDE: "path" [block-type] [language] [:lines "N-M"] [:minlevel N]} splices another document in at export time, before the first heading or in a heading's body. In a body it nests as children of that heading, one level deeper by default; at document level it keeps its own levels. The path is read from an explicit \texttt{github:}, \texttt{webdav:} or \texttt{local:} prefix, or else relative to the open file.

\begin{itemize}
\item With no block type, the file is parsed as org and its headings are spliced in (its own \texttt{\#+TITLE} and similar keywords are not). \texttt{:minlevel N} shifts its top level to N.
\item With a block type (\texttt{src}, \texttt{example}, \texttt{quote} or \texttt{export}, optionally with a language or backend, as in \texttt{\#+INCLUDE: "path" export html}), the raw text is wrapped in that block and placed in the body.
\item \texttt{:lines "N-M"}, \texttt{"-M"} or \texttt{"N-"} filters the text first. The end line is exclusive, as in org, despite the manual's wording.
\end{itemize}

\texttt{\#+HTML\_HEAD:} inserts raw HTML before \texttt{</head>}, in HTML export only and for subtree exports too; several lines are joined in order. \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_EXPORT <backend>} \ldots{} \texttt{\#+END\_EXPORT} passes its content through unescaped when the backend matches the current format (\texttt{html}, \texttt{ascii}, \texttt{odt}, where the content must already be ODF XML) and is omitted otherwise.

\textbf{Document type}: \texttt{\#+HTML\_DOCTYPE: html5} (or \texttt{org-html-doctype}, Settings → Export) picks the declaration; the default is \texttt{xhtml-strict}.

\textbf{Inline tasks}: with \texttt{org-inlinetask} in \texttt{org-modules}, a headline of 15 or more stars is an inline task, closed by an \texttt{END} headline of the same depth, and every export prints it in place (HTML \texttt{<div class="inlinetask">}, ASCII a box, \LaTeX{} a framed minipage, ODT a bordered paragraph).

\textbf{Header and footer}: \texttt{html-preamble:} and \texttt{html-postamble:} in \texttt{\#+OPTIONS:} take a quoted text placed above and below the page (\texttt{nil} drops it, \texttt{t} uses the format variable, \texttt{auto} the date, author and so on); \texttt{\%t} is the title, \texttt{\%s} the subtitle, \texttt{\%a} the author, \texttt{\%d} the date, \texttt{\%e} the email, \texttt{\%C} or \texttt{\%T} when exported. Example: \texttt{\#+OPTIONS: html-postamble:"Prepared by \%a, \%d"}. Without a text, the foot is Emacs's \texttt{auto} one (date, author, "Created" time, validation link); \texttt{\#+OPTIONS: timestamp:nil} leaves the "Created" line out, and \texttt{creator:t} adds the creator.

\subsubsection{ASCII}
\label{sec:org8184fa8}

Plain text laid out as \texttt{org-ascii-export-to-ascii} lays it out: a "Table of Contents", then numbered headings underlined by level with tags at the right margin (deeper than \texttt{H:} become bullets). Paragraphs are filled to \texttt{org-ascii-text-width} (default 72). Emphasis keeps its markers, \texttt{code} and \texttt{verbatim} read \texttt{`text'}, and a link reads \texttt{[description]} with its target listed after the section. Footnotes become \texttt{[1]} with definitions under "Footnotes". \texttt{\#+TITLE}, \texttt{\#+AUTHOR} and \texttt{\#+DATE} make a title block; a subtree export uses the heading as the title.

\texttt{org-ascii-charset} (Local Variables) is \texttt{ascii} (default), \texttt{latin1} or \texttt{utf-8}; entities such as \texttt{\textbackslash{}alpha} and \texttt{\textbackslash{}copy} are replaced to suit. UTF-8 also draws dashes, an ellipsis, checkboxes (☑ ☐ ☒), rules and block frames with box characters.

Example and source blocks and lines starting with a colon sit in a frame (a source block's caption follows as "Listing 1: …"). QUOTE and VERSE blocks are set in from the margin; CENTER blocks center, and \texttt{JUSTIFYLEFT} and \texttt{JUSTIFYRIGHT} align. \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_EXPORT ascii} and \texttt{\#+ASCII:} print as written. Lists keep bullets, numbers, counters and checkboxes. \texttt{\#+TOC: tables} and \texttt{\#+TOC: listings} list tables or listings. Tables are typeset with padded columns and right-aligned numbers; a row of \texttt{<N>} cells (\texttt{| <30> | <10> |}) sets column widths and \texttt{<l>}, \texttt{<c>}, \texttt{<r>} alignment (that row never appears in output); a caption follows as "Table 1: …". A horizontal rule takes its width from \texttt{\#+ATTR\_ASCII: :width N}. Of the \texttt{org-ascii-*} variables only the character set and text width are read.

\subsubsection{HTML}
\label{sec:orgbffe5f6}

A standalone page laid out like \texttt{ox-html}: the title as \texttt{h1}, top-level headings as \texttt{h2} in numbered containers, \texttt{org-ul}, \texttt{org-ol} and \texttt{org-dl} lists, tables with a header row (when a rule follows it), alignment and caption, figures, and numbered footnotes. Entities, timestamps, macros, \texttt{@@html:...@@} snippets, special blocks (\texttt{\#+BEGIN\_NOTE} is \texttt{<div class="note">}), \texttt{\#+TOC:} lists and \texttt{\#+ATTR\_HTML:} work; source blocks are colored for common languages. Pictures the app can read are embedded, so the file stands alone.

Tables follow ox's rules in HTML, \LaTeX{} and ASCII: a first column of \texttt{\#}, \texttt{*}, \texttt{!}, \texttt{\_}, \texttt{\textasciicircum{}}, \texttt{\$} or \texttt{/} marks is not written, nor are rows marked \texttt{/} \texttt{\textasciicircum{}} \texttt{\_} \texttt{\$} \texttt{!} or made only of alignment cookies; the last cookie of a column sets its alignment, and a header is what comes before the first rule. \texttt{|:nil} leaves tables out, \texttt{f:nil} leaves footnote references out, and \texttt{:UNNUMBERED: t} passes to sub-headings (\texttt{notoc} also keeps it out of the contents).

The CSS is print-aware, so \textbf{Print → Save as PDF} is the route to PDF. For a table of contents with page numbers, tick \textbf{Add TOC with page numbers} in Settings → Export → HTML (it adds the Paged.js script to \texttt{org-html-head}, loaded from the web) and set \texttt{\#+OPTIONS: toc:2}; open the page in Chrome, wait for the sheets to lay out, and print at Scale 100\%.

\subsubsection{ODT}
\label{sec:org12ef1fd}

A standalone \texttt{.odt} that opens in LibreOffice, Word (with the ODF filter) and Google Docs, a port of \texttt{ox-odt} with the same styles, style names and structure for headings, lists, tables (special rows and columns, alignment cookies, \texttt{\#+ATTR\_ODT:}), blocks, \texttt{\#+ODT:} and \texttt{@@odt:@@}, footnotes, links, the table of contents and captions, and \texttt{\#+OPTIONS:} such as \texttt{toc:}, \texttt{num:}, \texttt{tags:}, \texttt{todo:}, \texttt{pri:}, \texttt{p:}, \texttt{f:}, \texttt{|:}, \texttt{*:}, \texttt{stat:} and \texttt{prop:}. Images the app can read are embedded and sized from their pixels, \texttt{\#+ATTR\_ODT: :width :height :scale} or the page. \LaTeX{} fragments become embedded formula objects you can edit, with a number on display equations. Source blocks are colored with \texttt{OrgSrcFontLock} styles. \texttt{\#+ATTR\_ODT: :style NAME} picks a table style from \texttt{org-odt-table-styles}, which the Lisp init can extend.

\subsubsection{Line numbers and references in source blocks}
\label{sec:org1f139d4}
Source and example blocks follow Org's switches in HTML, ASCII, \LaTeX{} and ODT export. \texttt{-n} numbers lines from 1 and \texttt{-n 10} from 10; \texttt{+n} continues from the previous numbered block, \texttt{+n 5} adds 5 to that; \texttt{-i} keeps the indentation. A line ending in \texttt{(ref:label)} is a reference: \texttt{[[(label)]]} links to it and shows the line number (or the label when the block shows labels). \texttt{-r} removes the label from the printed line and makes links show numbers, \texttt{-k} keeps it, and \texttt{-l "[ref:\%s]"} changes how a label is written. \texttt{[[(label)][see (label)]]} replaces \texttt{(label)} in the description with the number.

HTML puts \texttt{<span class="linenr">} before each line and a \texttt{coderef} anchor on labeled lines, with Org's hover highlight. ASCII and \texttt{verbatim} put the number at the left and the label flush right; \texttt{listings} and \texttt{minted} number the lines themselves unless \texttt{org-latex-listings-options} or \texttt{org-latex-minted-options} says otherwise; ODT writes a numbered list with a bookmark on each labeled line.

\subsubsection{\LaTeX{}}
\label{sec:org9761731}

A \texttt{.tex} file that compiles with \texttt{pdflatex}, \texttt{xelatex} or \texttt{lualatex}, laid out as \texttt{org-latex-export-to-latex} lays it out: sections, lists, tables (\texttt{\#+ATTR\_LATEX:}), figures, footnotes, citations, links, math and source blocks. With pictures the app can read the export is a \texttt{.zip} with them in \texttt{images/}; otherwise just the \texttt{.tex}. Settings → Export → \LaTeX{} also has \textbf{Fix wide TOC numbers}, which adds the \texttt{tocloft} lines that keep numbers such as 1.11.1 from running into titles, as an \texttt{(add-to-list 'org-latex-packages-alist …)} form in the Lisp init. Examples with Emacs's results: \texttt{examples/export-latex.org}.

\begin{verbatim}
#+LATEX_CLASS: report
#+MACRO: stamp (eval (format-time-string "%Y" (current-time)))
#+OPTIONS: todo:nil tags:nil
\end{verbatim}

\texttt{\#+LATEX\_CLASS:}, \texttt{\#+LATEX\_CLASS\_OPTIONS:}, \texttt{\#+LATEX\_COMPILER:} and \texttt{\#+LATEX\_HEADER:} are read from the file; Settings → Export → \LaTeX{} sets class and compiler for files that do not. The Lisp init (Settings → Advanced) reads, as in an init file:
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{org-latex-classes} (an \texttt{add-to-list} of \texttt{("name" "\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}documentclass…" ("\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}section\{\%s\}" . "\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}section*\{\%s\}") …)}; the header may contain \texttt{[NO-DEFAULT-PACKAGES]}, \texttt{[PACKAGES]} and \texttt{[EXTRA]}) and \texttt{org-latex-packages-alist};
\item \texttt{org-latex-src-block-backend} (\texttt{'listings} or \texttt{'minted}; add the package to \texttt{org-latex-packages-alist} yourself) with \texttt{org-latex-listings-options}, \texttt{org-latex-listings-langs}, \texttt{org-latex-minted-options} and \texttt{org-latex-minted-langs};
\item \texttt{org-latex-tables-centered}, \texttt{org-latex-tables-booktabs}, \texttt{org-latex-default-table-environment}, \texttt{org-latex-default-table-mode}, \texttt{org-latex-caption-above}, \texttt{org-latex-images-centered}, \texttt{org-latex-default-figure-position}, \texttt{org-latex-title-command}, \texttt{org-latex-toc-command}, \texttt{org-latex-active-timestamp-format}, \texttt{org-latex-inactive-timestamp-format}, \texttt{org-latex-prefer-user-labels} and \texttt{org-latex-text-markup-alist};
\item \texttt{org-latex-format-headline-function}, a function called for each section title and low-level list headline with the keyword, its type (\texttt{todo} or \texttt{done}), the priority as a character code, the title, the tags and \texttt{nil} in place of the export info; what it returns is the headline.
\end{itemize}

\texttt{(eval ..)} macros run as Lisp. The export reads \texttt{\#+OPTIONS:} as Emacs does (\texttt{num:N}, \texttt{todo}, \texttt{pri}, \texttt{tags}, \texttt{stat}, \texttt{tasks}, \texttt{p}, \texttt{d}, \texttt{prop}, \texttt{arch}, \texttt{\textbackslash{}n}, \texttt{*}, \texttt{e}, \texttt{f}, \texttt{tex}, \texttt{title}, \texttt{email}, \texttt{creator}), \texttt{\#+SELECT\_TAGS:}, \texttt{\#+EXCLUDE\_TAGS:} and the \texttt{UNNUMBERED} property. Pictures follow \texttt{\#+ATTR\_LATEX:} (\texttt{:width}, \texttt{:height}, \texttt{:scale}, \texttt{:options}, \texttt{:float}, \texttt{:placement}, \texttt{:center}); pdf (\texttt{::page}), eps, svg and tikz files are written as Emacs writes them. Links to named blocks, equations, quotes and paragraphs get labels, \texttt{:booktabs t} tables, table special rows and columns, inline \texttt{src\_lang\{..\}}, \texttt{\#+LINK:} abbreviations, \texttt{\#+INDEX:} as \texttt{\textbackslash{}index\{\}}, letter counters (\texttt{[@c]}), the \texttt{\{\{\{n\}\}\}} counter, smart quotes (\texttt{':t}) with the quotes of each \texttt{\#+LANGUAGE:}, and sub- and superscripts (\texttt{a\_(b)}, \texttt{a\_b.c}, \texttt{x\_\textbackslash{}alpha}) follow Org. Presentations are under Beamer below.

\subsubsection{Beamer}
\label{sec:org8a35b7f}
