More → Export → Beamer writes a presentation as \texttt{org-beamer-export-to-latex} does, in class \texttt{beamer} unless the file sets \texttt{\#+LATEX\_CLASS:}. Compile it with a \TeX{} distribution; \texttt{examples/beamer-demo.org} is a working file.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Frames}: headings at the frame level (\texttt{H:} in \texttt{\#+OPTIONS:}, 1 by default; \texttt{:BEAMER\_env: frame} or \texttt{fullframe} sets it for one tree) become frames and headings above them sections. Below it a heading is a block, or the environment \texttt{BEAMER\_env} names: \texttt{block}, \texttt{alertblock}, \texttt{exampleblock}, \texttt{example}, \texttt{theorem}, \texttt{definition}, \texttt{proof}, \texttt{verse}, \texttt{quote}, \texttt{quotation}, \texttt{structureenv}, \texttt{beamercolorbox}, \texttt{columns} or \texttt{column}. \texttt{note} and \texttt{noteNH} write \texttt{\textbackslash{}note\{…\}}, \texttt{ignoreheading} writes only the text, \texttt{appendix} writes \texttt{\textbackslash{}appendix}, and \texttt{againframe} shows the frame named in \texttt{BEAMER\_ref} again. A frame with code, or \texttt{allowframebreaks}, is made fragile as in Emacs.
\item \textbf{Properties}: \texttt{BEAMER\_col} puts a heading in a column (neighbors share a \texttt{columns} environment), \texttt{BEAMER\_act} is the overlay (\texttt{<2->}), \texttt{BEAMER\_opt} the options.
\item \textbf{Document}: \texttt{\#+BEAMER\_THEME:}, \texttt{\_COLOR\_THEME:}, \texttt{\_FONT\_THEME:}, \texttt{\_INNER\_THEME:} and \texttt{\_OUTER\_THEME:} write the \texttt{\textbackslash{}use…theme} lines; \texttt{\#+BEAMER\_HEADER:} adds preamble lines; \texttt{\#+BEAMER:} lines go in as written; \texttt{\#+SUBTITLE:} is \texttt{\textbackslash{}subtitle\{\}}; \texttt{toc:t} gives the table of contents its own frame.
\item \textbf{Text}: \texttt{*bold*} is \texttt{\textbackslash{}alert\{\}}; \texttt{@@beamer:\textbackslash{}pause@@} is written as it stands, and \texttt{@@beamer:<2>@@} at the start of a list item, bold text or link description sets its overlay; \texttt{\#+ATTR\_BEAMER: :overlay <+->} and \texttt{:options} apply to a list.
\end{itemize}

The Lisp init reads \texttt{org-beamer-frame-level}, \texttt{org-beamer-theme}, \texttt{org-beamer-frame-default-options}, \texttt{org-beamer-outline-frame-title}, \texttt{org-beamer-outline-frame-options}, \texttt{org-beamer-subtitle-format} and \texttt{org-beamer-environments-extra} (with the \texttt{\%a} \texttt{\%A} \texttt{\%o} \texttt{\%O} \texttt{\%h} \texttt{\%r} \texttt{\%H} \texttt{\%R} escapes).

\subsubsection{Slides (HTML)}
\label{sec:org921cf0f}

More → Export → Slides (HTML) writes the same presentation as a web page of 16:9 slides. Open it in a browser or print it to PDF (also on a phone); each slide is one page. Emacs has no such export; Beamer export is Emacs's own.

The file is read as for Beamer (frame level, sections, blocks and \texttt{BEAMER\_env}, columns, \texttt{fullframe}, notes, \texttt{againframe}); \texttt{toc:t} adds an outline slide and \texttt{\#+TITLE:} a title slide. Text, tables, code, links and math look as in HTML export, and \texttt{*bold*} is colored as \texttt{\textbackslash{}alert} is. A slide is made for each overlay step: \texttt{BEAMER\_act} on a block or column (\texttt{<2->}, \texttt{<1,3>}, \texttt{<-2>}), \texttt{\#+ATTR\_BEAMER: :overlay <+->} on a list, or \texttt{- @@beamer:<2>@@ item}. An item not yet shown keeps its place; a block not yet shown takes none. \texttt{\#+BEAMER\_THEME:} names such as Madrid or Warsaw give a colored title bar, any other a plain page. The other Beamer themes, \texttt{\textbackslash{}setbeamertemplate} and other \LaTeX{} are not read, and a frame too tall for its page is cut at the edge.

\subsubsection{As-org}
\label{sec:orgdaac0a2}

Org's \texttt{org-org-export-as-org}: a fully processed copy of the document in a new unsaved buffer, \texttt{*Org ORG Export*}, leaving the original untouched. It resolves \texttt{\#+INCLUDE:} lines; expands macros; leaves out COMMENT headings, \texttt{\#+EXCLUDE\_TAGS:} (\texttt{noexport} by default) and \texttt{\#+SELECT\_TAGS:} exclusions and, with \texttt{tasks:nil}, TODO headings; writes what ox-org writes (keywords lower case, tags placed by \texttt{org-tags-column}, source and example blocks indented by two, tables aligned, ordered lists renumbered); follows \texttt{\#+OPTIONS:} for planning (\texttt{p:}), property drawers (\texttt{prop:}), drawers (\texttt{d:}), priorities, TODO keywords, tags, footnotes and the title lines; and shifts the top level to 1. In an Extras entry it is \texttt{'org-org-export-as-org}.

\textbf{Macros}: \texttt{\#+MACRO: name text} with \texttt{\$1}, \texttt{\$2} arguments, used as \texttt{\{\{\{name(arg1,arg2)\}\}\}} (\texttt{\textbackslash{},} is a literal comma). Built in: \texttt{\{\{\{title\}\}\}}, \texttt{\{\{\{author\}\}\}}, \texttt{\{\{\{email\}\}\}}, \texttt{\{\{\{date\}\}\}}, \texttt{\{\{\{date(FORMAT)\}\}\}}, \texttt{\{\{\{time(FORMAT)\}\}\}}, \texttt{\{\{\{property(NAME)\}\}\}}, \texttt{\{\{\{keyword(NAME)\}\}\}} \texttt{\{\{\{n\}\}\}} and \texttt{\{\{\{n(NAME)\}\}\}} (counters) and, in \LaTeX{} export, \texttt{\{\{\{input-file\}\}\}} and \texttt{\{\{\{modification-time(FORMAT)\}\}\}}. The first definition of a name wins; an undefined macro stops the export, as in Emacs. A macro whose text starts with \texttt{(eval \textasciitilde{} runs as Lisp with \textasciitilde{}\$1}, \texttt{\$2} \ldots{} as strings (\texttt{nil} when not given); an error in it stops the export, as in Emacs. This works in every export.

\subsubsection{Calendar (.ics)}
\label{sec:orgda74208}

An iCalendar file for any calendar app, written as \texttt{org-icalendar-export-to-ics} writes it. By default the events are the active timestamps in a heading's title and text, and the DEADLINE of a heading that is not a TODO item (summary \texttt{DL: Title}). Settings → Export changes that: \texttt{org-icalendar-use-scheduled} and \texttt{org-icalendar-use-deadline} say which SCHEDULED and DEADLINE dates become events (\texttt{S: Title}), \texttt{org-icalendar-include-todo} adds TODO items as tasks, \texttt{org-icalendar-with-timestamps} picks which timestamps count, and \texttt{org-icalendar-alarm-time} adds alarms. Re-exporting gives the same event IDs, so a calendar app updates events instead of duplicating them.

\textbf{To}: the file is downloaded. \textbf{To: file} opens the share sheet instead, which on an iPhone has \textbf{Save to Files} (a downloaded .ics there goes straight to Calendar); \textbf{To: new buffer} leaves the text in a new buffer.

\textbf{Scope}: \textbf{This file}, \textbf{Choose a heading…} and \textbf{This file + Agenda Files} write everything the settings select, with no window. \textbf{Agenda (as displayed)}, the last row, writes what \hyperref[sec:orgac99be7]{the calendar sync} sends: what View → Agenda shows, from a month back to six months ahead, with SCHEDULED, DEADLINE and alarms.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
Org source & vCalendar field & Notes\\[0pt]
\hline
A timestamp in the title or text & \texttt{DTSTART}, \texttt{DTEND}, \texttt{SUMMARY} (the title) & A date has an all-day end; a time without an end lasts two hours, or \texttt{org-agenda-default-appointment-duration}\\[0pt]
DEADLINE, SCHEDULED & The same, with \textasciitilde{}DL: \textasciitilde{} or \textasciitilde{}S: \textasciitilde{} before the title & \\[0pt]
A repeater (\texttt{+1w}, \texttt{++3d}, \texttt{.+1m}) & \texttt{RRULE} & The calendar app expands the recurrence\\[0pt]
The text below the heading & \texttt{DESCRIPTION} & As the ASCII export writes it, at most \texttt{org-icalendar-include-body} characters\\[0pt]
\texttt{:SUMMARY:}, \texttt{:DESCRIPTION:}, \texttt{:LOCATION:}, \texttt{:CLASS:}, \texttt{:TIMEZONE:} & The field of that name & \\[0pt]
Tags, \texttt{:CATEGORY:} & \texttt{CATEGORIES} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:APPT\_WARNTIME:} & \texttt{VALARM} & On a timed event\\[0pt]
org-contacts-anniversaries & \texttt{DTSTART} with a yearly \texttt{RRULE}, \texttt{SUMMARY} (\texttt{Birthday: Name}) & One yearly event cannot carry an age, so the date is in the description\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsubsection{Contacts (.vcf)}
\label{sec:org550ce79}

vCard 3.0 for any contacts app, modeled on \href{https://github.com/pinoaffe/org-vcard}{org-vcard} (compatible with org-contacts.el). \href{https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6350}{RFC 6350} requires only \texttt{FN}, so no email address is needed. There are two styles, and \textbf{Tree} is the default:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Flat}: every heading with at least one recognized contact property (\texttt{:EMAIL:}, \texttt{:PHONE:}, \texttt{:CELL:}, \texttt{:WORK\_PHONE:}, \texttt{:ADDRESS:}, \texttt{:ADR:}, \texttt{:NICKNAME:}, \texttt{:NOTE:}, \texttt{:ANNIVERSARY:} or the birthday property). \texttt{:IGNORE: t} excludes one. A heading with none is skipped.
\item \textbf{Tree}: a contact heading (\texttt{:KIND: individual}, \texttt{:FIELDTYPE: name}) with each field as a descendant heading carrying its own \texttt{:FIELDTYPE:}, at any depth. A contact with no fields still exports a minimal vCard (\texttt{FN}, \texttt{N}).
\end{itemize}

The \textbf{To: new buffer} checkbox sends the vCard text to a new unsaved document (a \texttt{vCard(s)} heading, titled \texttt{*scratch*}) instead of downloading a file; Import reads that shape back.

There are no name, tag or property filters. \textbf{This file} respects an active narrow restriction (\hyperref[sec:org6838b46]{subtree narrowing} or \hyperref[sec:org83d8646]{Search's Narrow}), and the screen says so; narrow first, then export. A narrow applies only to the open document, never to Contacts Files.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
Org source (flat) & vCard field & Notes\\[0pt]
\hline
Heading title & \texttt{FN} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:N:} & \texttt{N} & Used as given; if absent, split from the title (last word as family name)\\[0pt]
\texttt{:EMAIL:} & \texttt{EMAIL} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:EMAIL\_LABEL:} & \texttt{LABEL="..."} on the \texttt{EMAIL} line & When present\\[0pt]
\texttt{:PHONE:}, \texttt{:CELL:} & \texttt{TEL} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:PHONE\_LABEL:} & \texttt{LABEL="..."} on the \texttt{TEL} line & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:WORK\_PHONE:} & \texttt{TEL;TYPE=WORK} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:ADDRESS:}, \texttt{:ADR:} & \texttt{ADR} & Placed in the street component, since an address is one free-text string here\\[0pt]
\texttt{:ADDRESS\_LABEL:} & \texttt{LABEL="..."} on the \texttt{ADR} line & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:ADDRESS\_RAW:} & The structured \texttt{;;street;city;region;postal;country} part of \texttt{ADR} & The seven components, kept verbatim and used when present\\[0pt]
\texttt{:NICKNAME:} & \texttt{NICKNAME} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:ORG:} & \texttt{ORG} & Several \texttt{;}-separated parts are joined into one string\\[0pt]
\texttt{:JOB\_TITLE:} & \texttt{TITLE} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:URL:} & \texttt{URL} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:URL\_LABEL:} & \texttt{LABEL="..."} on the \texttt{URL} line & \\[0pt]
\texttt{:PHOTO:} & \texttt{PHOTO} & An \texttt{http} or \texttt{https} URL as is; an embedded photo as a \texttt{data:} URI (to display photos, see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{\texttt{org-xx-startup-with-show-photos}})\\[0pt]
\texttt{:NOTE:} & \texttt{NOTE} & \\[0pt]
A heading's tags & \texttt{CATEGORIES} & \texttt{:CATEGORIES\_RAW:} is preferred when present\\[0pt]
\texttt{:CATEGORIES\_RAW:} & \texttt{CATEGORIES} & The original comma-separated text; tags can't hold spaces, so "Other Account" would otherwise become \texttt{Other\_Account}\\[0pt]
\texttt{org-contacts-birthday-property} (default \texttt{BIRTHDAY}) & \texttt{BDAY} & Accepts a bare \texttt{YYYY-MM-DD} with no description\\[0pt]
\texttt{:ANNIVERSARY:} & \texttt{ANNIVERSARY} (\texttt{YYYYMMDD}) & A vCard 4.0 property, written in the 3.0 card as a phone's own export does\\[0pt]
\texttt{:SPOUSE:} & \texttt{RELATED;TYPE=spouse;VALUE=text} & Likewise\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
Tree style \texttt{:FIELDTYPE:} & vCard field & Notes\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{name} & The contact itself & Needs \texttt{:KIND: individual} on the same heading\\[0pt]
\texttt{n} & \texttt{N} & Used as given; else split from the title\\[0pt]
\texttt{cell} & \texttt{TEL;TYPE=CELL} & A \texttt{:LABEL:} property becomes a \texttt{LABEL="..."} parameter, here and in the rows below\\[0pt]
\texttt{phone}, \texttt{phone-work}, \texttt{phone-home} & \texttt{TEL}, \texttt{TEL;TYPE=WORK}, \texttt{TEL;TYPE=HOME} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{email}, \texttt{email-work}, \texttt{email-home} & \texttt{EMAIL}, \texttt{EMAIL;TYPE=WORK}, \texttt{EMAIL;TYPE=HOME} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{address} & \texttt{ADR} & Street component. A \texttt{:RAW:} property holds the seven preserved components, and a \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_VERSE} or \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_QUOTE} block in the body becomes the \texttt{LABEL}\\[0pt]
\texttt{address-work}, \texttt{address-home} & \texttt{ADR;TYPE=WORK}, \texttt{ADR;TYPE=HOME} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{nickname} & \texttt{NICKNAME} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{org} & \texttt{ORG} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{job-title} & \texttt{TITLE} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{url} & \texttt{URL} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{photo} & \texttt{PHOTO} & A URL is the heading's title. An embedded photo is titled "Photo", with its \texttt{data:} URI in a \texttt{:DATA:} property\\[0pt]
\texttt{note} & \texttt{NOTE} & Read from a \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_VERSE} or \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_QUOTE} block in the body, not the title\\[0pt]
\texttt{birthday} & \texttt{BDAY} & A bare \texttt{YYYY-MM-DD} is accepted\\[0pt]
\texttt{anniversary} & \texttt{ANNIVERSARY} & \\[0pt]
\texttt{spouse} & \texttt{RELATED;TYPE=spouse} & \\[0pt]

\end{tabular}

Both styles cover the same set of fields, which is smaller than org-vcard's full mapping. \texttt{:PREFERRED:} is read but does not change field order or add a \texttt{PREF} parameter.

\subsubsection{What is dropped}
\label{sec:orga2c5e1d}

Property drawers and \texttt{ARCHIVE\_*} properties (see \hyperref[sec:org2712015]{Archiving}) are not exported. SCHEDULED and DEADLINE show as a small italic line under the heading in HTML, and in ODT when \texttt{p:t} is set (Emacs leaves them out of ODT by default); Calendar is built from them.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Import}
\label{sec:orgdb5a142}
\textbf{More → Import} reads \textbf{Contacts (.vcf)} and \textbf{iCalendar (.ics)}, each in its own panel (palette: \texttt{org-vcard-import}, \texttt{icalendar-import-file}). Each import appends new headings to the end of the open document and touches nothing already there. The sources are \textbf{Choose a file…}, \textbf{Choose a heading…} and \textbf{This file} (headings whose bodies start with \texttt{BEGIN:VCARD} or \texttt{BEGIN:VCALENDAR}, such as Export's \textbf{To: new buffer} output). The \textbf{To: new buffer} checkbox sends the result to a new unsaved \texttt{*scratch*} document instead.

\textbf{Contacts (.vcf)} is the reverse of \hyperref[sec:org8e45f5f]{Contacts (.vcf) export}; one file can hold many contacts. Choose \textbf{Tree} (default) or \textbf{Flat}; exporting and importing again gives an equivalent vCard. Only \texttt{FN} is required; \texttt{N}, \texttt{EMAIL}, \texttt{TEL}, \texttt{ADR}, \texttt{URL}, \texttt{NICKNAME}, \texttt{ORG}, \texttt{TITLE}, \texttt{PHOTO}, \texttt{NOTE}, \texttt{BDAY}, \texttt{ANNIVERSARY}, \texttt{RELATED;TYPE=spouse} and \texttt{CATEGORIES} (as tags) are mapped, the reverse of Export's tables. \texttt{N} is kept as given, \texttt{ADR}'s components are joined into one string, folded lines are unfolded and escapes reversed.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Apple and Google labels}: \texttt{itemN.} grouping, with \texttt{X-ABLabel}, becomes \texttt{:EMAIL\_LABEL:}, \texttt{:PHONE\_LABEL:} or \texttt{:URL\_LABEL:} (Flat) or a \texttt{:LABEL:} on the field heading (Tree). Apple's placeholder forms are reduced to their inner name.
\item \textbf{Clean data (Google, Apple)}, on by default: keeps Google's eighth \texttt{ADR} component alongside the seven so export can rebuild the original, and turns Google's \texttt{\textbackslash{}:} back into \texttt{:}.
\item \textbf{Flat} keeps one value per field type (the first), so use Tree to keep them all. In Tree each value is its own descendant heading; \texttt{address-work} and \texttt{address-home} keep \texttt{TYPE=WORK} and \texttt{HOME}, and a value with newlines (a note, a multi-line address) becomes a fixed title with its text in a \texttt{\#+BEGIN\_VERSE} block.
\item Properties the importer doesn't know are listed once by name in the status message; a base64 \texttt{PHOTO} is kept as a \texttt{data:} URI and counted. A line that is not a property is named in the same message, and the rest is imported.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{iCalendar (.ics)} is the reverse of \hyperref[sec:org8e45f5f]{Calendar (.ics) export} and reads calendars from Google, Apple, Outlook or Nextcloud. Each event becomes a heading and each task a TODO heading.

\begin{itemize}
\item An event's time is a timestamp in the title: \texttt{* Dentist <2026-10-05 Mon 09:00-10:30>}. An all-day event has a date only; a multi-day event is a range.
\item Times are shown in this device's time zone; UTC and named zones (\texttt{TZID}) are converted, as \texttt{icalendar-import-file} does. A time with no zone, or in a zone name the browser doesn't know, is kept as written and the status line says so.
\item \texttt{LOCATION}, \texttt{URL} and \texttt{UID} become properties, \texttt{CATEGORIES} tags, \texttt{DESCRIPTION} the body, and a cancelled event keeps \texttt{:STATUS: CANCELLED}.
\item A recurrence a repeater can express (\texttt{FREQ} with \texttt{INTERVAL}, such as \texttt{+1w}) becomes one. Any other rule (an end date or \texttt{COUNT}, several weekdays, "the second Tuesday", \texttt{EXDATE} exceptions) becomes a diary expression, \texttt{<\%\%(and (org-cyclic 7 2026 10 5) (org-block 2026 10 5 2026 12 7))>}, built from Org's own \texttt{org-cyclic}, \texttt{org-date}, \texttt{org-block} and \texttt{diary-float}; the agenda has no time of day for these, so the time goes first in the title (\texttt{* 09:00 Standup}). \texttt{COUNT} is turned into an end date. Only a rule those cannot say (\texttt{INTERVAL} with several weekdays, or on a monthly or yearly rule, \texttt{FREQ=HOURLY}) is imported once at its first date with the rule in an \texttt{:RRULE:} property, and the status line counts them.
\item A task (\texttt{VTODO}) becomes \texttt{TODO}, or \texttt{DONE} with \texttt{CLOSED} once completed; \texttt{DUE} is its \texttt{DEADLINE}, \texttt{DTSTART} its \texttt{SCHEDULED}, \texttt{PRIORITY} becomes \texttt{[\#A]} to \texttt{[\#C]}.
\item \texttt{ORGANIZER} and \texttt{ATTENDEE} become \texttt{:ORGANIZER:} and \texttt{:ATTENDEES:} properties, \texttt{ATTACH} links become list lines under the heading, and a reminder (\texttt{VALARM}) becomes \texttt{:APPT\_WARNTIME:} in minutes, as \texttt{appt} reads it. Anything else not carried over is named in the status line.
\end{itemize}

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Help}
\label{sec:org43084b9}
Open Help from the palette's \textbf{Help} (or god-mode's \texttt{h SPC m}). It is this file, \texttt{README.org}, opened read-only in its own last tab, with \texttt{\#+STARTUP: show2levels}. The \texttt{examples/} folder has a file for each feature, with the results Emacs gives.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Settings}
\label{sec:org5be3190}
\textbf{More (⋮) → Settings} opens a list of six categories, each a page of small cards: \textbf{Appearance}, \textbf{Editing and startup}, \textbf{Agenda, diary and weather}, \textbf{Sync and storage}, \textbf{Export} and \textbf{Advanced}. A number on a category counts what you have set there. \textbf{Search settings} finds a card from any category. On a wide window (about 720 px) the categories become a sidebar. Settings reopens on the page you left. At the foot of the list \textbf{Check for updates} shows the version and, if a newer one is installed, a banner offers \textbf{Reload} (the Android app has no button). \textbf{Order of settings} (Advanced) moves categories and cards with ▲ ▼ and travels with \textbf{Export Settings}.

The cards:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Startup}, \textbf{Editing}, \textbf{Modeline}, \textbf{Keyboard}, \textbf{Progress logging}, \textbf{Search \& tags}, \textbf{Agenda}, \textbf{Diary}, \textbf{Weather}, \textbf{ASCII} and \textbf{Advanced (raw syntax)}: labeled controls for the Global and Local Variables (see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables}), each on the category page above that fits it; \textbf{Advanced (raw syntax)} holds those with complex syntax. They share storage with the \textbf{Global Variables} text box, so each reflects the other.
\item \textbf{GitHub} and \textbf{WebDAV}: connection details. Use a fine-grained GitHub token scoped to one repository (Contents read and write only), and for WebDAV an app-specific password if offered. \textbf{Calendar (CalDAV) / Contacts (CardDAV)} follow (see \hyperref[sec:orgac99be7]{Calendar and contacts sync}).
\item \textbf{Protect connections}: \textbf{Protect with a passphrase…} (at least 8 characters) encrypts the GitHub token and owner and the logins of WebDAV, the calendar and contacts. The passphrase is asked for when one of them is first used in a session and is not stored; \textbf{Export Settings} writes the logins encrypted and \textbf{Import Settings} asks for the file's passphrase.
\item \textbf{Settings history} (Advanced): \textbf{Undo} and \textbf{Redo} name the setting they change, the list shows this session's changes (up to 100) and a tap goes to that point, and \textbf{Restore from start of session} returns to the first entry. The palette has \textbf{Undo settings change} and \textbf{Redo settings change}. Logins and actions such as \textbf{Sync} are not followed, and Undo in a document never changes settings.
\item \textbf{Agenda notifications} (see \hyperref[sec:org3415eb2]{Agenda notifications}), \textbf{Attachments} (whether \textbf{Attach} adds a link; see \hyperref[sec:orgc5944b1]{Attachments}), \textbf{Extensions} (see \hyperref[sec:orgaf1b952]{Extensions}) and \textbf{Pending Local Changes} (files with edits not yet written back).
\item \textbf{Appearance}: theme (System, Light or Dark), fonts, independent sizes for main text, tables and menus, reading width, custom colors for Light and Dark, and \textbf{Paragraph Spacing} (0 to 32px, default 10px, separately for paragraphs and for tables and other blocks; where they meet the larger value applies).
\item \textbf{Backup}: \textbf{Export Settings} saves everything as JSON; \textbf{Import Settings} merges a file back in.
\item \textbf{Export} (ASCII, HTML, \LaTeX{}): one card per type. \textbf{HTML} sets a \textbf{Preamble}, \textbf{Postamble} and \textbf{Head}, with an option for a table of contents with page numbers when printing; \textbf{\LaTeX{}} sets the class and compiler, a Lisp box for classes, packages and the source block backend, and the wide-TOC fix. Each HTML and \LaTeX{} text item has a tick box and is off until ticked; a ticked item applies to every export whose file doesn't set its own. \textbf{Format codes} lists \texttt{\%t}, \texttt{\%a}, \texttt{\%d} and the rest. A text box opens in a large editor with \textbf{OK}, \textbf{Cancel} and \textbf{Reset}.
\end{itemize}

A file's own \texttt{\#+STARTUP:} or Local Variables block still overrides an app-wide default set here.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Offline behavior and sync}
\label{sec:org8e03395}
Edits are cached locally at once; writing to disk, GitHub or WebDAV happens only on an explicit Save.

\textbf{Conflict detection}: Save compares the file's current state with what the app last knew, so one version never silently overwrites the other. The app also checks for external changes when a file is opened, when the tab regains focus, and when you switch into a tab with real backing storage. A banner then appears with \textbf{Merge}, \textbf{Reload} and \textbf{Dismiss}. For a local file this background check never asks the browser for permission: it runs only if access is already granted, so the banner may not appear until you have saved or reloaded the file in the session. Save, Reload and Merge still ask when they need to.

\textbf{Saved in another window}: if another window of the app saved the same file while this one has unsaved edits, Save asks \textbf{Merge}, \textbf{Overwrite} or \textbf{Cancel}. Merge combines the two and leaves the Save to you, Overwrite replaces the other window's save, and Cancel (or Escape) saves nothing.

\textbf{Resolving a conflict}: the app keeps the full text of the file as of the last successful open or save, the common ancestor a three-way merge needs. When Save finds the file changed elsewhere under your unsaved edits, it compares the ancestor, your version and the other one line by line:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The other version has no real change, or matches yours}: Save just proceeds. A server that changes a file's ETag without changing its content isn't a conflict.
\item \textbf{Your changes and theirs are in different places}: they are combined automatically and Save completes with a status message (\texttt{Saved — merged with the changes made elsewhere}). The merge is its own undo step (\textbf{Merged with changes from elsewhere}), so Undo returns to your text from just before it.
\item \textbf{A subtree moved on one side and edited on the other}: when the line merge would clash, the app merges by heading instead. The moved subtree arrives in its new place with the other side's edits, a promoted or demoted heading keeps its children, and a heading is the same heading after a TODO state or tag change (or any title change, when it has an \texttt{:ID:}). Siblings reordered on one side merge with edits on the other. It merges only when it is sure: two headings with the same title and no \texttt{:ID:}, a heading deleted on one side and edited on the other, or one moved to two different places, still go to the dialog below.
\item \textbf{Both sides changed the same lines}, or adjacent lines with no unchanged line between them (the same place, as in git and GNU diff3): a dialog lists each such region with your version and the other one. Choose \textbf{Yours}, \textbf{Other} or \textbf{Both} (yours, then theirs) for each, or \textbf{All yours} or \textbf{All other} for every region at once. \textbf{Apply} stays disabled until every region has a decision, and everything outside the regions is already combined. \textbf{Cancel}, Escape or tapping outside changes nothing: the other version is untouched, your edits stay unsaved, and the next Save raises the same conflict.
\item \textbf{No common ancestor is known} (a file last synced by a version that didn't keep one, until its next open or save), or the two versions are too different to compare by lines: every difference, or the whole file as one choice, is shown for you to decide.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Two windows of the app}: saves of one file take turns, so they never interleave. When one window saves a file that another has open, the other reloads it if it has no unsaved edits, and otherwise shows the same banner.

\textbf{The banner's Merge} does the same without waiting for Save. It combines your unsaved edits with the version now stored, asks about clashing regions in the same dialog, and applies the result as an ordinary, undoable, still-unsaved edit. The other version becomes the new baseline, so the Save that follows is a plain write. With no unsaved changes Merge just reloads, and a read-only buffer can't be merged into (make it writable first).

\textbf{Same new heading on both sides}: two sides that each add the same new heading in different places keep both. A clean automatic merge is still worth a glance; that is what the undo step is for.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsubsection{Long lists}
\label{sec:orgcf461c4}
An outline or agenda with more than 400 rows draws only the rows near the screen, plus a couple of screens either side; the rest are blank space of the same height, so scrolling, folding, search, links, the back button, moving and dragging headings work as in a short file. \texttt{org-xx-windowing-threshold} (Settings → Editing) sets the row count, and \texttt{0} draws every row. Your browser's own Find (Ctrl-F) sees only the rows drawn, and so does Find on the Agenda; the app's Search looks through the whole file. Windowing is off while \texttt{display-line-numbers-mode} is on, and the Text view is not affected.

\subsubsection{Size limits}
\label{sec:orgfe6fddc}
A size variable that holds something that is not a size shows a message naming the variable and its value, and the action that needed it is not done. One that is not set keeps its default.

A large file can make the app slow, so each kind has a size at which it asks and one at which it refuses; the \texttt{org-xx-size-limit-*} variables change them in Global Variables, for example \texttt{(setq org-xx-size-limit-org-file "4MB")}, and \texttt{nil} removes a limit. An Org file above 500KB asks "This is large and may be slow. Open anyway?" and above 2MB is not opened; the same limit applies to a file read for the Agenda, a refile or a capture. A picture above 3MB is not shown inline: it appears as its size with a \textbf{Load} link. An attachment above 20MB asks before it is attached, and above 95MB is refused. Bibliography, \texttt{\#+SETUPFILE:} and \texttt{\#+INCLUDE:} files above their limits are skipped, and the app says so. A download that has not started answering after 30 seconds stops with a message. Pasting into the Text view asks or refuses at the same Org file sizes, and \texttt{\#+INCLUDE:} files together cannot grow a document past the limit. A calendar, CalDAV or WebDAV reply above 32MB is refused. Pictures linked from a web address are not limited.

\subsection{Platform support}
\label{sec:orgb821724}
Local file access ("Local", a live writable handle) requires the File System Access API -- Chrome/Edge, desktop or Android. Not supported on iOS, a WebKit limitation.

On unsupported platforms, \textbf{Import} replaces "Local": pick a file, edit it, and Save downloads the new version for you to move into place yourself. GitHub and WebDAV work the same everywhere, including iOS.

\textbf{Sharing into the app}: Android's Share sheet and the icon's \textbf{Capture} shortcut work for the installed app. iOS has no equivalent, so use the clipboard (\texttt{\%x}); see \hyperref[sec:orgaef253e]{Capturing from other apps}.

\subsubsection{Android app}
\label{sec:orgd336588}
The Android app is the same app in a native wrapper, with a few things done the Android way.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Local files}: \textbf{File → Open → This device} lists the org-pwa folder, and \textbf{Choose another file…} uses Android's file picker; the app keeps access to a picked file, so Save writes straight back and the file reopens from the recent list. \textbf{Save As → This device} names a new one. The picker starts in \texttt{Documents/org-pwa}, in the shared Documents folder where a file manager finds it, and you can choose any other folder. A file is known by its name, so two files with the same name from different folders replace each other.
\item \textbf{Agenda files}: \texttt{local:name.org} names a file in the org-pwa folder (below), like \texttt{github:journal.org;local:home.org}. It needs no prompt, and Refile and Replace can write into it while a local file is open; a file you opened with \textbf{Open → Local file} works too, and so does one added with the command \textbf{Add a local file} (command palette), which remembers the file without opening it.
\item \textbf{Attaching a file}: \textbf{Attach} opens Android's chooser with the camera apps beside your files, as the browser's does. Pick \textbf{Take a photo} or \textbf{Record a video}, and the result is attached. With \texttt{org-attach-method} \texttt{mv} or \texttt{ln} (or \textbf{Attach and move}, \textbf{Attach a link}) the document picker opens instead, with no camera: a move asks before deleting the original, and a link keeps reading the original file, so it stays where it is.
\item \textbf{Saving a file out}: exports and settings backups go straight into the \textbf{Downloads} folder, and the status line says so.
\item \textbf{The org-pwa folder}: the first time something needs it (a local file's first attachment, or a \texttt{local:} name that isn't found), the app asks you to choose a folder, starting at \texttt{Documents/org-pwa}. Attachments go under \texttt{data/} inside it, as on GitHub and WebDAV, and \texttt{local:} files are found in it by name, anywhere a \texttt{github:} or \texttt{webdav:} file can be named: \texttt{org-agenda-files}, \texttt{org-contacts-files}, \texttt{org-refile-targets}, a capture template's \texttt{file}, a link or \texttt{\#+INCLUDE}. \texttt{local:contacts.org} is \texttt{contacts.org} in that folder, and \texttt{local:areas/home.org} is \texttt{home.org} in its \texttt{areas} folder. A file you opened with the file picker is found by its name first. \textbf{Choose the org-pwa folder} changes it.
\item \textbf{Reminders}: agenda notifications (see \hyperref[sec:org3415eb2]{Agenda notifications}) are handed to Android, so they arrive with the app closed. Allow notifications when asked; without the \textbf{Alarms \& reminders} setting they may be a few minutes late.
\item \textbf{Long-press the app icon}: your capture templates are listed, in the order they are in the Lisp init, as many as the launcher shows. Tapping one opens that template. Drag one onto the home screen for an icon, or run \textbf{Add a capture icon to the home screen}.
\item \textbf{Sharing in}: share a link or text from any app to \textbf{org-pwa}; Capture opens with it (see \hyperref[sec:orgaef253e]{Capturing from other apps}).
\item \textbf{Separate from the browser}: the app keeps its own settings, tokens and documents, so enter GitHub, WebDAV, calendar and contacts settings again. A WebDAV, CalDAV or CardDAV server must allow the origin \texttt{https://localhost} (CORS).
\item \textbf{Updates}: the app is updated by installing a newer APK over the old one. \textbf{Settings → Updates} shows which version you have.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Screen size}: mobile-first below 900px wide. Above that, Settings and Help open in a resizable side panel next to the outline instead of replacing it, and the app uses the full window width. Reading width is unlimited by default; Settings → Appearance has an opt-in narrower column.

No auto-capitalization anywhere in this app.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Command palette}
\label{sec:org9fe54f3}
A searchable list of what the app can do, the touch counterpart of Emacs's \texttt{M-x}. Open it from \textbf{More → Commands} (first by default) or, from a keyboard, in \hyperref[sec:org24e47cb]{god-mode} with \texttt{g x} (which is \texttt{M-x}) or \texttt{h SPC a} (\texttt{C-h a}).

\textbf{Searching}: type a few letters or words. Each word must match the command's name, the real Org or Emacs command it corresponds to, or one of a few extra keywords (so \texttt{deadline} finds \textbf{Edit details}). Case doesn't matter. Real names work as you'd type them in \texttt{M-x}: \texttt{org-clock-in} finds \textbf{Clock in} but not \textbf{Clock out}, because a hyphenated word is matched as that exact phrase, while \texttt{clock in} typed with a space is two words that can match anywhere. A category name (\textbf{Clocking}, \textbf{Heading}, \textbf{Export}) also matches at the start of its words. There is no fuzzy or skip-letter matching.

\textbf{Order}: commands that can run now come first, then the rest, dimmed, each saying why it can't (\textbf{nothing is narrowed}, \textbf{no clock is running}, \textbf{the buffer is read-only}, \textbf{tap a heading first}). A command is never mysteriously absent, and choosing a dimmed one repeats the reason as a status message. With nothing typed, your most recently used commands come first (marked \texttt{↺}), remembered across sessions. ↑ and ↓ move the highlight, Enter or a tap runs it, and Escape or a tap outside closes it.

\textbf{What it acts on}: heading commands work on the heading whose action menu is open (tap a heading's title first), else the keyboard-focused heading. A command that needs a heading and can't find one says so, except \textbf{Add heading after} and \textbf{Add TODO heading after}, which also work with nothing selected (see the table in \hyperref[sec:org956255c]{Keybindings} for where the new heading lands).

\textbf{Names}: a command's real Emacs or Org function name is shown beside it and is searchable. The same name, quoted, names the command in an Extras-menu entry (see \hyperref[sec:org17e454c]{Extras menu}), so the palette, the god-mode chords and Extras share one vocabulary. The commands with no real name are this app's own: \textbf{New document}, \textbf{Undo history}, \textbf{Undo settings change}, \textbf{Redo settings change}, \textbf{Sync agenda to calendar}, \textbf{Rebuild calendar from the agenda}, \textbf{Show display measurements}, \textbf{Copy keyboard debug log}, \textbf{Copy update and startup log}, \textbf{Add a capture icon to the home screen}, \textbf{Choose the org-pwa folder} and \textbf{Add a local file}. A command with a \hyperref[sec:org24e47cb]{god-mode} key runs the same code as that key and shows it.

\textbf{What's in it}, by group:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Group & Commands\\[0pt]
\hline
\textbf{Heading} & cycle TODO state, set priority, set effort estimate, edit details (schedule, deadline, timestamps, tags, properties), add heading or TODO heading after, promote, demote, move up, move down, cut, paste, archive, unarchive, refile, attachments, narrow, widen\\[0pt]
\textbf{Clocking} & clock in, clock out, cancel clock, continue last clock, go to clocked task, go to a recently clocked task\\[0pt]
\textbf{Document} & save, save as, open, new, undo, redo, undo history, toggle read-only, capture, recalculate all tables\\[0pt]
\textbf{View} & agenda, TODO list, outline view, text view, cycle visibility of the whole document, calendar, search, sync agenda to calendar, rebuild calendar, sync contacts to the address book, rebuild contacts\\[0pt]
\textbf{Export} & the Export menu; this file as HTML, \LaTeX{} or ASCII\\[0pt]
\textbf{Import} & Contacts (.vcf), \texttt{org-vcard-import}; iCalendar (.ics), \texttt{icalendar-import-file}\\[0pt]
\textbf{App} & settings, help, show display measurements, copy keyboard debug log, copy security diagnostics, copy update and startup log, add a capture icon to the home screen and choose the org-pwa folder (Android app only)\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Also in it}: your own capture templates and \hyperref[sec:org17e454c]{Extras menu} entries, one command each. \textbf{Capture: <description>} (such as \textbf{Capture: Meeting}) runs that template of the Lisp init directly, and \textbf{Extras: <label>} runs that Extras entry as tapping it would. Both are read fresh each time the palette opens, so an edited Lisp init or a document's own Extras menu (set in its Local Variables) is current. The plain \textbf{Capture} command still opens the template picker.

\textbf{Commands}, like the other More entries, can be renamed, hidden or reordered with \hyperref[sec:orgdebc8db]{menu customization} (\texttt{org-xx-menu-aliases}). It is the ordinary \texttt{more:} label \texttt{Commands}, which renders first by default.


\subsection{Security and privacy}
\label{sec:org713f915}
There is no server of ours: the app talks only to the places you set up, and nothing is sent anywhere else.

\textbf{Where things are kept.} Your files stay where they are (a file on the device, GitHub or WebDAV). The app keeps its settings in the browser's own storage on this device, including the GitHub token, the WebDAV, calendar and contacts passwords, and the init script. They are stored as plain text, as in any browser app, so use a token limited to one repository and an app-specific password, and sign out of a shared device by clearing its site data. Nothing but what you set up is synced, exported or read from a file.

\textbf{What can run.} Only the app's own code runs in the page. The page's Content-Security-Policy refuses inline and injected scripts. Code from a document or the init script runs in a \hyperref[sec:orgaf1b952]{sandbox} with no access to the page, your files or your tokens. It reaches a server only if you allow it.

\textbf{Check the sandbox.} \texttt{Copy security diagnostics} (palette, App) starts the sandbox on your device and asks it what it can reach. The first line is \texttt{PASS: no native bridge reachable from sandboxed code}, or \texttt{FAIL:} with what was found. OK copies the report; paste it when reporting a problem.

\subsection{Keybindings}
\label{sec:org956255c}
A practical subset for a keyboard or mouse. On a phone or tablet it applies only to a paired Bluetooth keyboard.

These are \textbf{not org's own bindings}, on purpose. Org leans on the \texttt{C-c} prefix, and \texttt{C-c}, \texttt{C-v}, \texttt{C-a} and \texttt{C-f} are reserved by browsers for copy, paste, select-all and find, so a page can't reliably take them; org's \texttt{M-←} and \texttt{M-→} collide with the browser's back and forward. Where org's key is safe it is used as is; otherwise a safe key stands in. god-mode (below) reaches org's fuller set.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
Key & Action & Matches real org?\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{↓}, \texttt{↑} & Move keyboard focus to the next or previous visible line: any row (heading, paragraph, table, list item, block). Moving down into a folded heading reveals its first body row. A status message reports the first or last line & No equivalent\\[0pt]
\texttt{S-↓}, \texttt{S-↑}, \texttt{S-←}, \texttt{S-→} & Only with focus on a table: move cell by cell (the header row counts; a rule between rows doesn't). Outside a table they aren't intercepted. After you edit a cell by tap, \texttt{Enter} commits and \texttt{Escape} cancels (the \textbf{⎌} button does the same by tap), and the cell stays highlighted for more Shift+arrow navigation. Clicking anything that isn't a table cell clears it & No equivalent\\[0pt]
\texttt{i} & Edit the current line (heading title, paragraph, table cell or list item), cursor at the start & Like vim's \texttt{i}\\[0pt]
\texttt{j}, \texttt{k} & Move focus to the next or previous visible heading, faster than \texttt{↓} and \texttt{↑}. A status message reports the first or last heading & Vim-style\\[0pt]
\texttt{Tab} & Cycle the focused heading's fold state & Yes, \texttt{org-cycle}\\[0pt]
\texttt{Enter} & Open or close the focused heading's action row & No equivalent\\[0pt]
\texttt{/} & Focus the search box & A web convention\\[0pt]
\texttt{Escape} & The first that applies: cancel a god-mode sequence, exit god-mode, clear keyboard focus, enter god-mode & A web convention, extended for god-mode\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Keyboard focus, a thin highlight around the focused row, is separate from tapping a heading open. It starts unset; the first arrow, \texttt{j} or \texttt{k} picks the first or last visible heading, and shortcuts that need the focused heading do nothing until one exists. \texttt{Tab} follows the same archived-heading rule as the swipe gesture (see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables}). Shortcuts never fire while you are typing in a text field, and Ctrl and Cmd combinations are never intercepted, so the browser's copy, paste and find stay safe.

Cycling TODO state, moving a heading, promoting and demoting, and inserting a heading are available by tap, in god-mode (\texttt{c t}, \texttt{g↑} and \texttt{g↓}, \texttt{g←} and \texttt{g→}, \texttt{gRET}), and from the command palette (\textbf{Add heading after}).

\subsubsection{god-mode}
\label{sec:org24e47cb}
An alternate input mode that reaches org's fuller keybinding set (\texttt{C-c C-t}, \texttt{M-RET} and the rest) without the browser seeing a held Ctrl or Alt. \texttt{Escape} turns it on, or on a phone the \textbf{[g]} button does (\hyperref[sec:orgac2144a]{below}). While it is on, every key is part of a sequence, which the minibuffer (see \hyperref[sec:orgf259c86]{Modeline and minibuffer}) echoes; when one completes it names what ran, as \texttt{God-mode · C-c C-x C-j → Go to clocked task}. \texttt{examples/god-mode.org} has sequences to try.

God-mode starts on the heading you last used, or the row at the top of the screen. While a sequence is in progress, a card under the top bar lists the keys that would continue it, as which-key does; each entry is a button, so a whole chord can be completed by tapping (a key that leads on is marked \texttt{…}). \texttt{Escape} cancels. Opening an overlay panel (Extras, Settings, Capture, Search, the menus, History, the Calendar) exits god-mode, and \texttt{Escape} closes the open panel first; Help opened with \texttt{h SPC m} is the exception.

The translation rules follow real god-mode.el (github.com/emacsorphanage/god-mode), plus the \texttt{c} rule, which is this app's own:

\begin{itemize}
\item A plain key means Control: \texttt{t} is \texttt{C-t}.
\item \texttt{g} prefixes the next key with Meta (\texttt{g↑} is \texttt{M-↑}), so a bare \texttt{C-g} can't be typed. \texttt{G} (Shift+g) prefixes Control+Meta (\texttt{Gn} is \texttt{C-M-n}).
\item \texttt{SPC} toggles literal mode: following keys are typed with no modifier until \texttt{SPC} is pressed again. \texttt{c SPC g} is \texttt{C-c g}, not \texttt{C-c C-g}.
\item A named key (arrow, Tab, Return) typed bare is never controlled, so ordinary movement keeps working.
\item \texttt{c} as the first key gives \texttt{C-c} and starts an org-style chain: further letters are controlled too (\texttt{c t} is \texttt{C-c C-t}, \texttt{c c} is \texttt{C-c C-c}) while punctuation stays literal (\texttt{C-c .}, \texttt{C-c |}). One \texttt{c} is enough for any \texttt{C-c C-<letter>} command.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
god-mode sequence & Emacs chord & Action\\[0pt]
\hline
\texttt{↓}, \texttt{↑} & \texttt{<down>}, \texttt{<up>} & Next or previous visible line; inside a table, the next or previous row\\[0pt]
\texttt{←}, \texttt{→} & \texttt{<left>}, \texttt{<right>} & Collapse or expand the heading; inside a table, the previous or next column\\[0pt]
\texttt{S-↓}, \texttt{S-↑}, \texttt{S-←}, \texttt{S-→} (the floating \textbf{S} then an arrow, or Shift+arrow) & \texttt{S-<down>}, \texttt{S-<up>}, \texttt{S-<left>}, \texttt{S-<right>} & On a focused heading: move it down or up among its siblings, promote it (left) or demote it (right), like the heading's action buttons. In a table they move between cells. With nothing focused, \texttt{S-↓} and \texttt{S-↑} go to the next or previous heading. On a laptop, \textasciitilde{}Alt\textasciitilde{}+arrow moves, promotes and demotes the heading from anywhere, even in a table\\[0pt]
\texttt{S-←}, \texttt{S-→} & \texttt{S-<left>}, \texttt{S-<right>} & Table cell to the left or right\\[0pt]
\texttt{i} & (not a chord) & Edit the current line, cursor at the start (see \texttt{a} and \texttt{e})\\[0pt]
\texttt{a} & \texttt{C-a} & Before \texttt{i}: put the cursor at the start of the line\\[0pt]
\texttt{e} & \texttt{C-e} & Before \texttt{i}: put the cursor at the end of the line\\[0pt]
\texttt{Tab} & \texttt{Tab} & Cycle the focused heading's fold state\\[0pt]
\texttt{S-Tab} & \texttt{S-Tab} & Cycle the whole document (overview, fully shown)\\[0pt]
\texttt{←}, \texttt{→} & \texttt{<left>}, \texttt{<right>} & Collapse the focused heading fully, or expand it one level\\[0pt]
\texttt{g↑}, \texttt{g↓} & \texttt{M-↑}, \texttt{M-↓} & Move the focused heading up or down among its siblings (in a table: the row)\\[0pt]
\texttt{g←}, \texttt{g→} & \texttt{M-←}, \texttt{M-→} & Promote or demote the focused heading with its subtree (in a table: move the column)\\[0pt]
\texttt{gS-←}, \texttt{gS-→} & \texttt{M-S-←}, \texttt{M-S-→} & The same (there is no separate whole-subtree action); in a table: delete or insert a column\\[0pt]
\texttt{gS-↑}, \texttt{gS-↓} & \texttt{M-S-↑}, \texttt{M-S-↓} & In a table: delete the row; insert a row above\\[0pt]
\texttt{c -}, \texttt{c RET}, \texttt{c \textasciicircum{}} & \texttt{C-c -}, \texttt{C-c RET}, \texttt{C-c \textasciicircum{}} & In a table: insert a rule; insert a rule and go to the next row; sort\\[0pt]
\texttt{c f}, \texttt{c b} & \texttt{C-c C-f}, \texttt{C-c C-b} & Focus the next or previous heading at the same level; a status message says when there is none\\[0pt]
\texttt{c u} & \texttt{C-c C-u} & Focus the parent heading (a status message at the top level)\\[0pt]
\texttt{c n}, \texttt{c p} & \texttt{C-c C-n}, \texttt{C-c C-p} & Focus the next or previous visible heading, at any level\\[0pt]
\texttt{c SPC l} & \texttt{C-c l} & Copy an \texttt{[[id:…]]} link to the focused heading (\texttt{org-store-link})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c x w} & \texttt{C-c C-x C-w} & Cut the focused heading and its subtree to the clipboard (\texttt{org-cut-subtree})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c x y} & \texttt{C-c C-x C-y} & Paste a subtree after the focused heading at its level, shifting the pasted levels to match (\texttt{org-paste-subtree})\\[0pt]
\texttt{x SPC n s} & \texttt{C-x n s} & \hyperref[sec:org6838b46]{Narrow} to the focused heading's subtree\\[0pt]
\texttt{x SPC n w} & \texttt{C-x n w} & \hyperref[sec:org6838b46]{Widen}: remove any narrowing\\[0pt]
\texttt{x SPC x r} & \texttt{C-x x r} & \textbf{Rename buffer…} (\texttt{rename-buffer}): ask for a new name in the minibuffer. An empty name or one another buffer has is refused; the file is not touched\\[0pt]
\texttt{gRET} & \texttt{M-RET} & Insert a heading after the focused one, as its sibling. With nothing focused, an empty document gets a heading at the top and a document with headings gets one at the bottom\\[0pt]
\texttt{gS-RET} & \texttt{M-S-RET} & The same, with a TODO keyword\\[0pt]
\texttt{c t} & \texttt{C-c C-t} & Cycle the focused heading's TODO state; with no state and more than one \texttt{\#+TODO:} workflow, open a state picker\\[0pt]
\texttt{c ,} & \texttt{C-c ,} & Cycle priority (none, A, B, C)\\[0pt]
\texttt{c v} & \texttt{C-c C-v} & Switch to the TODO view\\[0pt]
\texttt{c .}, \texttt{c !}, \texttt{c d}, \texttt{c s} & \texttt{C-c .}, \texttt{C-c !}, \texttt{C-c C-d}, \texttt{C-c C-s} & Open the details editor (SCHEDULED, DEADLINE, timestamps)\\[0pt]
\texttt{c w} & \texttt{C-c C-w} & Refile the focused heading (\texttt{org-refile}, see \hyperref[sec:org183621b]{Refile})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c a} & \texttt{C-c C-a} & Open the attachment choices (\texttt{org-attach}, see \hyperref[sec:orgc5944b1]{Attachments})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c SPC a a} & \texttt{C-c a a} & Open the Agenda view (\texttt{C-c a} waits for a second key: \texttt{t} TODO list, \texttt{m} Match, \texttt{s} Keyword search)\\[0pt]
\texttt{c SPC a t} & \texttt{C-c a t} & Open the TODO view\\[0pt]
\texttt{c SPC a m} & \texttt{C-c a m} & Open the Match view\\[0pt]
\texttt{c SPC a s} & \texttt{C-c a s} & Open the Keyword search view\\[0pt]
\texttt{c SPC c} & \texttt{C-c c} & Open Capture, which exits god-mode (see below)\\[0pt]
\texttt{h SPC m} & \texttt{C-h m} & Open Help (\texttt{describe-mode}) without exiting god-mode\\[0pt]
\texttt{s} & \texttt{C-s} & Open search; on the Agenda, TODO, Match and Keyword search screens, the next match\\[0pt]
\texttt{r} & \texttt{C-r} & The previous match on those screens\\[0pt]
\texttt{x q} & \texttt{C-x C-q} & Toggle \texttt{buffer-read-only} (see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables})\\[0pt]
\texttt{x s} & \texttt{C-x C-s} & Save (\texttt{save-buffer})\\[0pt]
\texttt{x SPC s} & \texttt{C-x s} & Offer to save every modified tab that has a file, one key each (\texttt{save-some-buffers})\\[0pt]
\texttt{x w} & \texttt{C-x C-w} & Save under a new name or place (\texttt{write-file}, Save As)\\[0pt]
\texttt{x f} & \texttt{C-x C-f} & Open a file (\texttt{find-file})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c x SPC e} & \texttt{C-c C-x e} & Set the focused heading's effort estimate (\texttt{org-set-effort}, see \hyperref[sec:org2e62d01]{Clocking})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c x i} & \texttt{C-c C-x C-i} & Clock in (\texttt{org-clock-in})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c x o} & \texttt{C-c C-x C-o} & Clock out (\texttt{org-clock-out})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c x q} & \texttt{C-c C-x C-q} & Cancel the running clock without recording its time (\texttt{org-clock-cancel})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c x x} & \texttt{C-c C-x C-x} & Resume the most recently clocked heading (\texttt{org-clock-in-last})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c x j} & \texttt{C-c C-x C-j} & Jump to the clocked-in heading, in whichever tab it runs (\texttt{org-clock-goto})\\[0pt]
\texttt{u c x j} & \texttt{C-u C-c C-x C-j} & Choose from recently clocked tasks and jump to it (\texttt{org-clock-select-task})\\[0pt]
\texttt{c e} & \texttt{C-c C-e} & Open the export dispatcher (\texttt{org-export-dispatch}, see \hyperref[sec:org8e45f5f]{Export})\\[0pt]
\texttt{f} & \texttt{C-f} & Arm the next \texttt{/} to redo instead of undo\\[0pt]
\texttt{/} & \texttt{C-/} & Undo, or redo if armed\\[0pt]
\texttt{g x} & \texttt{M-x} & Open the \hyperref[sec:org9fe54f3]{command palette}\\[0pt]
\texttt{h SPC a} & \texttt{C-h a} & The same (\texttt{apropos-command}: find the commands that match)\\[0pt]
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

A valid sequence with no equivalent here (\texttt{c c}, \texttt{c |}, \texttt{c l}, \texttt{c o}) says so instead of doing nothing.

\textbf{Pickers}: \texttt{c SPC c}, and \texttt{c t} on a heading with no state and several workflows, exit god-mode and show a picker whose options are buttons, each with a one-character hotkey when no other option shares it. \texttt{Escape} cancels.

\textbf{Help}: \texttt{h SPC m} doesn't exit god-mode; while Help is the only thing open, \texttt{Escape} cancels a sequence and then exits god-mode instead of closing Help.

\textbf{Redo}: Emacs undoes the undo after something breaks the chain (conventionally \texttt{C-f} in god-mode). Here \texttt{f} arms the next \texttt{/} to redo; \texttt{/} keeps redoing while armed, any other key disarms it, and with nothing to redo \texttt{/} undoes.

\textbf{\texttt{i}, \texttt{a} and \texttt{e}} aren't chords; they are modeled on vim and act only as the first key of a fresh sequence (\texttt{g i} is still \texttt{M-i}). \texttt{a} and \texttt{e} set where the cursor lands the next time \texttt{i} opens the editor.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsubsection{God-mode without a hardware keyboard}
\label{sec:orgac2144a}
A phone has no \texttt{Escape} key, so a floating \textbf{[g]} button (above Extras, or in its place) enters god-mode, shows a floating keyboard and brings up the device's keyboard together; tap it again to end all three. Settings → Editing and startup → \textbf{Keyboard} has \textbf{Show the floating [g] god-mode button} (\texttt{org-xx-god-mode-button}, on by default; a document's Local Variables override it).

The floating keyboard has the keys a phone keyboard can't type, as a cross: a middle row of \textbf{⌨}, \texttt{Tab}, \texttt{←}, \texttt{→}, \texttt{S} and \texttt{g}, with \texttt{↑} above and \texttt{↓} below the arrow pair.

In the Text view, \textbf{[g]} only shows the floating keyboard, with no god-mode: the arrows move the cursor (with \textbf{S} they select), \texttt{Tab} indents, and \texttt{g} is a prefix that types nothing (\texttt{g} then \texttt{↑} or \texttt{↓} moves a page, \texttt{g} then \texttt{←} or \texttt{→} goes to the start or end of the line, and \texttt{S} \texttt{g} then \texttt{↑} or \texttt{↓} goes to the start or end of the text). The palette command \textbf{Copy keyboard debug log} copies a short trail of the last taps and cursor positions to send along.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{S} shifts the next key (\texttt{Tab} becomes \texttt{S-Tab}, \texttt{g} becomes \texttt{G}, the Control+Meta prefix). After an arrow it stays on, so \texttt{S} then \texttt{↑} \texttt{↑} \texttt{↑} moves the focused heading up three places; tap \textbf{S} again to turn it off. It also shifts the next key typed on the phone keyboard, so \texttt{gS-RET} (\texttt{M-S-RET}, a TODO heading) is: tap \texttt{g}, tap \textbf{S}, tap Return. A letter typed after \textbf{S} becomes its capital.
\item \textbf{⌨} hides or shows the device keyboard and changes nothing else. It is lit while the keyboard is up. After a popup closes, the keyboard doesn't return by itself; tap ⌨.
\item The move area (⠿) drags the panel, and its position is remembered. Tap it without dragging to minimize the panel to its handle, and tap the handle to restore it. The panel sits above the mode line and the floating buttons, so the device keyboard never hides it.
\item god-mode and the panel end through \textbf{[g]}, \texttt{Escape} or another panel opening, never because the device keyboard went away.
\end{itemize}

If a letter doesn't register on your keyboard app, the command palette reaches the same commands by name.


\subsection{Differences from Emacs org-mode}
\label{sec:org17920f6}
For readers who know Emacs org-mode: where org-pwa differs. A topic not listed here behaves as in org.

\textbf{Interaction} (see \hyperref[sec:org956255c]{Keybindings}): touch first. The \hyperref[sec:org9fe54f3]{command palette} is a curated list of commands, each with its Emacs name where it has one; your own capture templates and Extras entries join it. god-mode is described under \hyperref[sec:org24e47cb]{god-mode}.

\textbf{Inheritance} (see \hyperref[sec:orgcf34018]{Local Variables}): \texttt{org-use-property-inheritance} takes \texttt{t}, \texttt{nil}, a list of names or a regexp.

\textbf{Tables} (see \hyperref[sec:orgf56fea3]{Table formulas}): formulas recalculate on command, not on every keystroke. Calc is not embedded: \texttt{vvar}, \texttt{vsdev}, \texttt{vpvar}, \texttt{vpsdev} and \texttt{vmeane} over a vector holding a name can differ, because they need Calc's own simplifier.

\textbf{Clocking} (see \hyperref[sec:org2e62d01]{Clocking}): idle time counts only activity inside the app, and \texttt{org-clock-sound} plays a file only in the Android app.

\textbf{Agenda} (see \hyperref[sec:org8b51351]{Agenda}): the sexp evaluator is a Lisp subset; functions of your own come from an \hyperref[sec:orgaf1b952]{Extensions} script. \texttt{org-class} skips the days in your holiday lists. The diary file and \texttt{local:} agenda files feed the Agenda; to change one, open it (\textbf{File → Open}) and save as usual; in the Android app Refile and Replace also write into a \texttt{local:} agenda file while a local file is open.

\textbf{Babel}: \texttt{emacs-lisp} and \texttt{js} blocks run, with \texttt{:results}, \texttt{:var}, \texttt{:timeout}, \texttt{:wrap}, \texttt{:net}, \texttt{:location}, \texttt{:cache}, \texttt{:noweb} and tangling (see \hyperref[sec:orgf955b76]{Source blocks} and \hyperref[sec:org65d5d93]{Literate programming}). Source in \texttt{emacs-lisp}, \texttt{python}, \texttt{js} and \texttt{java} is colored as Emacs's font-lock colors it (keyword, string, comment and its starter, doc, constant, builtin, type, function-name, variable-name, operator, warning and annotation; numbers are plain), checked face by face against Emacs 29.3 on a sample of each; HTML export names the faces \texttt{org-keyword}, \texttt{org-doc} and so on, and ODT export has a style for each. Other languages get a simpler coloring. \texttt{go} is among them: Emacs 29.3 without \texttt{go-mode} shows Go plain, so Go is colored though Emacs would not be.

\textbf{Links and structure}: \texttt{[[id:...]]} links are followed through the open tabs and Agenda Files, then the files opened here before, using a table kept in this browser in place of \texttt{org-id-locations}. \texttt{<{}<{}targets>{}>{}} and radio targets work in the outline and in every export. \texttt{\#+SETUPFILE:} is read from the same place as the document, or from an http(s) URL, and kept for the session. One that cannot be read is named in a message with Emacs's words ("Unable to fetch file from …") and the export goes on without it. A web address is fetched only after you allow it: \textbf{Load once}, \textbf{Always load from this address} or \textbf{Never} (the same goes for a \texttt{\#+BIBLIOGRAPHY:} address).

\textbf{Citations} (see \hyperref[sec:org78fb33b]{Citations}): \LaTeX{} export honors \texttt{natbib} and \texttt{biblatex}; every other export uses the \texttt{basic} processor, so \texttt{csl} is exported as \texttt{basic} and \texttt{note} styles print as \texttt{text}. Set the processor per file with \texttt{\#+CITE\_EXPORT:}.

\textbf{Undo/redo} (see \hyperref[sec:org10b54c5]{Undo/redo and History}): a linear history; after an undo or redo jump the file's \texttt{\#+STARTUP} visibility is reapplied. The browser's field-level undo covers typing inside a field, much as Emacs batches consecutive typing.

\textbf{Search} (see \hyperref[sec:org83d8646]{Searching}): Search and Replace both reach every file in \texttt{org-agenda-files}, as org's \texttt{org-search-view} and \texttt{tags-query-replace} do. Subtree narrowing (see \hyperref[sec:org6838b46]{Narrowing}) and Search's Narrow survive a reload.

\textbf{Export} (see \hyperref[sec:org8e45f5f]{Export}): HTML export uses its own coloring in place of \texttt{htmlize} (see Babel above for the languages matched to Emacs) and KaTeX in place of MathJax. ODT is a port of ox-odt that follows it on the files compared. It differs on purpose in these places: \LaTeX{} becomes KaTeX formula objects (Emacs needs an outside converter and otherwise prints the source), source blocks are colored with this app's highlighter, verse blocks keep their line breaks, a link to a target without a description prints the target's name (Emacs prints "nil"), and a character such as \texttt{<} from an entity is escaped. A missing author is left out unless \texttt{user-full-name} is set. HTML, \LaTeX{}, ASCII and Org follow ox on tables, \texttt{UNNUMBERED} and the \texttt{f:} and \texttt{|:} options.

\textbf{Refile} (see \hyperref[sec:org183621b]{Refile}): the destination is an existing heading.

\textbf{Attachments} (see \hyperref[sec:orgc5944b1]{Attachments}): the same folder model as \texttt{org-attach} (an \texttt{ID} or \texttt{DIR} folder and the \texttt{:ATTACH:} tag) and the dispatcher keys \texttt{a} \texttt{b} \texttt{n} \texttt{o} \texttt{f} \texttt{d} \texttt{D} \texttt{s} \texttt{S} \texttt{z}, plus \texttt{r} to record audio. The Folder panel stands in for \texttt{org-attach-dired}: select files, then open, save or delete them. Needs GitHub, WebDAV, or the org-pwa folder in the Android app.

\textbf{Files view} (see \hyperref[sec:org97bb9ee]{Files view}): after Dired, with touch controls in place of keys. A copy or move reads the bytes and writes them at the new path (GitHub and WebDAV have no copy of their own), so a folder is copied file by file; GitHub and the Android folder have no empty folders, so a new folder there holds a \texttt{.gitkeep}. A listing gives a date only where the place does (WebDAV and the device, not GitHub). Find uses a regexp on the name only and has no narrowing of the folder in view (the \texttt{dired-narrow} package is not part of Emacs). Attach from Files is on \texttt{p}, which \texttt{org-attach} does not use.

\textbf{Conflict resolution} (see \hyperref[sec:org8e03395]{Offline behavior and sync}): a three-way merge by lines, and by heading for a subtree moved on one side and edited on the other, with a region-by-region resolver for what remains.

Each file in \texttt{examples/} ends with its own list of differences, checked against Emacs 29.3. What is planned is in \href{ROADMAP.org}{ROADMAP.org}.

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Known limitations}
\label{sec:org80f7f4d}
Platform limits, which no update can change:

\begin{itemize}
\item Local and relative images show a placeholder on local files (File System Access) and iOS imports, the same picker-permission limit as archiving and capture to a file. GitHub and WebDAV documents are unaffected.
\item iOS has no File System Access, so \textbf{Import} stands in for \textbf{This device} (see \hyperref[sec:orgb821724]{Platform support}).
\end{itemize}

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.5pt}

\subsection{Development}
\label{sec:orgfa6aea1}
A static site: \texttt{index.html} and ES modules, with no build step to run or deploy it. Serve it any way you like, including \texttt{python3 -m http.server} or GitHub Pages.

The one exception is \texttt{src/vendor/mathjs/mathjs-custom.min.js}, a tree-shaken custom mathjs build (Unit, BigNumber and Fraction, used by \hyperref[sec:orgf56fea3]{Table formulas}'s \texttt{uconv()}, \texttt{F} and \texttt{pN}). It is regenerated occasionally with \texttt{tools/build-mathjs-vendor.sh}, a dev-only step; the committed output is what ships, as with the vendored KaTeX files.

\textbf{Tests}: the engine (\texttt{src/}) and the browser adapters (\texttt{src-browser/}) use Node's built-in test runner, with no external dependencies:

\begin{verbatim}
npm test
\end{verbatim}

The tests run with a frozen clock, so they give the same result on any day. \texttt{npm run test:zones} runs them in three time zones at once.

Behavior that Emacs defines is held to Emacs itself. \texttt{tools/gen-repeat-oracle.mjs} and \texttt{tools/gen-agenda-oracle.mjs} ask Emacs 29.3 (with \texttt{faketime}) what completing a repeating task does and which days the agenda lists; \texttt{tools/gen-diary-oracle.mjs} does the same for diary rows, \texttt{tools/gen-latex-oracle.mjs} for \LaTeX{} export, and \texttt{tools/latex-compile-check.mjs} compiles the output. The answers are stored under \texttt{test/fixtures/}; the tests compare the app with them.

\texttt{npm run lint} (ESLint) and \texttt{npm run typecheck} (\texttt{tsc} on files that begin with \texttt{// @ts-check}) need \texttt{npm install -{}-{}no-save eslint @eslint/js globals typescript}. \texttt{node tools/release.mjs N} checks, bumps the cache name and writes \texttt{org-pwa-vN.zip}; \texttt{.github/workflows/ci.yml} runs the same checks and the smoke test on every push.

\texttt{node tools/roundtrip-corpus.mjs DIR} checks that every \texttt{.org} file in a directory comes back byte for byte after an open and save with no edit.

A test checks that every module the app imports is in the service worker's precache list, since a missing one would stop the app starting offline. Tests that hold the app to Emacs's results for the files in \texttt{examples/} are named \texttt{test/example-*.test.js}; \texttt{tools/gen-*-example.mjs} and the other \texttt{tools/gen-*.mjs} scripts write them from Emacs 29.3.

\textbf{Code layout}: \texttt{app.js} is the entry point (about 1,300 lines): it imports everything, sets up the shared state, wires event listeners and runs \texttt{bootstrap}. Features live in \texttt{src-browser/}, one module per area. All runtime state is one object, \texttt{S}, in \texttt{app-state.js}, and the page's DOM elements are looked up once in \texttt{dom.js}. The split is by file rather than decoupled (modules call each other, so the import graph has cycles), and browser modules need a DOM, so Node can't import them. \texttt{test/module-structure.test.js} and \texttt{tools/check-scope.mjs}, a scope analysis that needs the acorn and eslint-scope parsers installed once (\texttt{npm install -{}-{}prefix /tmp/acorn acorn eslint-scope}), keep the structure from decaying.

Everything the app asks of the device (files on the device, saving a file out, the clipboard, the service worker) goes through \texttt{src-browser/platform.js}, which has browser defaults. A native shell supplies its own by setting \texttt{window.orgPwaPlatform} before the app loads, and hands a share to \texttt{window.orgPwaLaunch()}. The browser tests use a fake platform the same way.

\textbf{Browser smoke test}: it covers what unit tests can't reach, since \texttt{app.js} is UI wiring:

\begin{verbatim}
node tools/smoke.mjs             # everything
node tools/smoke.mjs conflict    # only checks whose name contains "conflict"
SMOKE_SLICE=0:27 node tools/smoke.mjs    # only the first 27 checks; 27: runs the rest
\end{verbatim}

It drives the real app in headless Chromium through flows that have broken before, against a built-in static server and a small in-memory WebDAV server. It is dev-only, adds nothing to \texttt{package.json}, needs Playwright and a Chromium once (\texttt{npm install -g playwright \&\& npx playwright install chromium}, or set \texttt{CHROMIUM\_PATH}), and exits non-zero on any failure.
